subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: (a) Define maternal death and maternal mortality ratio, and state the present status of maternal mortality in India. (3 marks) (b) Explain the causes of maternal deaths, including the 'three delays' model. (6 marks) (c) Describe the strategies to reduce maternal mortality and the role of the nurse-midwife. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: The three delays model of maternal death
labels: Delay 1 – deciding to seek care (danger signs not recognised
fear or distrust) → Delay 2 – reaching the facility (distance
cost) → Delay 3 – receiving adequate care at the facility (shortage of staff
poor quality); under each delay the matching interventions: birth preparedness and community education; 102/108 ambulance and maternity waiting homes; EmONC

answer_html:
(a) Definitions and present status (3 marks)

Maternal death (WHO, ICD)

  • The death of a woman while pregnant or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy, whatever the duration or site of the pregnancy, from any cause related to or aggravated by the pregnancy or its management, but not from accidental or incidental causes.
  • A death from such causes between 42 days and one year after the end of pregnancy is called a late maternal death.

Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)

MMR = (Number of maternal deaths in a given period ÷ Number of live births in the same period) × 1,00,000

  • It is expressed per 1,00,000 (one lakh) live births and shows the risk a woman faces each time she becomes pregnant.
  • It differs from the maternal mortality rate, whose denominator is women of reproductive age (15–49 years), so the rate is also influenced by how often women become pregnant.

Present status in India

  • According to the Sample Registration System (SRS) Special Bulletin on Maternal Mortality 2022–24, India's MMR is 87 per lakh live births. It was 130 in 2014–16 and 88 in 2021–23.
  • India has achieved the National Health Policy 2017 target (MMR below 100) and is moving towards the Sustainable Development Goal target 3.1 – a global MMR below 70 by 2030.
  • The picture is uneven: states such as Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra are already below 70, while some large northern states, especially Uttar Pradesh, remain far above the national average.
  • The fall of only one point in the latest round shows that the remaining deaths are harder to prevent; they need better quality of care, not just more institutional births.

(b) Causes of maternal deaths (6 marks)

1. Direct obstetric causes These are complications of pregnancy, labour and the puerperium, or of the treatment given. In the Registrar General's study of maternal deaths in India (2001–03), haemorrhage caused about 38% of deaths, followed by sepsis (11%), abortion (8%), hypertensive disorders (5%) and obstructed labour (5%); "other conditions", largely anaemia and indirect causes, made up about one-third.

  • Haemorrhage – postpartum haemorrhage (atonic uterus, retained placenta, genital tract trauma, inverted uterus), antepartum haemorrhage (placenta praevia, abruption) and ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
  • Hypertensive disorders – pre-eclampsia, eclampsia and HELLP syndrome, causing cerebral haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, renal failure and abruption.
  • Sepsis – puerperal sepsis, septic abortion and chorioamnionitis; often linked to unclean deliveries, prolonged labour and retained products.
  • Unsafe abortion – haemorrhage, sepsis and uterine perforation after abortion by untrained persons.
  • Obstructed labour – ruptured uterus, sepsis, obstetric fistula.
  • Others – amniotic fluid embolism, pulmonary embolism, anaesthetic complications, molar pregnancy.

2. Indirect causes Diseases present before or developing during pregnancy that are made worse by it:

  • Severe anaemia – the commonest; it also turns a modest blood loss into a fatal one.
  • Heart disease (especially rheumatic), malaria, tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, diabetes, HIV, epilepsy and severe respiratory infections such as COVID-19.

3. Underlying social and health-system factors

  • Early marriage and teenage pregnancy – NFHS-6 (2023–24) found that 20.1% of women aged 20–24 were married before 18, and teenage pregnancy remains about 6.7%.
  • High parity and short birth intervals, malnutrition and anaemia.
  • Poverty, illiteracy, the low status of women and lack of decision-making power.
  • Home deliveries by untrained persons and harmful traditional practices.
  • Difficult terrain and poor transport in tribal and remote areas.
  • Health-system gaps – shortage of specialists, anaesthetists and blood; non-functional first referral units; delays in referral; disrespectful care; and out-of-pocket costs.

4. The 'three delays' model (Thaddeus and Maine, 1994) Most maternal deaths are preventable. They happen because of one or more delays between the start of a complication and its treatment.

Delay Meaning Common reasons
Delay 1 Delay in deciding to seek care Danger signs not recognised; decision left to elders or husband; fear of cost; cultural beliefs; previous bad experience at a facility
Delay 2 Delay in reaching the facility Long distance, no transport or road, night-time, cost of travel, being referred from facility to facility
Delay 3 Delay in receiving adequate care after arrival Shortage of staff, drugs or blood; delayed diagnosis; waiting for payment or documents; poor skills; lack of operation theatre

Some authors add a "Delay 0" (failure to prevent the complication through family planning and good antenatal care) and denial of care at the facility.

(c) Strategies to reduce maternal mortality and the role of the nurse-midwife (6 marks)

India follows the RMNCH+A continuum-of-care approach, which places effective interventions at every stage of a woman's life.

1. Before pregnancy

  • Delay marriage and the first pregnancy (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006; girls' education).
  • Family planning and birth spacing – PPIUCD, injectable MPA (Antara) and other spacing methods.
  • Adolescent nutrition, weekly iron–folic acid (WIFS), Anaemia Mukt Bharat and preconception folic acid.

2. During pregnancy

  • Early registration and at least four antenatal visits. NFHS-6 shows first-trimester registration has risen to 76.2%, but only 65.2% of mothers receive four or more visits.
  • Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) – assured antenatal check-up by a doctor on the 9th of every month; the extended PMSMA tracks high-risk pregnancies individually.
  • Screening and treatment of anaemia, hypertension, gestational diabetes, syphilis and HIV; IFA, calcium, Td and deworming.
  • Birth preparedness and complication readiness, recorded on the MCP card and the RCH portal.

3. During childbirth

  • Institutional delivery with a skilled birth attendant – NFHS-6 reports 90.6% institutional births.
  • Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) – cash assistance for institutional delivery; Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK) – free delivery including caesarean section, drugs, diagnostics, diet, blood and transport; 102/108 ambulances.
  • Evidence-based care: WHO Labour Care Guide, active management of the third stage, magnesium sulphate for eclampsia, early recognition of complications.
  • LaQshya (quality of labour rooms and maternity operation theatres), midwifery-led care units, respectful maternity care and a birth companion.
  • SUMAN – assured, free, dignified care with zero tolerance for denial of services.

4. Emergency obstetric care

  • Basic EmONC at PHCs and CHCs; comprehensive EmONC (caesarean section and blood) at first referral units; blood storage units; obstetric HDUs and ICUs; strong referral links.

5. After childbirth

  • Stay of at least 48 hours after delivery; postnatal check-ups; home visits by ASHA under HBNC; early detection of PPH, sepsis and postpartum hypertension; postpartum family planning.

6. Safe abortion services – comprehensive abortion care under the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021, with post-abortion contraception.

7. Accountability – Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) with notification within 24 hours, maternal near-miss reviews, and quality certification under the National Quality Assurance Standards.

8. Social measures – women's empowerment, PMMVY maternity benefit, community monitoring through VHSNCs and Mahila Arogya Samitis, and male involvement.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  1. Register every pregnancy early, preferably in the first trimester, and complete the MCP card and RCH entries.
  2. Identify high-risk mothers (severe anaemia, hypertension, previous caesarean, bad obstetric history, age under 18 or over 35, height under 145 cm) and ensure they reach PMSMA clinics and referral centres.
  3. Provide quality antenatal care – supplementation, screening and counselling about nutrition, rest and danger signs.
  4. Help each family make a birth preparedness plan – place of delivery, transport, money, blood donor and companion.
  5. Conduct safe deliveries – monitor with the Labour Care Guide, practise AMTSL, avoid unnecessary interventions and resuscitate the newborn.
  6. Recognise and stabilise emergencies – give the first dose of oxytocin, magnesium sulphate or antibiotics as per protocol, start IV fluids and refer with a note, a companion and an escort.
  7. Provide respectful maternity care so that women trust and use the facility.
  8. Give postnatal care – monitor for bleeding, infection and hypertension, and counsel on family planning.
  9. Notify every maternal death within 24 hours and take part honestly in death and near-miss reviews.
  10. Educate the community through VHSNDs and mothers' meetings, and keep her own knowledge and skills up to date.

Key clinical practices that prevent deaths at the facility

  1. Postpartum haemorrhage – active management of the third stage for every woman; measuring blood loss with a calibrated drape rather than guessing; a quick first response (uterine massage, oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth, IV fluids, bimanual compression) and early referral.
  2. Hypertensive disorders – blood pressure and urine protein at every antenatal visit; magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia; antihypertensives; and timely delivery.
  3. Sepsis – clean birth practices (the "cleans" of delivery), hand hygiene, limited vaginal examinations, antibiotics when membranes have been ruptured for long or the mother has fever, and temperature monitoring after birth.
  4. Anaemia – IFA for at least 180 days, intravenous iron for moderate or severe anaemia detected in the second and third trimesters, and blood transfusion when needed.
  5. Obstructed labour – labour monitoring with alert thresholds on the Labour Care Guide and timely referral for caesarean section.
  6. Unsafe abortion – easy access to safe abortion and post-abortion care, so that no woman needs to go to an untrained person.

These measures work only when the facility is ready 24 × 7 – trained staff on every shift, drugs and blood available, equipment working and a referral vehicle on call.

Nursing importance Nurses and midwives are present at almost every point of the continuum – the sub-centre, the labour room and the woman's home. Most maternal deaths are caused by conditions they can detect early and treat first, such as anaemia, hypertension, prolonged labour and PPH. Their skill, vigilance and respectful behaviour therefore decide whether a woman survives childbirth.

Conclusion Maternal death is the death of a woman during pregnancy or within 42 days of its end from a cause related to the pregnancy. India's MMR has fallen to 87 per lakh live births, but large state differences remain. Haemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, sepsis, unsafe abortion, obstructed labour and anaemia are the main causes, and the three delays explain why women die from them. Continuum-of-care programmes, emergency obstetric care, quality improvement and accountability – carried out by skilled and caring nurse-midwives – can bring India below the SDG target.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain the RMNCH+A strategy, with its continuum of care and key interventions.
tags: reproductive maternal newborn child adolescent health

diagram.caption: RMNCH+A continuum of care
labels: life stages in a circle – adolescence → reproductive age and pre-pregnancy → pregnancy → childbirth → postnatal mother and newborn → infancy and childhood → adolescence; an outer ring showing places of care – household and community

answer_html:
Introduction RMNCH+A stands for Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare launched this strategic approach in 2013 under the National Health Mission. The "+A" recognises adolescence as a distinct life stage. It brings the earlier separate programmes together so that each woman and child is cared for throughout life.

1. Continuum of care The strategy rests on two dimensions of continuity:

  • Across life stages – adolescence → pregnancy → childbirth → postnatal period → newborn → childhood → adolescence again. Each stage affects the next; for example, an anaemic adolescent girl later has a low birth weight baby.
  • Across places of care – household and community (ASHA, AWW), outreach (Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days) and health facilities (sub-centre/Ayushman Arogya Mandir, PHC, CHC/FRU, district hospital), linked by referral transport.

2. High-impact interventions (the 5 × 5 matrix) The strategy identifies five priority interventions for each of the five life stages, for example:

Life stage Key interventions
Reproductive Spacing methods and PPIUCD; community distribution of contraceptives by ASHAs; quality sterilisation services; comprehensive abortion care; management of RTIs/STIs
Maternal Early registration and quality antenatal care; skilled attendance at every birth; emergency obstetric care; postnatal care in the first 48 hours and at home; screening and management of anaemia and hypertension
Newborn Essential newborn care and resuscitation at every delivery point; early and exclusive breastfeeding; home-based newborn care; care of sick newborns in NBSUs and SNCUs; care of LBW babies including KMC
Child Infant and young child feeding; full immunisation; ORS and zinc for diarrhoea and antibiotics for pneumonia; vitamin A and iron supplementation; screening for 4 Ds (RBSK) and management of severe acute malnutrition
Adolescent Adolescent-friendly health clinics; weekly iron–folic acid supplementation; menstrual hygiene; counselling on nutrition, sexual and reproductive health and mental health; peer education

3. Cross-cutting strategies

  • High Priority Districts – districts with the poorest indicators receive extra funds, technical support and monitoring.
  • Name-based tracking of mothers and children with the MCP card and the RCH portal.
  • Convergence with ICDS/POSHAN, education, water and sanitation and Women and Child Development.
  • Supply chain for drugs and contraceptives, quality assurance, HMIS and supportive supervision.
  • Community processes through ASHAs and VHSNCs, behaviour change communication, gender and equity focus.

4. Major schemes under the umbrella – JSY, JSSK, PMSMA, LaQshya, SUMAN, HBNC and HBYC, RBSK, RKSK, Mission Indradhanush, the national family planning programme, Anaemia Mukt Bharat and the midwifery initiative.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  • Deliver the interventions at her level without missed opportunities – for example, offering family planning during postnatal care and checking immunisation during antenatal visits.
  • Track every mother and child by name, refer in time and keep records complete.

Conclusion RMNCH+A treats the health of women, newborns, children and adolescents as one continuous chain. By delivering a small set of high-impact interventions at every life stage and level of care, with extra focus on high-priority districts, it aims to end preventable maternal and child deaths.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Write a note on the history and present trends of midwifery and maternity care in India.

diagram.caption: Milestones of midwifery in India
labels: Ayurvedic texts and dais → 1854 midwives' school
Lying-in Hospital Madras → 1885 Dufferin Fund (Cama Hospital

Bombay) → early 1900s Victoria Memorial Scholarships for dais → 1946 Bhore Committee → 1947 INC Act → ANM cadre → 1977 MPW scheme → 1992 CSSM → 1997 RCH → 2005 NRHM and JSY → 2013 RMNCH+A → 2017 LaQshya → 2018 midwifery guidelines (NPM) → 2023 NNMC Act

answer_html:
Introduction Midwifery is one of the oldest caring practices. In India it has moved from traditional home births by dais to professional, facility-based and now woman-centred midwifery care.

Historical development

  1. Ancient period – Ayurvedic texts (Charaka, Sushruta and Kashyapa Samhitas) describe care in pregnancy, including a month-by-month regimen called garbhini paricharya. Births took place at home, attended by dais (traditional birth attendants) whose skills passed down through families.
  2. 1854 – a school for training midwives was set up at the Lying-in Hospital, Madras. It later grew into the training school of the Madras Government Maternity Hospital.
  3. 1885 – Lady Dufferin founded the Countess of Dufferin's Fund (the National Association for Supplying Female Medical Aid to the Women of India). It trained women doctors, nurses and midwives; the first school it financed was at Cama Hospital, Bombay.
  4. Early 1900s – the Victoria Memorial Scholarships for Dais, started with Lady Curzon's support, paid women's hospitals to train dais in safe midwifery.
  5. 1920s–1930s – maternity and child welfare leagues and the Maternity and Child Welfare Bureau of the Indian Red Cross trained health visitors and opened MCH centres.
  6. 1946 – Bhore Committee – recommended integrating MCH services into general health services and training more midwives and health visitors.
  7. 1947 – Indian Nursing Council Act – uniform standards for nursing and midwifery education and registration.
  8. 1950s–1970s – the auxiliary nurse-midwife (ANM) became the backbone of rural maternity care; the Multipurpose Worker scheme (1977) made her the female health worker of the sub-centre.
  9. 1992–2013 – Child Survival and Safe Motherhood (1992), RCH (1997), NRHM with Janani Suraksha Yojana (2005) and RMNCH+A (2013) – a major shift from home to institutional births.
  10. 2017–2023 – LaQshya (2017), Guidelines on Midwifery Services in India (2018) creating the Nurse Practitioner in Midwifery, INC NPM Programme Regulations (notified in 2021) and the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023.

Present trends

  • Institutional births have reached 90.6% (NFHS-6), but rising caesarean rates and over-medicalisation are new concerns.
  • Woman-centred, respectful care – birth companions, choice of birthing position, avoidance of routine episiotomy, and the WHO aim of a positive childbirth experience.
  • Professional midwifery – NPMs in midwifery-led care units working to ICM competencies.
  • Evidence-based tools – the WHO Labour Care Guide, the Safe Childbirth Checklist and skills training such as Dakshata.
  • Quality and accountability – LaQshya, NQAS certification, MDSR and SUMAN.
  • Continuum of care – ASHAs, PMSMA, home-based newborn care and postpartum family planning.
  • Digital health – RCH portal, ANMOL tablets for ANMs and tele-consultation.
  • Competency-based education – the INC 2021 B.Sc. Nursing curriculum includes the skilled birth attendant (SBA) module.

Conclusion Indian midwifery has travelled from dais and early colonial training schools to a regulated profession with its own specialist cadre. The present challenge is to combine high institutional coverage with high-quality, respectful and evidence-based midwifery care for every woman.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain the Midwifery Services Initiative in India, with the role and scope of practice of the Nurse Practitioner in Midwifery in midwifery-led care units.
tags: Guidelines on Midwifery Services in India 2018

diagram.caption: Collaborative care model of midwifery-led and obstetric-led care units
labels: every pregnant woman screened by NPM → low-risk women cared for in the MLCU (antenatal care
postnatal and newborn care) ↔ high-risk women or complications referred to the obstetric-led care unit located alongside → woman returns to NPM care when risk resolves

answer_html:
Introduction To improve the quality of maternity care, reduce unnecessary interventions and promote respectful care, the Government of India released the Guidelines on Midwifery Services in India in December 2018. They created a new cadre called the Nurse Practitioner in Midwifery (NPM), educated to International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) standards.

1. Who is an NPM?

  • A registered nurse-midwife (GNM or B.Sc. Nursing) who completes an additional 18-month NPM training programme designed by the Indian Nursing Council and based on the ICM essential competencies.
  • The INC notified the NPM Programme Regulations in January 2021.

2. Training structure (cascade model)

  • NPM Educators are trained for about 6 months at National Midwifery Training Institutes (NMTIs), with support from international midwifery educators.
  • The educators then train NPMs for 18 months at State Midwifery Training Institutes (SMTIs), followed by mentoring.
  • Trained NPMs are posted in midwifery-led care units (MLCUs) in high-caseload public health facilities.

3. Midwifery-led care unit (MLCU)

  • A unit, located alongside the obstetric-led care unit, where low-risk women are cared for by NPMs throughout pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period.
  • Works on a collaborative care model – every pregnant woman is screened by the NPM; women with risk factors or complications are referred to the obstetrician, and may return to midwifery care when the risk resolves.
  • Emphasises physiological birth, a birth companion, freedom of movement and choice of birthing position, and respectful maternity care.

4. Role and scope of practice of the NPM

  1. Preconception and antenatal care – history, examination, screening, supplementation, counselling and birth planning for low-risk women.
  2. Care in labour – monitoring with the Labour Care Guide, non-pharmacological pain relief, conducting normal births, AMTSL, perineal repair and immediate newborn care.
  3. Postnatal and newborn care – breastfeeding support, early identification of problems, postpartum family planning including PPIUCD.
  4. Emergency first response – first-line management of PPH, eclampsia (magnesium sulphate loading dose) and birth asphyxia, followed by timely referral.
  5. Use of protocols and selected medicines as allowed by state policy, with proper records.
  6. Health education and counselling of women and families.
  7. Mentoring of other staff, quality improvement and research.

5. Benefits

  • Continuity of care by a known provider, positive birth experience and greater satisfaction.
  • Fewer unnecessary interventions such as routine episiotomy and caesarean section.
  • Obstetricians are freed to concentrate on high-risk women.

Conclusion The midwifery initiative recognises that most births are normal and are best supported by skilled, autonomous midwives working closely with obstetricians. NPMs in midwifery-led care units are central to India's goal of safe and respectful childbirth.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Define respectful maternity care. Explain its components and the role of the nurse-midwife in promoting it.
tags: universal rights of women and newborns
answer_html:
Introduction Women stay away from facilities, or have a traumatic birth, when they are shouted at, slapped, left alone or examined without consent. Respectful maternity care (RMC) is therefore both a human right and a strategy to reduce maternal deaths.

Definition WHO (2018) describes RMC as care organised for and provided to all women in a way that maintains their dignity, privacy and confidentiality, ensures freedom from harm and mistreatment, and enables informed choice and continuous support during labour and childbirth.

Forms of disrespect and abuse (Bowser and Hill, 2010)

  1. Physical abuse – slapping, pinching, forceful restraint, fundal pressure.
  2. Non-consented care – procedures such as episiotomy or sterilisation done without consent.
  3. Non-confidential care – examinations without privacy; disclosing HIV status.
  4. Non-dignified care – shouting, scolding, insults, threats.
  5. Discrimination – based on caste, religion, age, poverty, HIV status or disability.
  6. Abandonment or denial of care – leaving women alone in labour, delivering unattended.
  7. Detention in facilities – for failure to pay, and demands for informal payments.

Components of respectful maternity care The Respectful Maternity Care Charter of the White Ribbon Alliance, updated in 2019 as the universal rights of women and newborns, includes:

  • Freedom from harm and ill-treatment.
  • Information, informed consent and respect for choices, including companionship and the right to refuse procedures.
  • Privacy and confidentiality.
  • Dignity and respect for every woman and newborn.
  • Equality and freedom from discrimination.
  • Healthcare of the highest attainable standard.
  • Liberty and autonomy – no detention.
  • The newborn's right to be with its parents, and to an identity (birth registration).
  • Adequate nutrition and clean water.

RMC in Indian programmes – LaQshya and SUMAN build RMC into labour room standards, and government policy permits a birth companion of the woman's choice in the labour room.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  1. Greet the woman, introduce herself and call her by name.
  2. Explain every examination and procedure and obtain consent before it.
  3. Ensure privacy with screens and curtains, and limit the number of people examining her.
  4. Allow a birth companion, oral fluids, movement and a birthing position of her choice.
  5. Avoid routine, unnecessary interventions – enema, shaving, routine episiotomy and fundal pressure.
  6. Offer pain relief and continuous support; never leave a woman alone in active labour.
  7. Use kind language; never shout, slap or threaten.
  8. Treat all women equally and maintain confidentiality.
  9. Keep mother and baby together; support early breastfeeding.
  10. Report and challenge disrespectful behaviour and take part in RMC training and audits.

Conclusion Respectful maternity care means safe care given with dignity, consent, privacy and continuous support. Practised by every nurse-midwife, it improves women's experience, builds trust in facilities and indirectly saves lives.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain the ethical issues in maternal and newborn care and the ethical responsibilities of the nurse-midwife.
tags: ICM International Code of Ethics for Midwives
answer_html:
Introduction Maternity care involves two patients – the mother and the fetus or newborn – and decisions that affect a whole family. Midwives therefore face frequent ethical dilemmas, which they resolve using ethical principles, law and professional codes.

Ethical principles applied

  • Autonomy – the woman's right to make informed decisions about her body and her baby.
  • Beneficence and non-maleficence – doing good and avoiding harm, including from unnecessary interventions.
  • Justice – fair and equal care and fair use of scarce resources.
  • Veracity, fidelity and confidentiality – honesty, keeping promises and protecting information.

Common ethical issues

  1. Informed consent and refusal – for vaginal examinations, episiotomy, caesarean section, blood transfusion and sterilisation, and for examination by students. A competent woman may refuse even life-saving treatment after full information.
  2. Maternal autonomy versus fetal welfare – for example, a woman refusing caesarean section for fetal distress. The midwife informs, persuades and documents, but cannot force treatment.
  3. Confidentiality – HIV or syphilis status, unmarried or adolescent pregnancy, domestic violence. Confidentiality may conflict with legal duties such as mandatory reporting under the POCSO Act for pregnancy in a minor.
  4. Sex selection – families may ask the sex of the fetus; disclosure is unethical and illegal under the PCPNDT Act.
  5. Termination of pregnancy – a provider with a conscientious objection must still refer the woman without delay and never obstruct legal care.
  6. Prenatal diagnosis of anomalies – counselling must be honest and non-directive so that parents decide.
  7. Newborn decisions – resuscitation of extremely preterm babies or those with lethal anomalies; withholding or withdrawing treatment; involving parents and ensuring comfort care.
  8. Resource allocation – a single ventilator or SNCU bed for several sick babies; decisions must follow clinical criteria, not ability to pay or influence.
  9. Disrespect and informal payments – violate dignity and justice.
  10. Research – pregnant women and newborns are vulnerable groups; research needs ethics committee approval and special consent.

Ethical responsibilities of the nurse-midwife

  • Follow the ICM International Code of Ethics for Midwives, which covers midwifery relationships, practice, professional responsibilities and the advancement of knowledge, together with the INC code of ethics.
  • Respect women's choices and give unbiased information.
  • Maintain competence and practise within her scope.
  • Protect confidentiality except where the law requires disclosure.
  • Document decisions and discussions carefully.
  • Use a systematic ethical decision-making process – identify the problem, gather facts, consider options and principles, consult the team or ethics committee, act and evaluate.
  • Advocate for women and newborns, especially the poor and marginalised.

Conclusion Ethical issues in maternity care range from everyday consent to life-and-death decisions for newborns. By applying ethical principles, the ICM code and the law, the midwife protects the rights of both mother and baby while keeping their trust.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain the legal provisions that a nurse-midwife must know for safe midwifery practice in India.
tags: Registration of Births and Deaths Act 1969
answer_html:
Introduction A nurse-midwife makes decisions that affect two lives. She must know the laws that govern her practice so that she can protect women and babies, and protect herself from charges of negligence.

1. Registration and scope of practice

  • Only nurses and midwives registered with the State Nursing Council may practise (INC Act, 1947; the National Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act, 2023 will replace it when the Commission is constituted).
  • Practise only within the scope defined by INC and Government of India guidelines. Under the SBA guidelines, trained staff nurses and ANMs are authorised to use the partograph/LCG, perform AMTSL, give first-line drugs such as oxytocin, misoprostol, the loading dose of magnesium sulphate and the first dose of antibiotics before referral, and resuscitate newborns.
  • Follow written protocols and standing orders, and never act beyond her training.

2. Consent – take valid, informed consent for procedures (episiotomy, PPIUCD insertion, sterilisation, blood transfusion) and record it. Consent for a minor is given by the guardian.

3. Documentation – the LCG, labour room register, delivery notes, MCP card, referral slips and drug records are legal documents; they must be accurate, timely, signed and never altered.

4. Registration of births and deaths – under the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969, the in-charge of the institution must report every birth, death and stillbirth within 21 days. The Amendment Act of 2023 (in force from 1 October 2023) provides for digital registration and makes the birth certificate a single document of date and place of birth.

5. Maternal death notification – every maternal death must be notified within 24 hours under the MDSR guidelines.

6. Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021) – only a registered medical practitioner may terminate a pregnancy, within the permitted gestation and conditions; the nurse assists, maintains confidentiality and never performs it herself.

7. PCPNDT Act, 1994 – sex determination is prohibited; the nurse must never disclose or hint at the sex of the fetus.

8. POCSO Act, 2012 – pregnancy in a girl under 18 must be reported to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit.

9. Medico-legal cases – suspected criminal abortion, assault, burns or poisoning in a pregnant woman are reported to the police and handled as MLCs.

10. Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 – an abandoned newborn must be reported to the police or Child Welfare Committee within 24 hours; sale of babies is a serious offence.

11. Other laws

  • Maternity benefit of 26 weeks for working women (now part of the Code on Social Security, 2020).
  • Infant Milk Substitutes Act, 1992 – no promotion of formula, bottles or teats.
  • Consumer Protection Act, 2019 – patients can claim compensation for deficient service; negligence may also attract criminal liability.
  • Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 – placenta and anatomical waste go in the yellow category.

Conclusion Safe midwifery practice is also legal practice: working within the registered scope, taking consent, documenting well and obeying laws on births, MTP, sex determination, child protection and waste. Knowing these laws protects mothers, babies and the midwife herself.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain the laws and procedure of adoption in India and the role of the nurse-midwife.

diagram.caption: Steps of adoption under the JJ Act
labels: abandoned or surrendered → reported to police/CWC → CWC declares child legally free for adoption → prospective adoptive parents register on CARINGS → home study by specialised adoption agency → referral and matching → acceptance → pre-adoption foster care → adoption order by District Magistrate → post-adoption follow-up

answer_html:
Introduction Adoption is the legal process by which a child becomes the lawful child of adoptive parents, with all the rights of a biological child. Midwives meet unwed or distressed mothers, abandoned newborns and families who want a baby, so they must know the law.

1. Laws governing adoption

  • Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act (HAMA), 1956 – applies to Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs; adoption by a registered deed between the families, with consent of the spouse.
  • Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 – a secular law open to all citizens; it governs adoption of orphaned, abandoned or surrendered (OAS) children through recognised agencies.
  • JJ (Amendment) Act, 2021 – in force from September 2022; District Magistrates now issue adoption orders instead of courts.
  • Adoption Regulations, 2022 – framed by the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA), the nodal body under the Ministry of Women and Child Development.

2. Agencies – CARA (national), State Adoption Resource Agencies, District Child Protection Units, Specialised Adoption Agencies (which care for the children) and the Child Welfare Committee (CWC), which declares a child legally free for adoption.

3. Procedure under the JJ Act

  1. An abandoned or orphaned child is reported to the police or CWC and placed in an agency; a surrendered child is surrendered by the parents before the CWC by a surrender deed, with 60 days allowed for them to reconsider.
  2. The CWC declares the child legally free for adoption after enquiry.
  3. Prospective adoptive parents register online on CARA's portal (CARINGS) with their documents.
  4. The agency conducts a home study of the family.
  5. A child is referred to the family; after acceptance, the child goes into pre-adoption foster care.
  6. The District Magistrate passes the adoption order.
  7. The agency carries out post-adoption follow-up for two years.

4. Eligibility of adoptive parents (main points) – physically, mentally and financially fit; a couple needs at least two years of stable marriage and the consent of both spouses; a single woman may adopt a child of any sex, but a single man may not adopt a girl; age limits depend on the age of the child.

5. Offences – adopting or giving a child without following the procedure, and selling or buying a child, are punishable; the punishment is more severe when the offender is a person in charge of the child, such as an employee of a hospital or maternity home.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  • Never take part in or arrange informal "handing over" of a newborn, even with the mother's consent.
  • Report an abandoned baby to the police, CWC or Childline (1098) within 24 hours, and give emergency care.
  • Counsel unwed or distressed mothers about legal surrender through the CWC and about support services, with strict confidentiality.
  • Keep accurate birth records and identification of every baby.
  • Support adoptive mothers in bonding, feeding and, where possible, induced lactation.

Conclusion In India adoption takes place under HAMA or, more commonly, under the JJ Act through CARA, with the District Magistrate issuing the final order. The midwife protects newborns by following the law, reporting abandonment and guiding mothers towards safe, legal options.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Explain Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR).

diagram.caption: MDSR cycle
labels: identification of maternal death → notification within 24 hours → review (facility-based review; community-based review by verbal autopsy) → analysis of causes and three delays → recommendations → response (action at facility

answer_html:
Introduction Every maternal death is a sentinel event that reveals a failure of the health system. Maternal Death Surveillance and Response (MDSR) is a continuous cycle of identifying, notifying and reviewing every maternal death and acting on the findings to prevent future deaths. India issued its MDSR guidelines in 2017, building on the earlier Maternal Death Review (2010) and placing more emphasis on response.

Objectives

  • To know the true number of maternal deaths and their distribution.
  • To find the medical causes and the avoidable factors (three delays).
  • To take corrective action at facility, district and state levels.
  • To monitor the effect of the actions.

Components

  1. Identification and notification
    • Maternal death is a notifiable event.
    • Any person – ASHA, ANM, AWW, staff nurse or doctor – who learns of the death of a woman during pregnancy, delivery or within 42 days after it acts as the primary informant.
    • The death is notified within 24 hours to the block or district nodal officer, using a notification form or helpline, and entered in the line list.
  2. Facility-based maternal death review (FBMDR)
    • For deaths in hospitals, the facility in-charge and the facility review committee review the case records, LCG and staff statements.
    • They identify the cause and gaps in care, in a no-blame, confidential manner.
  3. Community-based maternal death review (CBMDR)
    • For deaths at home or in transit, a trained block team conducts a verbal autopsy with the family, usually within about three weeks.
    • It reconstructs the events and delays.
  4. District MDSR committee – chaired by the District Collector/Magistrate; reviews deaths every month and approves action plans.
  5. State and national levels – analyse trends, conduct confidential reviews and revise policies.
  6. Response – the crucial step: for example, posting an anaesthetist at an FRU, ensuring blood storage, ambulance availability, staff training or community awareness about danger signs.

Guiding principles – no blame or punishment for providers, confidentiality, completeness of reporting, and timely action.

Complementary approach – Maternal near-miss review (2014) studies women who survived severe complications, which gives lessons without waiting for deaths.

Role of the nurse

  • Report every maternal death promptly and truthfully.
  • Keep complete records – LCG, drug charts and referral notes.
  • Prepare the case summary and take part honestly in reviews.
  • Implement the recommendations and educate the community about danger signs and BPCR.

Conclusion MDSR changes a maternal death from a private tragedy into public learning. By notifying, reviewing and – above all – responding to each death, it helps close the gaps that cause preventable maternal deaths.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: Define perinatal mortality rate.
answer_html:
• Perinatal mortality rate (PMR) is the number of stillbirths and early neonatal deaths (deaths in the first 7 days of life) per 1,000 total births (live births + stillbirths) in a year.

PMR = (Stillbirths + early neonatal deaths ÷ Live births + stillbirths) × 1,000

  • In India, a stillbirth is a fetal death at or after 28 weeks of gestation (or 1,000 g); WHO uses 22 weeks or 500 g for international comparison.
  • PMR reflects the quality of antenatal, intrapartum and immediate newborn care. Stillbirths are under-reported in routine data: SRS estimates are far lower than NFHS estimates.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)?
answer_html:
• JSY is a safe motherhood scheme launched on 12 April 2005 under the National (Rural) Health Mission to promote institutional delivery among poor pregnant women through cash assistance.
  • Low performing states (UP, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Jharkhand, MP, Chhattisgarh, Assam, Rajasthan, Odisha, J&K) – all women delivering in government or accredited facilities receive ₹1,400 (rural) or ₹1,000 (urban).
  • High performing states (such as Maharashtra) – BPL, SC and ST women receive ₹700 (rural) or ₹600 (urban).
  • ASHAs receive an incentive for antenatal care and facilitating delivery; BPL women who deliver at home get ₹500.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK)?
answer_html:
• JSSK, launched in June 2011, entitles every pregnant woman delivering in a public health facility to completely free care, with no user charges.
  • Free entitlements for the mother: normal delivery and caesarean section, drugs and consumables, diagnostics, diet (up to 3 days for normal delivery and 7 days for caesarean), blood, and transport from home to facility, between facilities on referral, and drop back home.
  • In 2013 it was extended to antenatal and postnatal complications and to sick infants up to one year, who receive the same free services.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA)?
answer_html:
• PMSMA was launched on 9 June 2016 to provide assured, comprehensive and free antenatal care to pregnant women in the second and third trimesters on the 9th of every month at government facilities.
  • Check-ups are done by obstetricians or medical officers, with private doctors volunteering their services; investigations and medicines are free.
  • High-risk pregnancies are identified and marked on the MCP card for follow-up.
  • Extended PMSMA (e-PMSMA, 2022) adds name-based tracking and follow-up of high-risk women until a safe outcome.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is LaQshya?
answer_html:
• LaQshya (Labour Room Quality Improvement Initiative) was launched by MoHFW on 11 December 2017.
  • It aims to reduce preventable maternal and newborn deaths and complications by improving the quality of care in labour rooms and maternity operation theatres (and obstetric HDUs/ICUs) during childbirth and the immediate postpartum period.
  • Facilities are assessed under the National Quality Assurance Standards; a score of 70% or more earns LaQshya certification, with platinum (≥90%), gold (≥80%) and silver (≥70%) badges and financial incentives.
  • It also promotes respectful maternity care and birth companions.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is Surakshit Matritva Aashwasan (SUMAN)?
tags: zero tolerance for denial of services
mothers up to six months after delivery
answer_html:
• SUMAN was launched by MoHFW on 10 October 2019 to provide assured, dignified, respectful and quality care at no cost, with zero tolerance for denial of services, to every woman and newborn visiting a public health facility.
  • Beneficiaries – all pregnant women, mothers up to six months after delivery, and sick newborns.
  • It brings together existing entitlements – free antenatal check-ups including PMSMA, free delivery and caesarean section, management of complications, free transport, home visits and postnatal care – as one guarantee, with the goal of zero preventable maternal and newborn deaths.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY)?
tags: Ministry of Women and Child Development
answer_html:
• PMMVY is a maternity benefit scheme of the Ministry of Women and Child Development (2017) that compensates for wage loss and promotes health-seeking behaviour of pregnant and lactating women.
  • Under PMMVY 2.0 (Mission Shakti, from April 2022), the mother gets ₹5,000 for the first child in two instalments – ₹3,000 after registration and at least one antenatal check-up, and ₹2,000 after birth registration and the first cycle of immunisation.
  • ₹6,000 is given in one instalment if the second child is a girl.
  • The money is paid by direct benefit transfer to the mother's account.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Introduction to Midwifery
question: What is a maternal near miss?
answer_html:
• A maternal near miss is a woman who nearly died but survived a complication that occurred during pregnancy, childbirth or within 42 days of the end of pregnancy (WHO).
  • It is identified by WHO criteria of organ dysfunction – clinical (shock, gasping, loss of consciousness), laboratory (severe hypoxaemia, very low platelets, high creatinine) or management-based (hysterectomy for infection or bleeding, transfusion of five or more units, intubation, dialysis, CPR).
  • Near-miss cases are more frequent than deaths, so reviewing them (GoI maternal near-miss review guidelines, 2014) gives quicker lessons for improving the quality of obstetric care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: (a) Describe the bones, joints and divisions of the female pelvis from the obstetric point of view. (3 marks) (b) Explain the planes and diameters of the pelvic inlet, cavity and outlet, with the pelvic inclination and axis. (8 marks) (c) Explain the types of pelvis according to the Caldwell–Moloy classification and their obstetric importance. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Female pelvis – inlet diameters and sagittal section
labels: (1) inlet seen from above: true conjugate 11 cm
sacrocotyloid 9.5 cm; (2) sagittal section: diagonal conjugate 12 cm
angle of inclination of brim 55–60° to the horizontal

answer_html:
(a) Bones, joints and divisions of the female pelvis (3 marks)

The female pelvis is the bony canal through which the fetus must pass during birth. Its size and shape decide whether labour will be easy, difficult or impossible, so every midwife must know it well.

Bones

  • Two innominate (hip) bones – each formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium and pubis at the acetabulum. Important landmarks are the iliopectineal line, the iliopectineal eminence, the ischial spine and the ischial tuberosity.
  • Sacrum – five fused vertebrae. The projecting upper border of the first sacral vertebra is the sacral promontory; the concave anterior surface forms the hollow of the sacrum.
  • Coccyx – four small fused vertebrae; it can move backwards during birth.

Joints

  • Symphysis pubis – a cartilaginous joint between the two pubic bones.
  • Two sacroiliac joints – between the sacrum and the ilia.
  • Sacrococcygeal joint – allows the coccyx to bend back by about 2 cm, enlarging the outlet in the second stage.
  • In pregnancy, relaxin and progesterone soften the ligaments, giving slight mobility to these joints and a little more room for the fetus (and causing backache and pubic pain).

Ligaments – sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments (which form the boundaries of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina), sacroiliac, interpubic, sacrococcygeal and inguinal ligaments.

Divisions

  • The pelvic brim (linea terminalis) divides the pelvis into two parts:
    • False pelvis – above the brim, formed by the iliac fossae. It supports the pregnant uterus and has little obstetric importance.
    • True pelvis – below the brim. It forms the bony birth canal and has an inlet (brim), a cavity and an outlet.

(b) Planes and diameters of the pelvis, inclination and axis (8 marks)

1. Pelvic inlet (brim)

  • Boundaries (from back to front) – sacral promontory, alae of the sacrum, sacroiliac joints, iliopectineal lines, iliopectineal eminences, superior pubic rami, upper border of the pubic bones and symphysis pubis.
  • Shape – in the normal female pelvis it is round or slightly oval transversely.
  • Diameters
    • Anteroposterior (true or anatomical conjugate) – from the middle of the sacral promontory to the upper inner border of the symphysis pubis – 11 cm.
    • Obstetric conjugate – from the sacral promontory to the most prominent point on the back of the symphysis, about 1 cm below its upper border – 10.5 cm. It is the shortest anteroposterior diameter through which the head must pass and is therefore the most important.
    • Diagonal conjugate – from the sacral promontory to the lower border of the symphysis – 12 cm. It is the only one that can be measured clinically by vaginal examination; the obstetric conjugate is about 1.5–2 cm less than the diagonal conjugate.
    • Oblique diameters – from one sacroiliac joint to the opposite iliopectineal eminence – 12 cm. The right oblique starts from the right sacroiliac joint. In LOA position the sagittal suture usually engages in the right oblique diameter.
    • Transverse diameter – between the farthest points of the iliopectineal lines – 13 cm; it is the largest diameter of the inlet.
    • Sacrocotyloid diameter – from the promontory to the iliopectineal eminence – 9.5 cm. It is the space for the parietal eminence in occipitoposterior positions.

2. Pelvic cavity

  • The space between the inlet above and the plane of least dimensions below. It is curved – the anterior wall (symphysis) is about 4 cm deep, the posterior wall (sacrum) about 12 cm.
  • The plane of greatest pelvic dimensions (through the middle of the symphysis and the junction of the second and third sacral vertebrae) is nearly round – about 12 cm in all diameters. Here the head can rotate easily.

3. Plane of least pelvic dimensions (mid-pelvis or obstetric outlet)

  • Passes through the lower border of the symphysis, the ischial spines and the tip of the sacrum.
  • The interspinous diameter (about 10–10.5 cm) is the narrowest transverse diameter of the pelvis. Arrest of descent commonly occurs at this level, for example deep transverse arrest in an android pelvis.
  • The ischial spines are the reference point for station of the presenting part during labour.

4. Pelvic outlet

  • Anatomical outlet – lozenge (diamond) shaped, bounded by the lower border of the symphysis, the pubic arch, the ischial tuberosities, the sacrotuberous ligaments and the tip of the coccyx. It is made of two triangles – the anterior (pubic arch) and the posterior sagittal triangle.
  • Diameters
    • Anteroposterior – from the lower border of the symphysis to the tip of the coccyx – 13 cm when the coccyx is pushed back during birth.
    • Oblique – from the middle of one sacrotuberous ligament to the opposite junction of the ischiopubic rami – 12 cm.
    • Transverse (intertuberous or bituberous) – between the inner borders of the ischial tuberosities – 11 cm.
  • Pubic arch – the angle below the symphysis; about 85–90° in the gynaecoid pelvis, so the occiput fits snugly under it.

Summary of diameters (in cm)

Plane Anteroposterior Oblique Transverse
Inlet 11 12 13
Cavity 12 12 12
Outlet 13 12 11

The table shows the key fact: at the inlet the widest diameter is transverse, at the outlet it is anteroposterior. The fetal head therefore enters the pelvis in the transverse or oblique diameter and must rotate to leave it in the anteroposterior diameter – this is the basis of internal rotation in the mechanism of labour.

5. Pelvic inclination

  • In the standing position the plane of the inlet makes an angle of about 55–60° with the horizontal; the plane of the outlet makes an angle of about 15°.
  • A high inclination (common in some women) may delay engagement of the head, and the uterus may fall forward (pendulous abdomen).

6. Pelvic axis (curve of Carus)

  • An imaginary line joining the centre points of the planes of the inlet, cavity and outlet.
  • It runs downwards and backwards to the level of the ischial spines and then curves downwards and forwards around the symphysis.
  • The fetus follows this curved path; the midwife supports the head and directs traction (for example, in forceps or vacuum delivery) along the axis.

(c) Types of pelvis – Caldwell–Moloy classification (4 marks)

Caldwell and Moloy (1933) classified pelves according to the shape of the inlet, using the posterior and anterior segments divided by the widest transverse diameter.

Feature Gynaecoid (about 50%) Android (about 20%) Anthropoid (about 25%) Platypelloid (about 5%)
Inlet Round or slightly transverse oval Heart-shaped, narrow forepelvis Anteroposterior oval, long and narrow Transversely oval, flat, short AP diameter
Side walls Straight, parallel Converging (funnel-shaped) Straight Straight or divergent
Ischial spines Not prominent Prominent Not prominent Not prominent
Sacrosciatic notch Wide Narrow Wide Narrow
Subpubic angle About 90° Narrow, less than 90° Normal or narrow Wide
Sacrum Well curved Straight, forward lower end Long Short, flat
Course of labour Normal; head engages in the transverse or oblique diameter and rotates easily Engagement in OP or transverse positions; deep transverse arrest, difficult or obstructed labour, perineal tears Head engages in the AP diameter; occipitoposterior or direct occipitoanterior delivery ("face to pubis") common Delay at the inlet; engagement in the transverse diameter with asynclitism; often normal once engaged

Obstetric importance

  • The gynaecoid pelvis is ideal for childbirth; most Indian women have a gynaecoid or near-gynaecoid pelvis.
  • Variations explain malpositions, prolonged labour and cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD).
  • A contracted pelvis may result from malnutrition, rickets, osteomalacia, injury or spinal deformity; short stature (height under 145 cm) is a clue.
  • On vaginal examination the midwife may note whether the promontory can be reached, the prominence of the ischial spines, the curve of the sacrum, the width of the subpubic angle and the intertuberous diameter (normally admitting four knuckles). Routine clinical pelvimetry of healthy women on admission in labour is no longer recommended (WHO, 2018); the best test of the pelvis is good progress of labour.

Assessment of the pelvis in practice

1. History

  • Childhood rickets, poliomyelitis, tuberculosis of the spine or hip, or a pelvic fracture.
  • Past obstetric performance – a previous prolonged or obstructed labour, difficult instrumental delivery or caesarean section for disproportion; on the other hand, the easy vaginal birth of a good-sized baby proves that the pelvis is adequate.

2. General and abdominal examination

  • Height under 145 cm, a limp, spinal deformity such as kyphoscoliosis.
  • A pendulous abdomen in a primigravida and a head that is not engaged at term in a primigravida.

3. Vaginal (clinical) pelvimetry – done only when indicated, for example in suspected disproportion near term

  • Inlet – in a normal pelvis the sacral promontory cannot be reached with two fingers; if it can, the diagonal conjugate is measured. Normally only the anterior part of the iliopectineal lines can be felt.
  • Cavity – the sacrum should be well curved, the sacrosciatic notch should admit two fingers, the ischial spines should not be prominent and the side walls should not converge.
  • Outlet – the subpubic angle should admit two fingers (about 90°), the intertuberous diameter should take four knuckles of the closed fist, and the coccyx should be mobile.

4. Imaging – X-ray pelvimetry is now obsolete; CT or MRI pelvimetry is used rarely, for example before a planned vaginal breech birth.

5. Trial of labour – in borderline cases, careful monitoring of labour under supervision in a facility with caesarean section available remains the best test, because the fetal head is the best pelvimeter.

Nursing importance Knowledge of the pelvis helps the midwife to understand the mechanism of labour, read station and descent correctly on the Labour Care Guide, suspect disproportion early (a high head in a primigravida at term, slow descent, severe moulding) and refer in time. It also explains common discomforts of pregnancy, such as backache and symphysis pain, so that she can reassure women.

Conclusion The female pelvis consists of two innominate bones, the sacrum and the coccyx, joined by the symphysis and sacroiliac joints. Its inlet is widest transversely and its outlet anteroposteriorly, which forces the fetal head to rotate as it passes along the curved pelvic axis. The gynaecoid pelvis is best suited to childbirth, while android, anthropoid and platypelloid types are associated with malpositions and difficult labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: (a) Describe the regions and landmarks of the fetal skull. (4 marks) (b) Explain the diameters of the fetal skull and their relation to the attitude and presentation. (7 marks) (c) Explain moulding and its significance in labour. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Fetal skull – regions and diameters
labels: submentovertical 11.5 cm and submentobregmatic 9.5 cm; superior view showing sagittal
biparietal 9.5 cm and bitemporal 8 cm diameters

answer_html:
(a) Regions and landmarks of the fetal skull (4 marks)

The fetal head is the largest and least compressible part of the fetus. If the head can pass through the pelvis, the rest of the body usually follows. Knowledge of the skull helps the midwife to identify the position and attitude of the head on vaginal examination.

Parts of the skull

  • Vault – the large dome-shaped part above the base, made of the two frontal, two parietal and the occipital bones (with parts of the temporal bones). The bones are thin, ossified in membrane and not firmly united at birth, so they can overlap during labour.
  • Base – firmly ossified and incompressible; it protects the brainstem.
  • Face – small at birth; its bones are firmly united.

Sutures (felt on vaginal examination)

  • Sagittal suture – between the two parietal bones; it is the key line used to judge the position of the head.
  • Frontal suture – between the two frontal bones.
  • Coronal sutures – between the frontal and parietal bones.
  • Lambdoid sutures – between the parietal and occipital bones.

Fontanelles (landmarks for position)

  • Anterior fontanelle (bregma) – a diamond-shaped membranous space where the frontal, sagittal and two coronal sutures meet. Four sutures lead from it.
  • Posterior fontanelle (lambda) – a small triangular space where the sagittal and two lambdoid sutures meet. Three sutures lead from it. In a well-flexed head it is the fontanelle felt during labour.

Regions of the skull

  1. Vertex – the area bounded by the anterior and posterior fontanelles and the two parietal eminences. It presents in a well-flexed head (about 95% of births).
  2. Sinciput (brow) – from the anterior fontanelle and coronal sutures to the root of the nose and the supraorbital ridges. It presents in brow presentation.
  3. Face – from the root of the nose and supraorbital ridges to the junction of the chin and neck.
  4. Occiput – the area behind the posterior fontanelle and lambdoid sutures. The occiput is the denominator of vertex presentation.

Important landmarks (used for measuring diameters)

  • Occipital protuberance; suboccipital region (the junction of the neck and occiput, the "nape").
  • Glabella (the elevated area between the orbital ridges) and nasion (root of the nose).
  • Mentum (chin) and submentum (junction of the chin and neck).
  • Parietal eminences – the most prominent points of the parietal bones; the biparietal diameter is measured between them.

(b) Diameters of the fetal skull and their relation to attitude and presentation (7 marks)

1. Anteroposterior (longitudinal) diameters

Diameter From – To Length Presents in
Suboccipitobregmatic Nape of the neck (below the occipital protuberance) to the centre of the anterior fontanelle 9.5 cm Fully flexed vertex – normal labour
Suboccipitofrontal Nape of the neck to the centre of the frontal suture 10 cm Incompletely flexed vertex
Occipitofrontal Occipital eminence to the root of the nose (glabella) 11.5 cm Deflexed head – "military" attitude, occipitoposterior position
Mentovertical Point of the chin to the highest point on the sagittal suture 14 cm Brow presentation – the longest diameter; cannot pass through a normal pelvis at term
Submentovertical Junction of the chin and neck to the highest point of the vertex 11.5 cm Incompletely extended face
Submentobregmatic Junction of the chin and neck to the centre of the anterior fontanelle 9.5 cm Completely extended face presentation

2. Transverse diameters

  • Biparietal – between the two parietal eminences – 9.5 cm. It is the widest transverse diameter that must pass the pelvic brim; when it has passed, the head is engaged.
  • Super-subparietal – from a point below one parietal eminence to a point above the other – 8.5 cm (in asynclitism).
  • Bitemporal – between the farthest points of the coronal sutures – 8 cm.
  • Bimastoid – between the tips of the mastoid processes – 7.5 cm; it is incompressible.

3. Circumferences – the plane of the suboccipitobregmatic and biparietal diameters is nearly round, with a circumference of about 27–28 cm; the occipitofrontal circumference (the head circumference measured after birth) is about 34–35 cm; the mentovertical circumference is about 38 cm.

4. Relation to attitude and presentation

  • Attitude – the relation of the fetal head to the trunk – decides which diameter presents and engages. As the head flexes, smaller diameters present; as it extends, larger diameters present, up to the brow, and then smaller ones again in full extension (face).
  • Well-flexed vertex – the suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm) and biparietal (9.5 cm) diameters present – a small, round presenting circle that fits the pelvis and dilates the cervix evenly. This is why flexion is the first and most important movement in normal labour.
  • Deflexed vertex and occipitoposterior position – suboccipitofrontal (10 cm) or occipitofrontal (11.5 cm) diameters present; labour is longer and the head may arrest in the cavity.
  • Brow presentation – the mentovertical diameter (14 cm) presents; vaginal birth of a term baby is impossible unless the head flexes or extends fully, so caesarean section is usually needed.
  • Face presentation – the submentobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm) presents; vaginal birth is possible in mentoanterior positions.
  • Engagement and descent – the midwife judges engagement by the fifths of the head palpable above the brim and by station on vaginal examination; the size of the presenting diameter explains why one baby descends easily and another does not.
  • After-coming head in breech – the head must flex quickly to present the smallest diameters, otherwise delivery is delayed and dangerous.

(c) Moulding and its significance (4 marks)

Definition Moulding is the alteration in the shape of the fetal head caused by the overlapping of the vault bones at the sutures as the head is compressed in the birth canal during labour.

Mechanism

  • The engaging diameter is compressed (shortened by up to about 1 cm) while the diameter at right angles to it elongates; the volume of the skull does not change.
  • In a flexed vertex (occipitoanterior) the suboccipitobregmatic diameter shortens and the mentovertical diameter lengthens, giving the newborn head an elongated shape towards the occiput.
  • The parietal bones override the occipital and frontal bones, and one parietal bone may override the other.

Grading (noted on the Labour Care Guide)

  • 0 – bones separated; sutures can be felt easily.
  • + (1) – bones just touching.
  • ++ (2) – bones overlapping but can be separated by gentle pressure.
  • +++ (3) – bones overlapping and cannot be separated – an alert sign.

Significance

  1. Physiological moulding helps the head adapt to the shape of the pelvis and pass through it; it disappears within a day or two after birth.
  2. Increasing moulding (+++) with poor progress is a sign of cephalopelvic disproportion or obstructed labour and calls for urgent review.
  3. Excessive or rapid moulding – in precipitate labour, preterm babies (soft bones) and the after-coming head of a breech – can tear the tentorium cerebelli or falx and cause intracranial haemorrhage.
  4. The direction of moulding tells the attitude and position after birth (for example, a flattened forehead after occipitoposterior labour).
  5. Moulding must be distinguished from caput succedaneum, which is soft-tissue swelling of the scalp; both may be present together.

Identifying position and attitude of the head on vaginal examination

  1. After cervical dilatation is assessed, the examining fingers locate the sagittal suture and note in which pelvic diameter it lies (transverse, oblique or anteroposterior).
  2. The fingers follow the suture to a fontanelle:
    • A small triangular posterior fontanelle with three sutures felt near the centre of the pelvis means the head is well flexed; its direction (for example, towards the left anterior quadrant) gives the position (LOA).
    • If both fontanelles can be felt easily, the head is deflexed.
    • If the diamond-shaped anterior fontanelle is felt near the centre, with the supraorbital ridges within reach, a brow presentation is likely.
  3. When caput hides the sutures, the fetal ear can be felt – the tragus points towards the face – to confirm the position.
  4. The midwife also notes asynclitism, the degree of moulding and caput, and the station in relation to the ischial spines.

Diameters of the fetal trunk – after the head, the shoulders must pass: the bisacromial diameter (12 cm) can be compressed and enters the pelvis obliquely, while the bitrochanteric diameter (10 cm) of the buttocks matters in breech birth. In a large baby, delay of the shoulders after birth of the head is called shoulder dystocia, a serious emergency.

Nursing importance On vaginal examination the midwife identifies the sutures and fontanelles to find the position, judges flexion from the fontanelle felt and grades moulding and caput. Together with descent and cervical dilatation, these findings are recorded on the Labour Care Guide and help her detect disproportion early. After birth she explains the temporary change in head shape to anxious parents.

Conclusion The fetal skull has a compressible vault with sutures and fontanelles, and four regions – vertex, sinciput, face and occiput. In a well-flexed vertex the smallest diameters (suboccipitobregmatic and biparietal, 9.5 cm each) present, which makes normal birth possible; deflexion and extension bring larger diameters into play. Moderate moulding aids birth, while severe moulding warns of obstruction and brain injury.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Describe the development and structure of the placenta at term. Add a note on the placental barrier.

diagram.caption: Structure of the placenta
labels: section through placenta showing decidua basalis
spiral arteries opening into the intervillous space
chorionic plate with amnion and cord vessels; inset of a villus showing the layers of the placental barrier

answer_html:
Introduction The placenta is a temporary organ shared by mother and fetus. Through it the fetus breathes, feeds and excretes, and it produces the hormones that maintain pregnancy.

Development

  1. After implantation (6–7 days after fertilisation), the trophoblast differentiates into an inner cytotrophoblast and an outer syncytiotrophoblast, which erodes the endometrium.
  2. Lacunae appear in the syncytium and fill with maternal blood from eroded vessels; these later form the intervillous space.
  3. Villi develop – primary villi (cytotrophoblast core), secondary villi (mesoderm core) and, by the end of the third week, tertiary villi containing fetal blood vessels, which connect with the embryo's circulation as the heart begins to beat.
  4. Villi facing the decidua basalis multiply to form the chorion frondosum (the future placenta); those facing the uterine cavity degenerate to form the smooth chorion laeve (part of the membranes).
  5. Trophoblast invades and remodels the spiral arteries into wide, low-resistance channels; failure of this process underlies pre-eclampsia and fetal growth restriction.
  6. The placenta is fully formed by about 12 weeks and continues to grow until late pregnancy.

Structure at term

  • Shape and size – a round, flat disc about 15–20 cm in diameter and 2.5–3 cm thick at the centre; weight about 500 g, roughly one-sixth of the baby's weight.
  • Fetal surface – smooth and shiny, covered by amnion; the umbilical cord is attached near the centre, with its vessels radiating under the amnion.
  • Maternal surface – rough, dark red and spongy, covered by a thin layer of decidua basalis, and divided by septa into 15–20 cotyledons.
  • Margin – continuous with the chorion and amnion (the membranes).
  • Internal structure – the chorionic plate (fetal side) and basal plate (maternal side) enclose the intervillous space, filled with about 150 ml of maternal blood that is replaced several times a minute. Fetal villi float in this blood, so maternal blood is in direct contact with the trophoblast – a haemochorial placenta. Uteroplacental blood flow at term is about 500 ml per minute.

Placental barrier (placental membrane)

  • The tissue that separates maternal blood from fetal blood; the two bloods never mix normally.
  • Layers – syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast (which becomes thin and patchy after mid-pregnancy), basement membrane, connective tissue of the villus, and the endothelium of the fetal capillary.
  • The barrier becomes thinner as pregnancy advances, which increases exchange.
  • It is a selective, not a complete, barrier:
    • Oxygen, carbon dioxide and water cross by diffusion; glucose by facilitated diffusion; amino acids, calcium and iron by active transport; maternal IgG antibodies cross and give the newborn passive immunity.
    • Many drugs, alcohol and nicotine cross; large molecules such as heparin, insulin and IgM do not.
    • Some microorganisms cross – rubella, cytomegalovirus, HIV, hepatitis B, Treponema pallidum and Toxoplasma – causing congenital infections.
    • Anti-D (IgG) antibodies of a sensitised Rh-negative mother cross and cause haemolytic disease of the newborn.

Conclusion The placenta develops from the chorion frondosum and decidua basalis and at term is a 500 g disc with a shiny fetal and a lobulated maternal surface. Its barrier allows the exchange that the fetus needs, but it also lets drugs, infections and antibodies through – which is why medicines and infections in pregnancy need special care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Describe the formation, composition and functions of amniotic fluid. Add a note on the fetal membranes.

diagram.caption: Fetal membranes and amniotic fluid circulation
labels: chorion and amnion surrounding the amniotic cavity; fetus with arrows showing fluid production (fetal urine
absorption across the fetal surface of the placenta)

answer_html:
Fetal membranes

  • Amnion – the inner, thin, tough, smooth and avascular membrane lining the amniotic cavity; it covers the fetal surface of the placenta and the umbilical cord.
  • Chorion – the outer, thicker membrane (the chorion laeve), attached to the decidua and continuous with the edge of the placenta.
  • The two membranes come into contact by about 12 weeks, obliterating the chorionic cavity.
  • Functions – enclose the fetus and fluid, form a barrier to ascending infection, produce prostaglandins that help start labour, and form the bag of forewaters, which helps dilate the cervix in early labour.

Formation and circulation of amniotic fluid

  • Early pregnancy – mainly a transudate of maternal plasma across the membranes and of fetal plasma across the non-keratinised fetal skin.
  • From the second half of pregnancy – mainly fetal urine (the major source near term) and fluid secreted by the fetal lungs.
  • Removal – fetal swallowing, absorption across the fetal surface of the placenta into fetal vessels, and transfer across the membranes.
  • The fluid is constantly renewed, so it is in dynamic balance.

Volume – about 50 ml at 12 weeks, 400 ml at 20 weeks, a peak of about 1,000 ml at 36–38 weeks, then about 800 ml at term, decreasing further after 40 weeks.

Composition

  • Water 98–99% and solids 1–2%.
  • Organic substances – proteins, glucose, urea, creatinine, uric acid, hormones, enzymes and phospholipids (lecithin and sphingomyelin) from the fetal lungs.
  • Inorganic salts – sodium, chloride, potassium.
  • Suspended matter – lanugo hair, vernix caseosa and shed fetal cells (used for chromosome studies).
  • Normally clear and colourless early, pale straw-coloured near term, slightly alkaline.
  • Abnormal colours – green (meconium) in fetal hypoxia or post-maturity; golden yellow in Rh haemolytic disease; blood-stained or port-wine in abruption; dark brown in long-standing intrauterine death.

Functions During pregnancy

  1. Protects the fetus from injury by cushioning blows.
  2. Allows free movement and symmetrical growth and prevents adhesions between the fetus and amnion.
  3. Maintains an even temperature.
  4. Helps lung and gut development – fetal breathing movements and swallowing of fluid.
  5. Supplies a little water and nutrients and has some antibacterial activity.

During labour

  1. The forewaters in the bag of membranes help dilate the cervix evenly.
  2. Equalises the pressure of contractions and protects the fetus and placenta while the membranes are intact.
  3. After rupture, it flushes and lubricates the birth canal.

Clinical importance

  • Amniocentesis – for chromosomal studies and fetal lung maturity (lecithin–sphingomyelin ratio of 2 or more).
  • Ultrasound amniotic fluid index – normal about 5–25 cm; oligohydramnios (AFI below 5 cm) suggests fetal growth restriction, renal anomaly or leaking membranes; polyhydramnios (AFI above 25 cm) suggests diabetes, twins or fetal anomalies such as oesophageal atresia.
  • Colour of liquor in labour – thick meconium is an alert sign on the Labour Care Guide.

Conclusion The amnion and chorion enclose the fetus in amniotic fluid, which is formed mainly from fetal urine and lung fluid and removed mainly by swallowing. About one litre at its peak, it protects the fetus, allows growth and movement, and helps labour; its volume and colour give the midwife valuable information about fetal well-being.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Explain the growth and development of the fetus from conception to term.
answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy lasts about 280 days (40 weeks) from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), or 266 days from fertilisation. Clinically, age is counted from the LMP (gestational age), which is about two weeks more than the fertilisation age.

Periods of intrauterine life

  1. Pre-embryonic period (first two weeks after fertilisation) – cleavage, blastocyst formation and implantation.
  2. Embryonic period (weeks 3–8 after fertilisation) – organogenesis; all major organs form. This is the period of greatest vulnerability to teratogens such as drugs, radiation, alcohol and rubella.
  3. Fetal period (from the 9th week to birth) – growth and maturation of organs already formed.

Development at different stages (gestational age)

Gestation Approximate length / weight Main features
8 weeks About 2–3 cm Human form; head very large; limbs with fingers and toes; heart beating (seen on ultrasound from about 6 weeks)
12 weeks About 9 cm; 15–20 g External genitalia begin to differ; nails appear; kidneys produce urine; fetal heart audible with Doppler; placenta formed
16 weeks About 16 cm; 100 g Lanugo appears; sex can be seen on ultrasound; active movements; multigravida may feel quickening
20 weeks About 25 cm; 300 g Vernix caseosa forms; scalp hair; primigravida feels quickening; heart sounds heard with a fetal stethoscope
24 weeks About 30 cm; 600–700 g Skin red and wrinkled; eyelids still fused; surfactant production begins; survival possible only with intensive care
28 weeks About 35 cm; about 1,000–1,100 g Eyelids open; testes begin to descend; legal age of viability in India; good survival with newborn care
32 weeks About 40 cm; 1,600–1,800 g Subcutaneous fat accumulates; skin less wrinkled
