36 weeks About 45 cm; 2,500 g Body plump; lanugo decreasing; nails reach fingertips
40 weeks About 50 cm; 2,800–3,500 g Smooth pink skin; vernix in folds; nails beyond fingertips; testes in scrotum or labia majora covering minora; firm ear cartilage; plantar creases over the whole sole; good muscle tone and cry

Haase's rule – a simple guide to fetal length: in the first five months, length in cm = (month)²; after that, length = month × 5. For example, 3 months = 9 cm; 7 months = 35 cm; 10 months = 50 cm.

Factors affecting fetal growth

  • Maternal – nutrition and weight gain, anaemia, hypertension, diabetes, infections, smoking, tobacco chewing, alcohol, drugs, age and height.
  • Placental – adequacy of uteroplacental blood flow, infarcts, abnormal implantation.
  • Fetal – genetic potential, chromosomal anomalies, congenital infections, multiple pregnancy.

Nursing implications

  • Counselling to avoid teratogens, especially in the first trimester, and early folic acid.
  • Using fundal height, weight gain and ultrasound to monitor growth.
  • Interpreting the signs of maturity at birth.

Conclusion The fetus develops from a single cell to a mature baby of about 3 kg in 40 weeks. Organs form in the embryonic period and then grow and mature in the fetal period. Knowing these milestones helps the midwife counsel mothers, assess growth and judge maturity at birth.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Explain the fetopelvic relationship – lie, attitude, presentation, presenting part, denominator, position, engagement and station.

diagram.caption: Positions of the vertex
labels: diagram of the pelvic inlet seen from below with the occiput in six positions – LOA
ROP; a side view showing stations −3 to +3 in relation to the ischial spines

answer_html:
Introduction The fetopelvic relationship describes how the fetus lies in the uterus in relation to the mother's pelvis. These terms are used every day in antenatal examination, labour notes and handovers.

1. Lie

  • The relationship of the long axis of the fetus to the long axis of the uterus.
  • Longitudinal (about 99%), transverse or oblique (usually unstable and temporary).

2. Attitude

  • The relationship of the fetal parts to one another.
  • Normal attitude is universal flexion – head flexed on the chest, back curved, limbs flexed – making the fetus an ovoid that fits the uterus.
  • Deflexion (military attitude) and extension produce brow and face presentations.

3. Presentation

  • The part of the fetus that occupies the lower pole of the uterus, over the pelvic brim.
  • Cephalic (about 96–97%) – vertex (commonest), brow or face; breech (about 3%); shoulder (with transverse lie); compound (for example, hand with head).

4. Presenting part

  • The part of the presentation felt first on vaginal examination, lying over the cervical os – for example, the posterior part of the vertex (the parietal bone) in vertex presentation, or the anterior buttock in breech.

5. Denominator

  • A fixed bony point on the presenting part used to name the position: occiput in vertex, mentum (chin) in face, sacrum in breech and acromion in shoulder presentation.

6. Position

  • The relationship of the denominator to the six regions of the maternal pelvis – right and left, anterior, lateral (transverse) and posterior.
  • Vertex positions are LOA, LOT, LOP, ROA, ROT and ROP. LOA is the commonest; ROP is the commonest posterior position.

7. Engagement

  • The head is engaged when its greatest transverse diameter (biparietal) has passed through the pelvic inlet.
  • Abdominally – only two-fifths or less of the head is palpable above the brim.
  • Vaginally – the leading part of the skull is at or near the level of the ischial spines.
  • In primigravidae the head usually engages by 36–38 weeks; a non-engaged head at term in a primigravida suggests disproportion, placenta praevia or another cause and needs evaluation. In multiparae engagement often occurs only in labour.

8. Station

  • The level of the leading bony part of the presenting part in relation to the ischial spines.
  • 0 at the spines; −1 to −5 cm above and +1 to +5 cm below; +5 is at the vulva (crowning).
  • It is recorded at each vaginal examination to assess descent.

9. Synclitism and asynclitism

  • Synclitism – the sagittal suture lies midway between the symphysis and the sacrum.
  • Anterior asynclitism (Naegele's obliquity) – the anterior parietal bone leads.
  • Posterior asynclitism (Litzmann's obliquity) – the posterior parietal bone leads.

Clinical importance – these are determined by abdominal palpation (Leopold manoeuvres) and vaginal examination; they predict the mechanism of labour, alert the midwife to malpresentation and malposition and help decide the mode of delivery.

Conclusion Lie, attitude, presentation, presenting part, denominator, position, engagement and station together describe the fetus in relation to the pelvis. A longitudinal lie with a well-flexed vertex in the LOA position, engaging by term, is the most favourable for normal birth.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Write a note on menstrual hygiene – practices, products, problems and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Menstrual hygiene means that women and girls use a clean material to absorb or collect menstrual blood, change it as often as needed in privacy, wash with soap and water, dispose of used materials safely, and understand menstruation as a normal biological process without shame. According to NFHS-6 (2023–24), 79.2% of women aged 15–24 use hygienic methods of protection; the rest still use unclean cloth or other materials.

1. Menstrual products

  • Disposable sanitary pads – convenient; change every 4–6 hours.
  • Reusable cloth pads – economical and eco-friendly; must be washed with soap, dried in sunlight and stored clean.
  • Menstrual cups – medical-grade silicone cups worn inside the vagina; can be used for up to about 8–12 hours, reusable for years after boiling; need teaching.
  • Tampons and period underwear – less used in India.

2. Healthy practices

  • Change the pad or empty the cup regularly; never use the same pad all day.
  • Wash the genitals from front to back with clean water; wash hands before and after changing.
  • Bathe daily – there is no harm in bathing during periods.
  • Dispose of used pads wrapped in paper or a bag into a covered bin or incinerator; never flush them or throw them in the open.
  • Eat a normal, iron-rich diet and continue normal activities and exercise.
  • Keep a menstrual calendar.

3. Problems due to poor menstrual hygiene

  • Rashes, reproductive tract and urinary infections from unclean cloth and infrequent changing.
  • School and work absenteeism and dropping out, embarrassment and stress.
  • Myths and taboos – not entering the kitchen or temple, not touching pickles, not bathing, being kept separate.
  • Lack of toilets, water, privacy and disposal facilities in schools and workplaces.

4. Government initiatives

  • Menstrual Hygiene Scheme (2011) – subsidised sanitary napkins for rural adolescent girls through ASHAs, with education sessions.
  • Rashtriya Kishor Swasthya Karyakram and school health programmes – education by peer educators and teachers.
  • Jan Aushadhi "Suvidha" sanitary napkins sold at ₹1 per pad.
  • Toilets, sanitary napkin vending machines and incinerators in schools under the Swachh Bharat and Samagra Shiksha programmes.
  • Menstrual Hygiene Day – 28 May.

Role of the nurse

  1. Educate girls before menarche, and their mothers, about menstruation as a normal process.
  2. Demonstrate the use, change and disposal of pads, washing and drying of cloth pads, and the use of cups.
  3. Dispel myths and taboos with a respectful, culturally sensitive approach.
  4. Ensure availability of pads through ASHAs, schools and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
  5. Advocate for toilets, water and disposal facilities in schools and workplaces.
  6. Identify menstrual problems – severe dysmenorrhoea, heavy or irregular bleeding, anaemia – and refer them.
  7. Include menstrual hygiene in adolescent health, antenatal and postnatal education.

Conclusion Good menstrual hygiene depends on clean products, privacy, water, safe disposal and correct knowledge. By educating, demonstrating and challenging taboos, the nurse helps girls and women manage menstruation with health and dignity.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Define decidua and name its parts.
answer_html:
• Decidua is the endometrium of pregnancy. After implantation, under the influence of progesterone, the endometrial stromal cells enlarge and store glycogen and fat (the decidual reaction).
  • Parts – according to the site of implantation:
    • Decidua basalis – between the embryo and the myometrium; forms the maternal part of the placenta.
    • Decidua capsularis – covers the embryo on the side facing the uterine cavity; later fuses with the parietalis.
    • Decidua parietalis (vera) – lines the rest of the uterine cavity.
  • The placenta separates through its spongy layer in the third stage of labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Human Reproductive System and Conception
question: Describe the umbilical cord at term.
answer_html:
• The umbilical cord connects the fetus to the placenta. At term it is about 50 cm long (range 30–100 cm) and about 1–2 cm thick, covered by amnion.
  • It contains two umbilical arteries (carrying deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta) and one umbilical vein (carrying oxygenated blood to the fetus), embedded in Wharton's jelly, which protects the vessels from compression.
  • It is usually inserted near the centre of the placenta; marginal (battledore) and velamentous insertions are abnormal. A single umbilical artery may be associated with fetal anomalies.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: (a) Explain the changes in the reproductive organs and breasts during pregnancy. (5 marks) (b) Explain the systemic changes during pregnancy – cardiovascular, haematological, respiratory, renal, gastrointestinal, endocrine, metabolic, skin and musculoskeletal – with their nursing implications. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Main physiological changes of pregnancy
labels: central figure of a pregnant woman with labelled boxes – uterus (weight 50–60 g to about 1

answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy brings remarkable changes in almost every system of the woman's body. They are caused mainly by the hormones of the placenta and corpus luteum (hCG, oestrogen, progesterone, hPL and relaxin), by the growing uterus and by the increased metabolic demands of the fetus. These changes are normal adaptations, but they produce symptoms, alter normal laboratory values and can unmask disease, so the midwife must know them well.

(a) Changes in the reproductive organs and breasts (5 marks)

1. Uterus

  • Size and weight – it grows from about 7.5 cm long and 50–60 g in weight to about 35 cm long and about 1,000 g at term; its capacity increases about 500-fold, to nearly 5 litres.
  • Mechanism – mainly hypertrophy and stretching of the existing muscle fibres under oestrogen, with some hyperplasia in early pregnancy; later growth is due to distension by the fetus.
  • Shape and position – pear-shaped in early pregnancy, globular by 12 weeks, then ovoid. It rises out of the pelvis at about 12 weeks and becomes an abdominal organ, usually rotated to the right (dextro-rotation).
  • Muscle – the three layers of muscle fibres become well developed; the middle layer of interlacing fibres later acts as "living ligatures" after delivery of the placenta.
  • Lower uterine segment – the isthmus elongates and thins from about 12 weeks to form the lower segment, which becomes fully formed in late pregnancy and labour; it is the site of the caesarean incision.
  • Contractions – painless, irregular Braxton Hicks contractions begin early and become more noticeable in late pregnancy.
  • Blood flow – increases to about 500–750 ml per minute at term, mostly to the placenta.
  • Consistency – becomes soft; softening of the isthmus produces Hegar's sign.

2. Cervix

  • Becomes soft (Goodell's sign), bluish and more vascular.
  • The glands secrete thick mucus that forms the mucus plug (operculum), which protects against ascending infection; it is shed as the "show" at the onset of labour.
  • The columnar epithelium may evert (ectropion) and bleed on contact.

3. Vagina and perineum

  • Increased vascularity gives a bluish-violet colour (Chadwick's or Jacquemier's sign).
  • The walls become soft and thick, and secretions increase (physiological leucorrhoea); the pH falls (acidic), which limits some infections but favours candida.
  • The perineum becomes soft and vascular, ready to stretch in labour.

4. Ovaries and fallopian tubes

  • Ovulation stops.
  • The corpus luteum of pregnancy secretes progesterone and oestrogen until the placenta takes over at about 10–12 weeks.
  • The tubes become more vascular.

5. Breasts

  • Early tenderness, fullness and tingling (from 6–8 weeks).
  • Enlargement with visible superficial veins, due to growth of ducts (oestrogen) and alveoli (progesterone).
  • The nipples enlarge and become more erectile; the primary areola darkens, and Montgomery's tubercles (enlarged sebaceous glands) appear around the nipple.
  • A secondary areola (mottled pigmentation outside the primary areola) appears at about 20 weeks.
  • Colostrum can be expressed from the second trimester; striae may appear.
  • High oestrogen and progesterone inhibit full milk secretion until after delivery.

(b) Systemic changes and nursing implications (10 marks)

1. Cardiovascular system

  • Blood volume increases by 40–50% (about 1.5 litres), reaching its peak by 30–34 weeks. This meets the needs of the enlarged uterus and protects against blood loss at delivery.
  • Cardiac output rises by about 40–50%, mainly from increased stroke volume early and increased heart rate later (by 10–15 beats per minute). It increases further in labour and immediately after delivery, when blood returns from the contracting uterus.
  • Peripheral resistance falls (progesterone), so blood pressure falls in the second trimester, especially the diastolic, and returns to normal by term.
  • The heart is pushed upwards and to the left; a soft systolic murmur and a third heart sound may be normal.
  • Venous pressure in the legs rises due to pressure of the uterus on the pelvic veins → oedema of the feet, varicose veins and haemorrhoids.
  • In the supine position the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava → supine hypotensive syndrome.
  • Nursing implications – women with heart disease may decompensate at 28–34 weeks, in labour and just after delivery; advise left lateral position and leg elevation; measure blood pressure in the sitting position.

2. Haematological changes

  • Plasma volume increases more (about 50%) than red cell mass (about 20–30%) → haemodilution, the so-called physiological anaemia of pregnancy. Haemoglobin below 11 g/dl is still considered anaemia (WHO).
  • Iron requirement increases greatly; without supplementation iron-deficiency anaemia develops.
  • White cell count rises (up to about 15,000/mm³, more in labour); ESR rises and is not a useful test in pregnancy.
  • Hypercoagulable state – fibrinogen and clotting factors VII, VIII, IX and X increase, while fibrinolysis decreases. This protects against bleeding at delivery but increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.
  • Nursing implications – give IFA and calcium as per protocol, check haemoglobin at every visit, encourage mobility and hydration, and watch for calf pain and swelling, especially after caesarean section.

3. Respiratory system

  • The diaphragm rises by about 4 cm, but the chest widens, so breathing is not restricted.
  • Tidal volume increases by about 40% and minute ventilation rises (progesterone stimulates the respiratory centre); the respiratory rate changes little.
  • PaCO₂ falls (mild, compensated respiratory alkalosis), which helps transfer of CO₂ from the fetus.
  • Functional residual capacity falls; oxygen consumption rises.
  • Nasal congestion and nosebleeds are common.
  • Nursing implications – mild breathlessness of pregnancy is common, but breathlessness at rest, with palpitations or chest pain, needs evaluation; pregnant women desaturate quickly during anaesthesia or convulsions.

4. Renal and urinary system

  • Kidneys enlarge; renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rate increase by about 50%, so serum urea and creatinine are lower than in non-pregnant women.
  • Glycosuria may occur because more glucose is filtered than the tubules can reabsorb; it is not by itself diagnostic of diabetes.
  • Ureters and renal pelves dilate (right more than left), due to progesterone and pressure of the uterus → urinary stasis and risk of urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis.
  • Frequency of micturition in the first trimester (uterus pressing on the bladder) and again near term (engagement of the head).
  • Sodium and water are retained – about 6–8 litres of extra water by term.
  • Nursing implications – encourage fluids and frequent voiding, teach perineal hygiene, test urine for protein and sugar at every visit, and report burning, fever or loin pain.

5. Gastrointestinal system

  • Nausea and vomiting in the first trimester (hCG, oestrogen).
  • Gums become swollen and bleed easily; increased salivation (ptyalism) may occur.
  • Heartburn – progesterone relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter, and the uterus raises intra-abdominal pressure.
  • Constipation – reduced bowel motility (progesterone), pressure of the uterus and iron tablets.
  • Gall bladder emptying is slow, favouring gallstones; cholestasis may cause itching.
  • Appetite and thirst increase; some women develop cravings or pica.
  • Nursing implications – advise small frequent meals, avoid lying down after meals, a high-fibre diet with fluids, dental care, and report persistent vomiting or itching of the palms and soles.

6. Endocrine system

  • Placenta – produces hCG (peaks at 10–12 weeks; the basis of pregnancy tests), oestrogen (mainly oestriol), progesterone, human placental lactogen (hPL) and relaxin.
  • Pituitary enlarges; prolactin rises steadily, preparing the breasts for lactation.
  • Thyroid may enlarge slightly; total T3 and T4 rise because of increased binding protein, but free hormone levels remain normal. In early pregnancy hCG mildly stimulates the thyroid.
  • Adrenal – cortisol and aldosterone increase.
  • Pancreas and carbohydrate metabolism – in the second half of pregnancy hPL, cortisol and progesterone cause insulin resistance (the "diabetogenic" effect), which ensures a steady supply of glucose to the fetus; fasting blood sugar tends to be lower, but sugar rises more after meals. Women with limited insulin reserve develop gestational diabetes.
  • Nursing implications – screen all pregnant women for gestational diabetes; interpret thyroid tests with pregnancy reference values.

7. Metabolic changes and weight gain

  • Basal metabolic rate increases by about 10–20%.
  • Protein is retained for the growth of the fetus, uterus and breasts; fat is stored, especially in the first half of pregnancy, as an energy reserve for late pregnancy and lactation.
  • Calcium absorption from the gut increases to meet fetal needs.
  • Average weight gain is about 11 kg in a woman of normal weight (more if underweight, less if obese) – the fetus, placenta, liquor, uterus, breasts, blood volume, extracellular fluid and fat stores together.
  • Nursing implications – record weight at every visit; poor weight gain suggests fetal growth restriction, while sudden excessive gain suggests oedema and pre-eclampsia.

8. Skin

  • Pigmentation – linea nigra (dark line in the midline of the abdomen), darkening of the areola, vulva and scars, and chloasma (the "mask of pregnancy" on the face) due to melanocyte-stimulating effects of oestrogen and progesterone.
  • Striae gravidarum – pinkish or purplish stretch marks on the abdomen, breasts and thighs; they later become silvery white.
  • Spider naevi, palmar erythema, increased sweating and hair growth may occur.
  • Nursing implications – reassure the woman that most changes fade after delivery; advise sunscreen or covering the face; persistent severe itching needs investigation.

9. Musculoskeletal system

  • Relaxin and progesterone soften pelvic ligaments and joints, increasing mobility of the sacroiliac joints and symphysis pubis.
  • The growing uterus shifts the centre of gravity forward, causing lumbar lordosis, backache and a waddling gait in late pregnancy.
  • Leg cramps, carpal tunnel syndrome (fluid retention) and diastasis of the rectus muscles may occur.
  • Nursing implications – teach good posture, low-heeled footwear, correct lifting, back-care exercises and the use of a firm mattress.

10. Nervous system and mind

  • Fatigue and sleepiness in early pregnancy, emotional lability, sleep disturbance in late pregnancy.
  • Changes in body image and anxiety about labour and parenthood are common; the midwife provides emotional support and watches for antenatal depression.

11. Immune system – maternal immune responses are modulated so that the fetus is not rejected; some infections (such as malaria, tuberculosis and influenza) may become more severe, and autoimmune diseases may change in activity.

Nursing importance Many complaints of pregnant women – breathlessness, frequent urination, oedema, constipation, backache, fainting – are explained by these normal changes. Knowing them allows the midwife to reassure and teach the woman, to interpret findings such as a lower haemoglobin, higher white cell count or glycosuria correctly, and – most importantly – to recognise when a change goes beyond the normal and indicates disease, such as severe anaemia, pre-eclampsia, heart failure or gestational diabetes.

Conclusion Pregnancy causes growth and softening of the reproductive organs, preparation of the breasts and adaptive changes in every body system: expanded blood volume and cardiac output, haemodilution and a hypercoagulable state, increased ventilation and renal filtration, slower gut movement, insulin resistance, pigmentation and joint laxity. These changes support the fetus and prepare the mother for birth and lactation, and they form the basis of good antenatal assessment and counselling.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: (a) Define antenatal care and state its objectives. (3 marks) (b) Describe the schedule of antenatal visits and the components of an antenatal check-up as per Government of India guidelines. (8 marks) (c) Explain the identification of high-risk pregnancies and the counselling given during antenatal care. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Government of India antenatal visit schedule
labels: timeline from conception to 40 weeks showing: 1st visit (registration) within 12 weeks; 2nd visit 14–26 weeks; 3rd visit 28–34 weeks; 4th visit 36 weeks to term; PMSMA check-up on the 9th of the month in the 2nd/3rd trimester; boxes listing key activities at each visit

answer_html:
(a) Definition and objectives (3 marks)

Definition Antenatal care is the systematic supervision of a woman during pregnancy – through regular examination, investigations, preventive treatment and advice – to maintain her health and that of her fetus, to detect and manage complications early and to prepare her for childbirth and motherhood.

Objectives

  1. To promote, protect and maintain the health of the mother during pregnancy.
  2. To detect high-risk factors and complications early and manage or refer them.
  3. To prevent complications – anaemia, tetanus, pre-eclampsia, infections.
  4. To ensure the birth of a healthy, mature baby with the least risk to the mother.
  5. To prepare the woman and family for childbirth – birth preparedness and complication readiness.
  6. To prepare the mother for breastfeeding, newborn care and family planning.
  7. To reduce maternal, perinatal and neonatal mortality and morbidity.
  8. To give psychological support and a positive experience of pregnancy.

(b) Schedule of visits and components of an antenatal check-up (8 marks)

1. Schedule of visits (GoI) Every pregnant woman should have at least four antenatal visits, including registration:

Visit Timing
1st (registration) Within 12 weeks, as soon as pregnancy is suspected
2nd 14–26 weeks
3rd 28–34 weeks
4th 36 weeks to term
  • In addition, every woman in the second or third trimester should have at least one check-up by a doctor under PMSMA, held on the 9th of every month.
  • High-risk women need more frequent visits.
  • WHO (2016) recommends a minimum of eight contacts (at 12, 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks) for a positive pregnancy experience.
  • NFHS-6 shows first-trimester registration has risen to 76.2%, but only 65.2% of mothers receive four or more visits – a gap the midwife must close.

2. Components of the antenatal check-up

A. History (mainly at the first visit, updated at each visit)

  • Personal – name, age, address and contact number, education, occupation, husband's details, socio-economic status, habits (tobacco, alcohol).
  • Menstrual – first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), regularity and length of cycles; calculation of the expected date of delivery (EDD) by Naegele's rule, confirmed by an early ultrasound when available.
  • Obstetric – gravida and parity; outcome and mode of each previous delivery; abortions, stillbirths, neonatal deaths; previous caesarean section, PPH, eclampsia, birth weights.
  • Present pregnancy – symptoms, bleeding, fever, fetal movements, minor discomforts.
  • Medical and surgical – hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, tuberculosis, asthma, epilepsy, thyroid disease, HIV, previous surgery, blood transfusion, drug allergy.
  • Family – diabetes, hypertension, twins, congenital anomalies, genetic disorders (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease).
  • Contraceptive history.

B. Physical examination

  • General – height (less than 145 cm is a risk factor), weight at every visit, blood pressure at every visit, pulse, pallor, oedema, jaundice, thyroid, teeth, heart and lungs.
  • Breasts – nipples (flat or inverted), lumps.
  • Abdominal examination – from the second trimester: inspection, fundal height, obstetric palpation for lie, presentation and engagement, and fetal heart sounds.
  • Pelvic examination – only when indicated (bleeding, discharge, suspected disproportion near term), not routinely.

C. Investigations

  • Haemoglobin – at every visit.
  • Blood group and Rh type; indirect Coombs test for Rh-negative women.
  • Urine – albumin and sugar at every visit; culture if symptoms suggest infection.
  • HIV, syphilis (VDRL/RPR or rapid test) and hepatitis B (HBsAg) – at the first visit (with counselling).
  • Blood sugar – single-step 75 g oral glucose test for gestational diabetes at the first visit and again at 24–28 weeks.
  • Ultrasound – for dating in the first trimester and an anomaly scan at 18–20 weeks where available; later scans for growth when indicated.
  • Other tests where indicated – thyroid function, malaria, sickle cell screening in tribal areas, blood sugar in high-risk women.

D. Preventive interventions

  • Folic acid in the first trimester, then iron–folic acid (IFA) daily from the second trimester for at least 180 days, continued after delivery; intravenous iron for moderate or severe anaemia as per protocol.
  • Calcium supplementation from the second trimester.
  • Tetanus–diphtheria (Td) – two doses, or one booster dose if she received two doses in a pregnancy within the previous three years.
  • Albendazole once after the first trimester for deworming.

E. Recording and reporting – entries in the MCP card, the ANC register and the RCH portal, so that every woman is tracked by name.

(c) Identification of high-risk pregnancies and counselling (4 marks)

High-risk factors to be identified

  • Maternal characteristics – age under 18 or over 35, height under 145 cm, low body weight, grand multiparity, birth interval under 18–24 months.
  • Past obstetric history – previous caesarean section, stillbirth, two or more abortions, preterm birth, PPH, eclampsia, birth of a malformed or very small baby.
  • Present pregnancy – severe anaemia, hypertension (BP 140/90 mmHg or more), gestational diabetes, antepartum haemorrhage, multiple pregnancy, malpresentation after 36 weeks, poor or excessive uterine growth, Rh-negative mother, post-term pregnancy.
  • Medical disorders – heart disease, diabetes, tuberculosis, epilepsy, thyroid disease, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B.
  • Social factors – poverty, domestic violence, substance use, lack of family support.

High-risk women are marked on the MCP card, referred to PMSMA clinics, CHCs or first referral units, followed up individually (extended PMSMA) and advised institutional delivery at a facility capable of managing the complication.

Counselling during antenatal care

  1. Diet – an extra meal every day, a balanced diet with green leafy vegetables, pulses, milk, fruits and iron-rich foods; regular IFA and calcium; avoid tea or coffee with meals.
  2. Rest and activity – about 8 hours of sleep at night and 2 hours of rest in the day, lying on the left side in later pregnancy; continue light housework and walking; avoid heavy lifting.
  3. Personal hygiene – daily bath, care of breasts and teeth, comfortable loose clothing and low-heeled footwear.
  4. Avoid harmful practices – tobacco, alcohol, self-medication and X-rays without advice.
  5. Sexual activity – may continue in normal pregnancy; avoid in bleeding, leaking, previous abortions or placenta praevia.
  6. Danger signs – bleeding, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, swelling of the face, fever, severe abdominal pain, leaking of fluid and reduced fetal movements – report immediately.
  7. Birth preparedness – place of delivery, transport, money, blood donor, companion and documents; government entitlements (JSY, JSSK, PMMVY).
  8. Breastfeeding and newborn care – early initiation, colostrum, exclusive breastfeeding.
  9. Postpartum family planning – options and timing.
  10. Emotional health – encourage expression of fears, involve the husband and family, and refer women with signs of depression.

What is done at every follow-up visit

  • Ask about complaints, fetal movements, danger signs and compliance with IFA and calcium (and their side effects).
  • Record weight, blood pressure, pallor and oedema; test haemoglobin and urine for protein and sugar.
  • Measure fundal height, palpate the abdomen and listen to the fetal heart; compare with the expected growth for the gestation.
  • Review test results and the woman's risk status; refer if a new risk appears.
  • Give the next supply of IFA and calcium, complete Td, and fix the date of the next visit.
  • Counsel according to the stage of pregnancy:
    • First trimester – nutrition, folic acid, nausea, avoidance of drugs and X-rays, early ultrasound.
    • Second trimester – IFA and calcium, Td, fetal movements, anomaly scan, minor disorders, GDM test at 24–28 weeks.
    • Third trimester – BPCR and micro-birth plan, signs of labour, breastfeeding preparation, birth companion, postpartum family planning.

Making antenatal care woman-centred

  • WHO stresses a positive pregnancy experience – care that is respectful, private and unhurried, with clear explanations and continuity of the same provider.
  • Use the visit to build trust: greet the woman by name, listen to her concerns, involve her husband or mother-in-law when she wishes, and never scold her for missed visits.
  • Outreach through Village Health, Sanitation and Nutrition Days, home visits by ASHAs and tracking on the RCH portal help reach women who do not come on their own, especially the poor, adolescents and migrants.

Nursing importance Antenatal care is the main contact between the health system and the pregnant woman. Through careful history, examination, tests and counselling, the midwife can prevent or detect early most of the conditions that kill mothers and babies – anaemia, hypertension, diabetes, infection and malpresentation – and ensure a planned, safe institutional birth. Respectful, unhurried care also encourages the woman to return for every visit.

Conclusion Antenatal care is the planned supervision of pregnancy to keep the mother and fetus healthy and prepare them for birth. The Government of India recommends at least four visits plus a PMSMA check-up, each including history, examination, investigations, preventive supplements and Td, risk assessment and counselling. Identifying high-risk women and ensuring they deliver in the right facility is the key to reducing maternal and perinatal deaths.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: (a) Explain the presumptive symptoms and signs of pregnancy. (5 marks) (b) Explain the probable and positive signs of pregnancy, including laboratory and ultrasound diagnosis. (7 marks) (c) State the differential diagnosis of pregnancy. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Signs of pregnancy by gestational age
labels: timeline 0–40 weeks: amenorrhoea and positive urine test around the missed period; gestational sac on transvaginal scan at about 5 weeks and cardiac activity at about 6 weeks; Hegar's and Goodell's signs 6–10 weeks; Doppler fetal heart from 10–12 weeks; quickening 16–20 weeks; ballottement 16–28 weeks; fetal heart with Pinard stethoscope and fetal parts palpable from about 20 weeks

answer_html:
Introduction Early and accurate diagnosis of pregnancy allows early registration, dating, supplementation and timely detection of problems such as ectopic pregnancy. Signs of pregnancy are traditionally grouped into presumptive (suggestive), probable (strongly suggestive) and positive (certain) signs.

(a) Presumptive symptoms and signs (5 marks) These are mostly subjective symptoms felt by the woman; each can have other causes.

1. Amenorrhoea – sudden stopping of menstruation in a woman of reproductive age with previously regular cycles is the earliest and most important symptom. Other causes include lactation, stress, illness, thyroid disease, polycystic ovaries and approaching menopause.

2. Nausea and vomiting ("morning sickness") – begins at about 6 weeks and usually settles by 12–14 weeks; worse in the morning; related to rising hCG and oestrogen.

3. Frequency of micturition – in the first trimester, due to pressure of the enlarging uterus on the bladder and pelvic congestion.

4. Breast changes – tenderness, fullness and tingling from 6–8 weeks; later enlargement, prominent veins, darkened areola, Montgomery's tubercles, a secondary areola (about 20 weeks) and colostrum.

5. Fatigue – common in the first trimester.

6. Quickening – the first perception of fetal movements by the mother, at 18–20 weeks in a primigravida and 16–18 weeks in a multigravida. It helps date pregnancy but may be imagined (pseudocyesis) or confused with intestinal movements.

7. Skin changes – linea nigra, chloasma and striae gravidarum.

8. Vaginal changes – bluish discolouration of the vaginal mucosa and vulva (Chadwick's or Jacquemier's sign) at about 8 weeks, due to increased vascularity; it can also occur with pelvic congestion.

9. Other early symptoms – food cravings or aversions, increased salivation, mood changes, mild abdominal bloating.

(b) Probable and positive signs (7 marks)

Probable signs (objective findings by the examiner, but still not certain)

  1. Enlargement of the abdomen and uterus – the uterus is palpable above the symphysis at about 12 weeks and enlarges progressively in keeping with the period of amenorrhoea.
  2. Changes in the uterus on bimanual examination
    • Hegar's sign (6–10 weeks) – on bimanual examination the softened, compressible isthmus allows the fingers of both hands to almost meet below the firm body of the uterus.
    • Palmer's sign (4–8 weeks) – rhythmic contractions of the uterus felt during bimanual examination.
    • Piskacek's sign – asymmetrical enlargement of the uterus at the site of implantation.
  3. Changes in the cervix
    • Goodell's sign (about 6 weeks) – softening of the cervix; it feels like the lips rather than the tip of the nose.
    • Osiander's sign (about 8 weeks) – increased pulsation felt in the lateral vaginal fornices.
  4. Braxton Hicks contractions – painless, irregular uterine contractions felt by the examiner from about the second trimester; they also occur with soft fibroids or haematometra.
  5. Ballottement (16–28 weeks) – when the fetus in the amniotic fluid is pushed sharply by a finger in the vagina (internal) or a hand on the abdomen (external), it floats away and returns to strike the examining hand.
  6. Outline of the fetus on abdominal palpation – a firm mass in the uterus, before fetal parts can be clearly identified.
  7. Uterine souffle – a soft blowing sound, synchronous with the maternal pulse, heard over the uterus from about 16 weeks; it is due to blood flow in the uterine vessels and also occurs with large fibroids.
  8. Positive pregnancy tests (biochemical)
    • Based on human chorionic gonadotrophin (hCG), secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast. It can be detected in maternal blood about 8–10 days after ovulation, doubles about every two days in early pregnancy and peaks at about 10 weeks.
    • Urine pregnancy card test – a simple immunochromatographic test, usually positive by the time of the missed period; it is available free with ASHAs (Nischay kit) and used for early registration.
    • Serum β-hCG – quantitative; useful in suspected ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and molar pregnancy.
    • Tests are called "probable" because hCG can be raised in molar pregnancy, choriocarcinoma, after recent abortion or hCG injections.

Positive signs (certain proof of a fetus)

  1. Fetal heart sounds
    • Heard with a Doppler device from about 10–12 weeks and with a Pinard fetal stethoscope from about 18–20 weeks.
    • Rate 110–160 beats per minute, not synchronous with the mother's pulse (always check the maternal pulse at the same time).
  2. Fetal movements felt by the examiner – after about 20 weeks.
  3. Fetal parts palpable – head, back and limbs can be identified on abdominal palpation from about 20–24 weeks.
  4. Ultrasound – the most reliable and earliest positive evidence:
    • Gestational sac in the uterus at about 5 weeks on transvaginal scan (about a week later on abdominal scan).
    • Yolk sac and then a fetal pole with cardiac activity at about 6 weeks (transvaginal).
    • Crown–rump length at 7–13 weeks gives the most accurate dating.
    • It also confirms the site (intrauterine or ectopic), number of fetuses and viability.
  5. Radiological visualisation of the fetal skeleton (after about 16 weeks) is now obsolete because of radiation risk.

(c) Differential diagnosis of pregnancy (3 marks) Conditions that may be mistaken for pregnancy because they cause amenorrhoea and/or abdominal enlargement:

Condition Distinguishing features
Pseudocyesis (false pregnancy) A woman with an intense desire for (or fear of) pregnancy believes she is pregnant; amenorrhoea, abdominal enlargement due to fat or gas, "movements" are imagined; uterus normal size; pregnancy test and ultrasound negative; needs sensitive counselling
Full bladder (retention of urine) Cystic, dull swelling arising from the pelvis; disappears after catheterisation
Fibroid uterus Firm, irregular uterus; menstruation usually present or heavy; negative pregnancy test; ultrasound shows fibroids
Ovarian cyst or tumour Swelling separate from the uterus, often to one side; menses present; ultrasound confirms
Ascites Shifting dullness, fluid thrill, flanks full; other signs of liver, kidney or heart disease
Hydatidiform mole Uterus larger than dates, bleeding, severe vomiting, very high hCG, no fetal heart; "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound
Other causes of amenorrhoea Lactation, stress, polycystic ovary syndrome, thyroid disease, contraceptive use; pregnancy test negative

Estimating the duration (gestational age) of pregnancy Once pregnancy is confirmed, the midwife estimates how far it has advanced:

  1. From the LMP – calculating the EDD by Naegele's rule, if the woman is sure of her dates and her cycles were regular.
  2. From the date of quickening – roughly 20 weeks in a primigravida and 18 weeks in a multigravida (only a rough guide).
  3. From fundal height – using abdominal landmarks or symphysis–fundal height in centimetres after 24 weeks.
  4. From ultrasound – crown–rump length in the first trimester (most accurate, within about a week); biparietal diameter, head circumference and femur length in the second trimester.

Warning features while diagnosing pregnancy

  • Pain or bleeding with a positive test, especially with fainting or shoulder-tip pain – suspect ectopic pregnancy; ultrasound shows an empty uterus. Refer urgently.
  • Bleeding with an open cervix or passage of tissue – miscarriage.
  • Uterus much larger than dates, severe vomiting, very high hCG and no fetal heart – molar pregnancy.
  • Uterus smaller than dates – wrong dates, missed miscarriage or fetal growth restriction.

Practical approach at the sub-centre or clinic

  1. Take a careful menstrual history and ask about symptoms.
  2. Do a urine pregnancy test on an early-morning sample.
  3. If positive, register the pregnancy immediately, start folic acid, check haemoglobin and blood pressure, and advise an early ultrasound.
  4. If negative but amenorrhoea continues, repeat the test after one week, and look for other causes of amenorrhoea.
  5. Counsel the woman sensitively – some pregnancies are unplanned, and she may need information about safe options under the MTP Act.

Nursing importance The midwife or ANM is usually the first to see a woman who has missed a period. By asking the right questions, doing a urine pregnancy test and recognising early signs, she can register the pregnancy in the first trimester, start folic acid, calculate the EDD and refer for early ultrasound. She must also recognise warning features – pain or bleeding with a positive test (ectopic pregnancy), or a uterus much larger than dates (mole or twins) – and refer at once.

Conclusion Pregnancy is first suspected from amenorrhoea, morning sickness, breast changes and urinary frequency (presumptive signs); it becomes probable with uterine and cervical changes, ballottement and a positive hCG test; and it is confirmed by fetal heart sounds, fetal movements and parts felt by the examiner, or by ultrasound. Careful assessment also excludes conditions such as pseudocyesis, fibroids, ovarian tumours and molar pregnancy.

question: Explain the abdominal (obstetric) examination of a pregnant woman, including Leopold manoeuvres.

diagram.caption: Four Leopold manoeuvres
labels: (1) fundal grip – both hands on the fundus

facing the woman's face; (2) lateral grip – hands on the sides of the uterus to find the back and limbs; (3) Pawlik's (first pelvic) grip – one hand grasping the lower pole above the symphysis; (4) pelvic (second pelvic) grip – facing the feet
both hands sliding into the pelvic inlet to assess engagement and flexion

answer_html:
Introduction Abdominal examination from the second trimester tells the midwife about the growth of the fetus, its lie, presentation, position and engagement, and its well-being. It is done at every antenatal visit and on admission in labour.

Preparation

  • Explain the procedure and obtain consent; ensure privacy; ask the woman to empty her bladder.
  • Position her supine with a pillow under the head and knees slightly flexed; expose the abdomen from the xiphisternum to the symphysis; keep her covered otherwise.
  • Avoid prolonged supine position (supine hypotension); warm hands; stand on her right side.

1. Inspection

  • Size and shape of the abdomen – a longitudinal ovoid suggests a longitudinal lie; a broad abdomen suggests a transverse lie or twins.
  • Skin – linea nigra, striae gravidarum, scars of previous operations (especially caesarean section).
  • Umbilicus (flat or everted near term), visible fetal movements, pendulous abdomen.

2. Fundal height

  • By landmarks – the fundus is just palpable above the symphysis at 12 weeks, about one-third of the way to the umbilicus at 16 weeks, at the umbilicus at about 24 weeks, one-third of the way between the umbilicus and xiphisternum at 28 weeks, two-thirds at 32 weeks and near the xiphisternum at 36 weeks; at 40 weeks it sinks to about the 32-week level as the head engages (lightening).
  • Symphysis–fundal height (SFH) with a tape measure, from the top of the symphysis to the top of the fundus – after 24 weeks the SFH in centimetres roughly equals the weeks of gestation (± 2 cm).
  • A uterus smaller than dates suggests wrong dates, fetal growth restriction or oligohydramnios; larger than dates suggests wrong dates, twins, polyhydramnios or a large baby.

3. Palpation – Leopold manoeuvres

  1. Fundal grip (first manoeuvre) – facing the woman's head, both hands palpate the fundus to find which pole lies there: the breech feels soft, broad and irregular and does not move independently; the head feels hard, round and ballottable.
  2. Lateral (umbilical) grip (second manoeuvre) – hands on either side of the uterus, one steadying while the other palpates: the back feels smooth, firm and continuous; the limbs feel like small irregular knobs that may move. This gives the lie and position.
  3. Pawlik's grip (third manoeuvre) – the lower pole is grasped between the thumb and fingers of the right hand just above the symphysis to identify the presenting part and whether it is free (ballottable) or fixed.
  4. Pelvic grip (fourth manoeuvre) – facing the woman's feet, the fingers of both hands are pressed gently downwards and inwards along the sides of the lower uterus towards the pelvic inlet to judge engagement and flexion (the cephalic prominence is felt on the side opposite the back in a flexed head). Engagement is recorded as fifths of the head palpable above the brim (5/5 to 0/5); two-fifths or less means engaged.

4. Auscultation of the fetal heart

  • Using a Pinard stethoscope (from about 20 weeks) or a hand-held Doppler, listen over the fetal back; in LOA position this is below the umbilicus on the left side.
  • Count for a full minute while feeling the mother's pulse; normal rate 110–160 per minute, regular.

5. Recording and explanation – record fundal height, lie, presentation, position, engagement and FHR in the MCP card, and explain the findings to the woman, who often enjoys hearing the baby's heartbeat.

Conclusion Inspection, measurement of fundal height, the four Leopold manoeuvres and auscultation of the fetal heart give a complete picture of fetal growth, position and well-being. Done gently and explained clearly, the examination also strengthens the bond between mother, baby and midwife.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
