question: Explain the minor disorders of pregnancy and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Minor disorders are common discomforts caused by the normal physiological changes of pregnancy. They are not dangerous, but they cause distress, and some can mask serious conditions. The midwife's role is to reassure, give simple remedies and recognise when a symptom is not "minor".

Disorder Cause Management and advice
Nausea and vomiting (6–14 weeks) hCG, oestrogen, emotional factors Dry toast or biscuits before getting up; small frequent meals; avoid fatty, spicy food and strong smells; ginger; plenty of fluids between meals; refer if vomiting is persistent, with dehydration or weight loss (hyperemesis)
Heartburn Progesterone relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter; pressure of the uterus Small frequent meals; avoid lying down for 2 hours after meals; sleep with extra pillows; avoid spicy, fried food; antacids if prescribed
Constipation Reduced bowel motility, iron tablets, less exercise High-fibre diet, fruits, green vegetables, 8–10 glasses of water, regular walks, regular bowel habit; mild laxatives only if prescribed
Haemorrhoids Constipation, pressure on pelvic veins Prevent constipation; warm sitz baths; local soothing applications as prescribed
Frequency of micturition Pressure of the uterus on the bladder (first trimester and near term) Reassure; reduce fluids before bedtime but not during the day; refer if burning, fever or pain (urinary infection)
Backache Lordosis, relaxed joints, poor posture, high heels Good posture, low-heeled footwear, correct lifting (bend knees), firm mattress, back-care and pelvic tilt exercises, local warmth
Leg cramps Altered calcium–phosphorus balance, fatigue, pressure on nerves Calcium supplementation; stretching the calf (pulling the toes upwards) during the cramp; massage; warmth; avoid pointing the toes
Varicose veins Increased venous pressure, relaxation of vein walls Avoid standing for long periods; elevate the legs; avoid crossing legs; elastic stockings; leg exercises
Oedema of the feet Pressure on pelvic veins, water retention Rest with legs raised, lying on the left side; avoid long standing; check BP and urine protein – oedema of the face or hands, or sudden swelling, may be pre-eclampsia
Leucorrhoea Increased vaginal secretions Perineal hygiene, cotton underwear; avoid douching; refer if itching, foul smell or coloured discharge (infection)
Fainting and dizziness Low blood pressure, supine hypotension, hypoglycaemia, anaemia Rise slowly, avoid standing in crowds and lying flat on the back, eat regularly, check haemoglobin
Insomnia Fetal movements, frequency, discomfort, anxiety Rest in the day, warm milk at bedtime, left lateral position with pillows, relaxation; no sleeping pills without advice
Breathlessness Raised diaphragm, progesterone Good posture, rest, extra pillows; refer if severe, at rest, or with palpitations or cough
Carpal tunnel syndrome Fluid retention compressing the median nerve Rest, wrist splint at night, raising the hands; resolves after delivery
Ptyalism, gum bleeding Hormonal effects Oral hygiene, soft toothbrush, dental check
Itching (pruritus) Stretching of skin, dryness Light cotton clothing, moisturiser; refer if severe itching of palms and soles (cholestasis)
Round ligament pain Stretching of round ligaments Rest, change of position, warmth; refer if pain is severe or with bleeding

General principles

  • Explain that these complaints are due to normal changes and usually disappear after delivery.
  • Avoid self-medication; use simple non-drug measures first.
  • Continue IFA and calcium, but take iron after meals and not with tea, to reduce side effects.
  • Refer when "red flags" appear – persistent vomiting, severe headache, visual disturbance, swelling of the face, bleeding, severe abdominal pain, fever or reduced fetal movements.

Conclusion Minor disorders of pregnancy are common and usually harmless. Reassurance, simple dietary and postural measures and timely recognition of warning signs allow the mother to remain comfortable and safe.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: Explain the methods of assessing fetal well-being during pregnancy.

diagram.caption: Components of the biophysical profile
labels: five boxes each scored 2 or 0 – non-stress test (reactive)
fetal breathing movements (one episode of 30 seconds or more in 30 minutes)
gross body movements (three or more in 30 minutes)
fetal tone (one episode of extension and return to flexion)
amniotic fluid (single deepest pocket 2 cm or more); total score 8–10 normal

answer_html:
Introduction Fetal well-being means that the fetus is growing normally and is not short of oxygen. Assessment is especially important in high-risk pregnancies – hypertension, diabetes, fetal growth restriction, post-term pregnancy, reduced fetal movements, Rh isoimmunisation and previous stillbirth.

1. Clinical methods

  • Fetal movements – the mother's own record is the simplest test.
    • Daily fetal movement count (DFMC) from 28 weeks, for example the Cardiff "count to ten" – the mother notes the time taken to feel ten movements, starting in the morning.
    • Fewer than 10 movements in 12 hours, or a clear reduction from her usual pattern, must be reported the same day.
  • Fundal height and weight gain at each visit, plotted against gestation.
  • Auscultation of the fetal heart with a Pinard stethoscope or Doppler.

2. Ultrasound

  • Dating, number and site of pregnancy in the first trimester; anomaly scan at 18–20 weeks.
  • Fetal biometry (biparietal diameter, head and abdominal circumference, femur length) and estimated fetal weight to detect growth restriction or macrosomia.
  • Amniotic fluid index (normal about 5–25 cm), placental site and maturity.

3. Non-stress test (NST)

  • A cardiotocograph records the fetal heart rate and uterine activity for 20 minutes (extended to 40) with the mother in a semi-sitting or left lateral position.
  • Reactive (normal) – at least two accelerations of 15 beats per minute lasting 15 seconds in 20 minutes, a baseline of 110–160 and normal variability.
  • Non-reactive – needs further testing; the fetus may simply be asleep.
  • Vibroacoustic stimulation – a sound–vibration device placed on the abdomen over the fetal head for a few seconds wakes a sleeping fetus and reduces false non-reactive results.

4. Biophysical profile (BPP – Manning)

  • Five components, each scored 2 (normal) or 0: NST, fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, fetal tone and amniotic fluid volume, observed by ultrasound over 30 minutes.
  • 8–10 normal; 6 equivocal (repeat or deliver if mature); 4 or less abnormal – consider delivery.
  • Modified BPP – NST plus amniotic fluid index; quicker and widely used.

5. Doppler velocimetry

  • Umbilical artery Doppler in fetal growth restriction – absent or reversed end-diastolic flow indicates serious compromise.
  • Middle cerebral artery Doppler – shows "brain sparing" in hypoxia and detects fetal anaemia in Rh disease.

6. Contraction stress test – the fetal heart response to induced contractions; rarely used now.

7. Biochemical and invasive tests

  • Maternal serum screening for chromosomal anomalies – the double marker in the first trimester (with nuchal translucency) and the triple or quadruple marker in the second.
  • Amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling for diagnosis when screening is positive.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  • Teach every mother to monitor fetal movements and to report reduced movements at once.
  • Prepare the woman for NST, BPP and Doppler, position her in the left lateral or semi-sitting position, explain the results and record them.
  • Ensure high-risk women attend for serial testing and act promptly on abnormal results.

Conclusion Fetal well-being is assessed by fetal movement counts, fundal height, auscultation, ultrasound, non-stress test, biophysical profile and Doppler studies. Used wisely, especially in high-risk pregnancies, these tests allow timely delivery before the fetus is harmed.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: Explain preconception care and counselling.
answer_html:
Introduction Many important events in fetal development – such as closure of the neural tube and formation of the heart – occur before a woman knows she is pregnant. Preconception care is the set of biomedical, behavioural and social interventions given to women and couples before conception to improve their health and the outcome of a future pregnancy (WHO). It supports planned parenthood.

1. Assessment

  • Medical history – diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, thyroid disease, heart disease, tuberculosis, HIV, kidney disease, mental illness.
  • Medications – identify teratogenic drugs (for example sodium valproate, warfarin, ACE inhibitors, isotretinoin, methotrexate) and change them before conception under medical advice.
  • Obstetric history – previous abortions, stillbirths, caesarean section, babies with anomalies.
  • Family history – genetic disorders (thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, haemophilia), consanguinity.
  • Lifestyle – nutrition, tobacco (smoking or chewing), alcohol, drugs, occupational exposure to chemicals or radiation.
  • Examination – weight and BMI, blood pressure, pallor, thyroid, breasts, dental health.

2. Investigations (as indicated) – haemoglobin, blood group and Rh, blood sugar, thyroid function, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, rubella immunity, screening for thalassaemia or sickle cell disease in high-prevalence groups.

3. Interventions

  • Folic acid 400 micrograms daily from at least three months before conception until 12 weeks of pregnancy to prevent neural tube defects; a higher dose (4–5 mg) for women with a previous baby with a neural tube defect, epilepsy on treatment or diabetes.
  • Correct anaemia with iron and a good diet.
  • Immunisation – rubella (MR) vaccine for non-immune women, with advice to avoid pregnancy for one month; hepatitis B and Td as needed.
  • Control chronic diseases – good blood sugar control in diabetes, blood pressure control, stable epilepsy on the safest drug.
  • Achieve a healthy weight – underweight and obesity both increase risk.
  • Stop tobacco and alcohol (for both partners) and avoid harmful exposures.
  • Treat infections – RTIs/STIs, dental infections.

4. Counselling

  • Ideal timing – avoid pregnancy before 18–20 years; birth spacing of at least 24 months between a birth and the next pregnancy, and at least 6 months after a miscarriage or abortion.
  • Genetic counselling for couples at risk.
  • Awareness about normal birth – that labour and birth are normal physiological processes; the benefits of normal birth over unnecessary caesarean section; birth companions and choices in labour.
  • Nutrition, exercise, stress management and mental health.
  • Involvement of the male partner in planning and support.
  • Information about antenatal registration and government schemes.

Role of the nurse

  • Use every contact – newly-wed couples, family planning clinics, adolescent clinics, postnatal visits and NCD screening – to offer preconception advice.
  • Distribute folic acid, check haemoglobin and immunisation status, and refer women with chronic illness to a doctor before they conceive.

Conclusion Preconception care prepares a woman's body and mind for pregnancy. Folic acid, correction of anaemia, immunisation, control of chronic disease, avoidance of teratogens and harmful habits, and planned birth spacing can prevent many birth defects and maternal complications.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: Explain birth preparedness and complication readiness, including micro-birth planning.

diagram.caption: Components of birth preparedness and complication readiness
labels: central box "birth plan" linked to – place of delivery and skilled attendant; transport (102/108
local vehicle); money and documents; blood donor; decision-maker and companion; items for mother and baby; knowledge of danger signs; facility for emergencies

answer_html:
Introduction Most obstetric complications cannot be predicted, but every woman can be prepared. Birth preparedness and complication readiness (BPCR) is a strategy that helps the woman, her family and the community plan for a normal birth and for an emergency, so that the first two of the three delays are avoided.

Components of a birth plan

  1. Place of delivery – an identified health facility with a skilled birth attendant (institutional delivery), suitable to her risk status.
  2. Transport – how she will reach the facility at any hour – the 102/108 ambulance number written on the MCP card, and a back-up local vehicle.
  3. Money – savings for travel, food and emergencies, with knowledge of free services under JSSK and cash benefits under JSY and PMMVY.
  4. Blood donor – at least one or two relatives with a compatible blood group willing to donate.
  5. Decision-maker – who will decide and accompany her if she needs referral when her husband is away.
  6. Birth companion – a female relative or friend to support her in labour.
  7. Items for mother and baby – clean clothes, sanitary pads, soap, baby clothes, cap, socks and wraps.
  8. Documents – MCP card, ANC records, ID card and bank details.
  9. Knowledge of danger signs in pregnancy, labour and after birth, and of the signs of labour, so that she leaves home in time.
  10. Facility for emergencies – the nearest centre that can provide caesarean section and blood (FRU).

Micro-birth planning

  • An individual, written birth plan for each pregnant woman, prepared by the ANM and ASHA together with the woman and her family, usually by the seventh month.
  • It lists the EDD, risk status, blood group, chosen facility, transport arrangement, phone numbers of the ASHA, ANM and ambulance, and the escort, and is recorded in the MCP card and the sub-centre's due list.
  • The ASHA keeps a list of women due each month and checks the plan at home visits.
  • High-risk women are planned for delivery at an appropriate higher facility, sometimes with admission before labour.

Complication readiness at other levels

  • Community – emergency transport systems, community funds, blood donor lists, VHSNC support.
  • Facility – 24-hour skilled staff, drugs (oxytocin, magnesium sulphate, antibiotics), blood, equipment and referral linkages.

Role of the nurse-midwife

  • Discuss BPCR at every antenatal visit, involving the husband and mother-in-law.
  • Explain danger signs and how to act on them.
  • Help prepare and update the micro-birth plan, and follow up women close to their EDD.

Conclusion BPCR turns a pregnant woman's family into an active partner in safe motherhood. A clear micro-birth plan – where, how, with whom and with what money and blood – prevents delays and saves lives when complications occur.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: Explain the antenatal care of an Rh-negative mother, with anti-D prophylaxis.
answer_html:
Introduction When an Rh-negative woman carries an Rh-positive fetus (from an Rh-positive husband), fetal red cells entering her circulation may cause her to form anti-D antibodies (isoimmunisation). These IgG antibodies cross the placenta in a later pregnancy and destroy fetal red cells, causing haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn – anaemia, jaundice, hydrops and stillbirth. The first pregnancy is usually not affected. Isoimmunisation is largely preventable with anti-D immunoglobulin.

Sensitising events (fetomaternal haemorrhage) – delivery, abortion, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, antepartum haemorrhage, abdominal trauma, external cephalic version and manual removal of placenta.

1. Antenatal assessment

  • Blood group and Rh type of every woman at the first visit; if Rh-negative, check the husband's blood group (if he is also Rh-negative, the fetus is Rh-negative and there is no risk).
  • Indirect Coombs test (ICT) at the first visit to detect existing antibodies, and repeated at about 28 weeks.
  • History of previous pregnancies, anti-D received, affected babies, transfusions.

2. Unsensitised woman (ICT negative)

  • Antenatal prophylaxis – anti-D immunoglobulin 300 micrograms intramuscularly at 28 weeks where recommended and available.
  • After any sensitising event – anti-D within 72 hours: 50 micrograms before 12 weeks and 300 micrograms after 12 weeks.
  • After delivery – collect cord blood for the baby's blood group, Rh and direct Coombs test; if the baby is Rh-positive, give 300 micrograms anti-D within 72 hours of birth. This dose neutralises about 30 ml of fetal blood; a Kleihauer–Betke test measures a larger bleed (for example after abruption) so that more can be given.

3. Sensitised woman (ICT positive)

  • Refer to a specialist centre; anti-D is not useful once antibodies are present.
  • Antibody titres are repeated every 2–4 weeks; when they reach a critical level, the fetus is monitored for anaemia by middle cerebral artery Doppler and ultrasound for hydrops.
  • Severe fetal anaemia may need intrauterine transfusion; delivery is timed carefully; the newborn may need phototherapy or exchange transfusion.

4. Care in labour

  • Avoid unnecessary manipulation – no fundal pressure, gentle placental delivery, avoid manual removal unless essential.
  • Collect cord blood (for blood group, Coombs test, haemoglobin and bilirubin) and inform the paediatrician.

Role of the nurse

  • Identify every Rh-negative mother early and flag her record.
  • Explain the condition, the purpose of tests and anti-D in simple language, and obtain consent.
  • Store anti-D at 2–8°C (cold chain), check the label and expiry, give it deep intramuscularly (deltoid), and record the dose and batch number.
  • Advise the woman to keep a record and to inform health workers in every future pregnancy, abortion or transfusion.

Conclusion Careful blood grouping, ICT screening and timely anti-D prophylaxis after delivery and every sensitising event protect Rh-negative mothers from isoimmunisation and their future babies from haemolytic disease.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: Explain childbirth preparation (antenatal) classes – objectives, content, methods and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Fear of the unknown makes labour more painful and difficult. Childbirth preparation classes are structured group sessions that give pregnant women and their partners the knowledge, skills and confidence to cope with pregnancy, labour, birth and early parenthood.

Objectives

  • To reduce fear and anxiety and break the fear–tension–pain cycle described by Grantly Dick-Read.
  • To teach coping skills for labour – breathing, relaxation, positions and massage.
  • To help women make informed choices and develop a birth plan.
  • To prepare for breastfeeding, newborn care and parenthood.
  • To involve the husband or birth companion as an active supporter.

Organisation

  • Small groups of about 8–12 women with their partners, usually 4–8 weekly sessions from about 28–32 weeks.
  • Held in antenatal clinics, Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, hospitals or community halls, at a convenient time.
  • Conducted by nurse-midwives, with doctors, dietitians and physiotherapists as resource persons.

Content

  1. Changes of pregnancy, nutrition, rest, exercise and minor disorders.
  2. Danger signs and birth preparedness.
  3. Signs of labour – show, regular painful contractions, leaking of fluid – and when to go to hospital.
  4. Stages of labour and what happens in the labour room – examinations, monitoring and common procedures.
  5. Coping with labour pain – slow deep breathing, patterned breathing, relaxation, massage, warm compresses, walking, upright positions, birth ball.
  6. Birthing positions and pushing in the second stage.
  7. Role of the birth companion.
  8. Pain relief options and reasons for interventions such as caesarean section.
  9. Breastfeeding – early initiation, positioning and attachment.
  10. Newborn care, postnatal care, emotional changes and baby blues, family planning.
  11. A tour of the labour room to make it familiar.

Approaches to childbirth preparation

  • Dick-Read method (natural childbirth) – education and relaxation to remove fear.
  • Lamaze method (psychoprophylaxis) – conditioned responses: focused attention and patterned breathing during contractions.
  • Bradley method – husband-coached childbirth with deep abdominal breathing.
  • Hypnobirthing, yoga and prenatal exercise – relaxation, visualisation and controlled breathing.

Methods of teaching – short talks with discussion, demonstration and return demonstration, videos, charts, models and dolls, role play, practice sessions and sharing by mothers who have recently delivered.

Benefits – less fear and anxiety, better coping, fewer requests for unnecessary interventions, greater satisfaction with birth, more successful breastfeeding and active participation of fathers.

Role of the nurse

  • Plan sessions according to the needs, language and culture of the group.
  • Create a friendly, interactive atmosphere and encourage questions.
  • Teach and supervise practice of breathing, relaxation and positions.
  • Evaluate learning and continue support in the labour room.

Conclusion Childbirth preparation classes replace fear with knowledge and skill. They empower women and their partners to take an active part in birth, making labour safer and the experience more positive.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is Naegele's rule?
tags: add nine months and seven days
answer_html:
• Naegele's rule is used to calculate the expected date of delivery (EDD) from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP).
  • EDD = LMP + 9 calendar months + 7 days (or LMP − 3 months + 7 days + 1 year), which gives about 280 days.
  • Example – LMP 10 March 2026 → EDD 17 December 2026.
  • It assumes a regular 28-day cycle; for longer cycles, the extra days are added. Only a few women deliver on the exact EDD; most deliver within two weeks of it. An early ultrasound (crown–rump length) is more accurate when the LMP is uncertain.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is the obstetric score (GTPAL)?
answer_html:
• The obstetric score summarises a woman's past and present pregnancies, commonly written as GTPAL:
    • G – Gravida: total number of pregnancies, including the present one.
    • T – Term births (at or after 37 weeks).
    • P – Preterm births (after the age of viability but before 37 weeks).
    • A – Abortions (pregnancy losses before viability).
    • L – Living children.
  • Example – a woman pregnant for the fourth time who has had one term birth, one preterm birth and one abortion, with two living children, is G4 T1 P1 A1 L2.
  • Twins count as one pregnancy for gravida but as two for living children.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is supine hypotensive syndrome?
answer_html:
• Supine hypotensive syndrome (aortocaval compression) occurs in late pregnancy when a woman lies flat on her back: the heavy uterus compresses the inferior vena cava (and aorta), reducing venous return and cardiac output.
  • Features – a fall in blood pressure, faintness, dizziness, pallor, sweating, nausea and a change in pulse; placental blood flow falls and the fetus may become hypoxic.
  • Management and prevention – turn the woman immediately to her left side; avoid the flat supine position; use a wedge under the right hip (left uterine displacement) during examinations, procedures and caesarean section.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is lightening?
answer_html:
• Lightening is the descent of the presenting part into the pelvis (engagement of the head) during the last two to three weeks of pregnancy in a primigravida, so that the uterus sinks down.
  • The mother feels lighter – breathing and heartburn improve because pressure on the diaphragm and stomach is reduced.
  • At the same time she may notice increased frequency of micturition, pelvic pressure and leg cramps.
  • The fundal height falls to about the 32-week level. In multiparae it may occur only at the onset of labour. It is one of the signs of approaching labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is the double marker test?
answer_html:
• The double marker test is a first-trimester maternal blood screening test, done at 11–14 weeks, that measures free β-hCG and pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A).
  • Combined with the nuchal translucency ultrasound and the mother's age, it calculates the risk of chromosomal anomalies such as Down syndrome (trisomy 21) and trisomy 18; in Down syndrome β-hCG tends to be high and PAPP-A low.
  • It is a screening test, not a diagnosis – a "high-risk" result is followed by counselling and a diagnostic test (chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis).

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: List the danger signs in pregnancy.
answer_html:
• Vaginal bleeding at any stage of pregnancy.
  • Severe headache, blurred vision, or pain in the upper abdomen.
  • Convulsions (fits) or loss of consciousness.
  • Swelling of the face and hands.
  • High fever, with or without foul-smelling discharge.
  • Severe abdominal pain.
  • Leaking or gush of watery fluid from the vagina.
  • Reduced or absent fetal movements.
  • Breathlessness, palpitations or severe weakness and pallor.
  • Persistent vomiting, or labour pains before 37 weeks.
  • Any of these needs immediate transfer to a health facility; the family should keep the 102/108 ambulance number and the birth plan ready.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Management of Normal Pregnancy (Antenatal Care)
question: What is the Mother and Child Protection (MCP) card?
answer_html:
• The MCP card is a joint card of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the Ministry of Women and Child Development, given to every pregnant woman at registration and kept by her.
  • It records her antenatal check-ups, investigations, Td, IFA, risk status, birth plan, delivery and postnatal care, and the newborn's and child's care – immunisation, growth monitoring charts, feeding and development milestones.
  • It also gives health messages, danger signs and information on entitlements (JSY, JSSK, PMMVY).
  • It links services of ASHAs, ANMs, anganwadi workers and facilities, and must be carried to every visit.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: (a) Define normal labour and list its stages with their duration. (3 marks) (b) Explain the physiology of the first stage of labour. (6 marks) (c) Explain the monitoring of the first stage with the WHO Labour Care Guide and the evidence-based care of a woman in the first stage. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: WHO Labour Care Guide – seven sections
labels: Section 1 identifying information and labour characteristics at admission; Section 2 supportive care (companion
posture); Section 3 care of the baby (baseline FHR
moulding); Section 4 care of the woman (pulse
descent O); Section 6 medication; Section 7 shared decision-making (assessment and plan); an "alert" column beside each parameter

answer_html:
(a) Definition and stages of labour (3 marks)

Labour is the series of events by which the fetus, placenta and membranes are expelled from the uterus through the birth canal.

Normal labour (eutocia) is labour that:

  • begins spontaneously at term (37–42 completed weeks);
  • has the fetus in vertex presentation;
  • ends with the spontaneous birth of a live baby without undue prolongation or artificial aids;
  • has no complications for the mother or the baby.

Stages of labour and their duration

Stage From – To Usual duration (WHO 2018)
First stage Onset of true labour to full dilatation of the cervix (10 cm) Latent phase (regular painful contractions with cervical change up to 5 cm) – variable and may last many hours; active phase (5 cm to full dilatation) – usually up to 12 hours in a first labour and 10 hours in later labours
Second stage Full dilatation to birth of the baby Usually up to 3 hours in a first labour and 2 hours in later labours
Third stage Birth of the baby to expulsion of the placenta and membranes About 5–30 minutes; shorter with active management
Fourth stage First 1 hour (up to 2 hours) after delivery of the placenta A period of close observation of mother and baby

(b) Physiology of the first stage (6 marks)

1. Uterine contractions – the primary power

  • Involuntary and intermittent – periods of contraction alternate with relaxation, which restores blood flow to the placenta.
  • Painful – pain is due to hypoxia of the contracting muscle and stretching of the cervix and lower segment; it is felt in the back and lower abdomen and radiates to the thighs.
  • Fundal dominance – each contraction starts near the cornua (pacemaker areas), spreads downwards, and is strongest and longest at the fundus, so the fetus is pushed downwards.
  • Polarity – the upper segment contracts and retracts actively, while the lower segment and cervix relax and dilate; this co-ordination is essential for progress.
  • Progressive – contractions become more frequent, longer and stronger; in the active phase there are usually 3–5 contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 40–60 seconds.

2. Retraction

  • A unique property of uterine muscle: after each contraction the fibres do not return to their original length but remain a little shorter.
  • The upper segment therefore becomes progressively thicker and shorter, its cavity smaller, while the lower segment becomes thinner and longer.
  • Retraction maintains the progress gained by each contraction and, after delivery, closes the blood vessels of the placental site.

3. Formation of the lower uterine segment and retraction ring

  • The isthmus and upper cervix are stretched and thinned to form the lower uterine segment.
  • The junction between the thick upper and thin lower segment is the physiological retraction ring; in obstructed labour it rises and becomes visible as a pathological (Bandl's) ring.

4. Effacement (taking up) of the cervix

  • The cervical canal is drawn upwards and merges with the lower segment until the cervix is paper-thin.
  • In a primigravida effacement precedes dilatation; in a multigravida both occur together.

5. Dilatation of the cervix

  • The cervix opens from closed to full dilatation (10 cm), wide enough for the head to pass.
  • Causes – pull of the retracting upper segment, the hydrostatic wedge of the bag of forewaters and, after rupture of the membranes, direct pressure of the well-applied presenting part.

6. Formation of the bag of forewaters

  • As the lower segment stretches, the membranes separate from it; the fluid in front of the head (forewaters) is cut off from the hindwaters by the head fitting into the lower segment.
  • The bag bulges through the cervix with each contraction and helps dilatation. Membranes usually rupture near full dilatation.

7. Show – a blood-stained mucus discharge formed by the expelled mucus plug and blood from small decidual vessels torn as the membranes separate; a sign of the onset of labour.

8. Descent and flexion – with each contraction the fetus is pushed down by fundal pressure transmitted along its spine (fetal axis pressure); the head flexes further as it meets resistance.

9. Changes in mother and fetus – cardiac output and blood pressure rise with each contraction, breathing quickens, and gut activity slows; placental blood flow falls briefly during each contraction, which a healthy fetus tolerates well.

(c) Monitoring with the Labour Care Guide and evidence-based care (6 marks)

WHO Labour Care Guide (LCG) The LCG (WHO, 2020) replaced the traditional partograph. It is started when a woman is in the active first stage (5 cm or more), whatever her parity, and continues to the end of the second stage. Instead of a fixed 1 cm/hour alert line, it uses evidence-based time limits at each centimetre and an "alert" column for every observation.

Section What is recorded Alert values (examples)
1. Identifying information and labour characteristics Name, parity, onset of labour, time of active labour diagnosis and rupture of membranes, risk factors –
2. Supportive care Companion, pain relief, oral fluid, posture "N" (not provided) for companion, pain relief or oral fluid; supine posture
3. Care of the baby Baseline FHR, decelerations, amniotic fluid, fetal position, caput, moulding FHR below 110 or 160 and above; late decelerations; thick meconium or blood; posterior or transverse position; caput or moulding +++
4. Care of the woman Pulse, systolic and diastolic BP, temperature, urine protein and acetone Pulse below 60 or 120 and above; systolic BP below 80 or 140 and above; diastolic BP 90 or above; temperature below 35°C or 37.5°C and above
5. Labour progress Contractions per 10 minutes and their duration; cervical dilatation (X); descent (O) Contractions 2 or fewer, or more than 5, in 10 minutes; duration under 20 or over 60 seconds; no progress for 6 hours at 5 cm, 5 hours at 6 cm, 3 hours at 7 cm, 2.5 hours at 8 cm, 2 hours at 9 cm; second stage 3 hours or more (first labour) or 2 hours or more (later labours)
6. Medication Oxytocin, other medicines, IV fluids –
7. Shared decision-making Assessment and plan, agreed with the woman –

Any alert value is circled, the senior midwife or doctor is informed, and the assessment and action are recorded.

Frequency of observations in the active first stage

  • Fetal heart rate by intermittent auscultation (Pinard or Doppler) every 15–30 minutes, for a full minute after a contraction.
  • Contractions every 30 minutes.
  • Vaginal examination about every 4 hours (or earlier if there is a clinical need), with consent and privacy.
  • Pulse, blood pressure and temperature about every 4 hours (more often if abnormal); urine each time it is passed.
  • Supportive care checked regularly.

Evidence-based care in the first stage (WHO 2018 recommendations)

  1. Respectful maternity care – dignity, privacy, consent, no verbal or physical abuse.
  2. Effective communication – explain progress and plans in simple words; involve her in decisions.
  3. A companion of her choice throughout labour.
  4. Admission – women in the latent phase can often be cared for at home or in an antenatal area with reassurance and follow-up, which avoids unnecessary interventions.
  5. Admission assessment – history, MCP card, vital signs, abdominal palpation, fetal heart and vaginal examination; use the Safe Childbirth Checklist.
  6. Oral fluids and light food for low-risk women; avoid routine IV fluids.
  7. Mobility and upright positions of her choice – walking, sitting, kneeling, birth ball; avoid lying flat on the back.
  8. Pain relief according to her wishes – relaxation and breathing techniques, massage and warm packs; epidural or opioid analgesia where available.
  9. Bladder care – encourage her to pass urine every 2 hours.
  10. Infection prevention – hand hygiene, limited vaginal examinations, clean surroundings.
  11. Practices NOT recommended routinely – pubic shaving, enema, routine CTG on admission for low-risk women, vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine, routine amniotomy or early oxytocin to speed labour, antispasmodics, and routine antibiotics.
  12. Act on alerts – for example, an FHR below 110 needs repositioning, assessment for cord problems, review of contractions and urgent help.
  13. Prepare for birth – delivery tray, warm newborn corner, working bag-and-mask, oxytocin ready, and a trained person available.

Nursing importance The first stage is the longest part of labour and the period when most problems – prolonged labour, fetal distress, infection, rising blood pressure – first appear. Through regular monitoring on the LCG, prompt response to alerts and kind, continuous support, the midwife can keep labour normal, intervene only when needed and give the woman a positive childbirth experience.

Conclusion Normal labour begins spontaneously at term with a vertex presentation and ends in a spontaneous birth without complications. In the first stage, co-ordinated contractions with fundal dominance and retraction efface and dilate the cervix, helped by the bag of forewaters. Monitoring with the WHO Labour Care Guide and evidence-based, respectful care – companion, mobility, fluids, pain relief and avoidance of unnecessary interventions – make the first stage safe for mother and baby.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: (a) Explain the factors involved in labour (passage, passenger and powers). (4 marks) (b) Describe the mechanism of normal labour in the left occipito-anterior position. (11 marks)

diagram.caption: Cardinal movements of labour in LOA position
labels: eight panels – engagement (sagittal suture in the right oblique diameter) → descent → flexion → internal rotation (occiput rotates one-eighth of a circle anteriorly to lie behind the symphysis) → crowning and extension (occiput pivots under the pubic arch
face sweeps over the perineum) → restitution (occiput turns to the left) → internal rotation of shoulders with external rotation of head → expulsion of shoulders and trunk by lateral flexion

answer_html:
Introduction The mechanism of labour is the series of passive movements of the fetus – mainly its head – by which it adapts itself to the changing shape and size of the birth canal and passes through it with the least resistance. Knowing it allows the midwife to understand what she feels on examination, to assist birth correctly and to recognise abnormal labour.

(a) Factors involved in labour (4 marks) The outcome of labour depends on the interaction of the "three Ps" – passage, passenger and powers – together with the mother's position and psychological state.

1. Passage (birth canal)

  • Bony pelvis – its size, shape (gynaecoid is ideal) and diameters. The inlet is widest transversely and the outlet anteroposteriorly, which makes rotation of the head necessary.
  • Soft tissues – the lower uterine segment, cervix, vagina, pelvic floor (levator ani) and perineum. The gutter-shaped pelvic floor directs the leading part forward, causing internal rotation.

2. Passenger (fetus and placenta)

  • Size of the fetus and especially of the head, its attitude (flexion presents the smallest diameters), lie, presentation and position, ability of the skull to mould, and the number of fetuses.
  • Position and health of the placenta (for example, placenta praevia obstructs the passage).

3. Powers

  • Primary powers – involuntary uterine contractions with fundal dominance and retraction, which efface and dilate the cervix and push the fetus down.
  • Secondary powers – in the second stage, voluntary bearing down by the diaphragm and abdominal muscles.

4. Position of the mother – upright and lateral positions use gravity, improve contractions and enlarge the pelvic outlet.

5. Psyche – fear and anxiety release catecholamines that can weaken contractions; support and confidence help labour.

(b) Mechanism of normal labour in the LOA position (11 marks)

Position before labour

  • Lie – longitudinal; presentation – vertex; attitude – flexed; denominator – occiput.
  • Position LOA – the occiput is directed towards the left iliopectineal eminence, the sinciput towards the right sacroiliac joint.
  • The sagittal suture lies in the right oblique diameter of the pelvic inlet (or in the transverse diameter).
  • Presenting diameters – suboccipitofrontal (10 cm), becoming suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm) with good flexion, and biparietal (9.5 cm).

Cardinal movements These movements overlap and occur together with continuous descent.

1. Engagement

  • The biparietal diameter passes through the pelvic brim.
  • In a primigravida this usually occurs in the last weeks of pregnancy; in a multigravida at the onset of labour or during it.
  • The head usually engages in synclitism, with slight anterior asynclitism being common.

2. Descent

  • Continues throughout labour; it is slow in the first stage and faster in the second stage.
  • Caused by uterine contractions and retraction, fundal pressure on the breech transmitted along the fetal spine, the bearing-down efforts of the mother in the second stage, and, to a small extent, the forewaters.

3. Flexion

  • As the descending head meets resistance from the cervix, the pelvic walls and the pelvic floor, its flexion increases – the chin approaches the chest.
  • Lever theory – the head is attached to the spine nearer the occiput, so it acts as a lever with a short posterior arm and a long anterior arm; resistance pushes the longer anterior arm up and the occiput down.
  • The presenting diameter changes from the suboccipitofrontal (10 cm) to the suboccipitobregmatic (9.5 cm), and the posterior fontanelle becomes the leading part.

4. Internal rotation of the head

  • When the occiput (the leading part) reaches the pelvic floor, it rotates forwards through one-eighth of a circle (45°), from the left anterior position to lie behind the symphysis pubis (direct occipito-anterior).
  • The sagittal suture now lies in the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet, which is the largest diameter at that level.
  • Causes – the gutter-shaped, forward-sloping pelvic floor (levator ani) directs the leading part forwards; the shape of the pelvis and good flexion help. The general rule is that whichever part of the fetus first meets the pelvic floor rotates forward.
  • The neck is twisted by one-eighth of a circle because the shoulders remain in the oblique diameter.
  • Internal rotation usually occurs late in the first stage or in the second stage, especially in a primigravida.

5. Crowning

  • The head distends the vulva; when the biparietal diameter passes through the vulval ring and the head no longer recedes between contractions, it is said to be crowned.

6. Extension

  • The suboccipital region (nape) pivots under the pubic arch, and the head is born by extension – the occiput, vertex, forehead, face and chin sweep in turn over the perineum.
  • The force is the resultant of the downward push of the uterus and the upward and forward resistance of the pelvic floor.
  • This is the moment of greatest stretching of the perineum, when tears are most likely.

7. Restitution

  • Once the head is born, the twist of the neck undoes itself – the head turns back one-eighth of a circle in the direction from which it came, so that the occiput turns towards the mother's left side (in LOA).
  • Restitution restores the normal relation between the head and the shoulders; its direction tells the original position.

8. Internal rotation of the shoulders

  • The shoulders enter the pelvis in the left oblique diameter. The anterior (right) shoulder, reaching the pelvic floor first, rotates forwards one-eighth of a circle to lie behind the symphysis.
  • The bisacromial diameter (12 cm) now lies in the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet.

9. External rotation of the head

  • At the same time, the born head rotates a further one-eighth of a circle in the same direction as restitution; the occiput faces the mother's left thigh and the face her right thigh.

10. Expulsion (birth of the shoulders and trunk)

  • The anterior shoulder is born first, from under the symphysis pubis; the posterior shoulder is born over the perineum by lateral flexion of the trunk.
  • The rest of the body follows easily by lateral flexion along the curve of the birth canal (curve of Carus).

Mechanism in other positions (brief)

  • ROA – the same movements on the opposite side; the sagittal suture engages in the left oblique diameter and restitution is to the right.
  • Occipitoposterior positions – the occiput usually makes a long rotation of three-eighths of a circle forwards and delivers normally, but labour is longer; if the occiput rotates backwards, the baby is born "face to pubis" (persistent occipitoposterior), with more perineal trauma; arrest may occur (deep transverse arrest).

Role of the midwife during the mechanism

  1. Encourage upright or lateral positions and pushing with the woman's own urge, which helps descent and rotation.
  2. During crowning, keep the head flexed with gentle pressure on the occiput and control the speed of extension, delivering the head slowly between contractions to protect the perineum.
  3. Wait for restitution and external rotation; do not rotate the head forcibly.
  4. Deliver the anterior shoulder by gentle downward traction and the posterior shoulder by upward traction, then the trunk by lateral flexion.
  5. Observe the direction of restitution to confirm the position; recognise delay (for example, in occipitoposterior positions or shoulder dystocia) and call for help.

How the midwife recognises each movement clinically

  • Engagement – only two-fifths or less of the head palpable abdominally; leading part near the ischial spines on vaginal examination.
  • Flexion – the small posterior fontanelle is felt near the centre of the pelvis and the anterior fontanelle is out of reach.
  • Internal rotation – the sagittal suture moves from the oblique to the anteroposterior diameter, with the posterior fontanelle behind the symphysis.
  • Crowning and extension – the head stays visible between contractions, then the face sweeps over the perineum.
  • Restitution – the born head turns towards the mother's left thigh in LOA (right in ROA), confirming the position.
  • External rotation – the head turns further in the same direction as the shoulders rotate inside.

Factors that disturb the normal mechanism

  • Deflexion of the head and occipitoposterior positions.
  • An android or flat pelvis and a rigid pelvic floor.
  • Weak or incoordinate contractions, an exhausted mother or a full bladder.
  • A large baby, and epidural analgesia that relaxes the pelvic floor (rotation may be delayed).

When these are present, the midwife expects delay, monitors closely on the Labour Care Guide, encourages upright or all-fours positions and calls for medical help early.

Nursing importance Every vaginal examination finding – position of the sagittal suture, the fontanelle felt, flexion and station – makes sense only in the light of the mechanism of labour. Understanding these movements allows the midwife to assist the birth gently, prevent perineal tears and sudden compression of the fetal head, and detect malpositions and obstruction early.

Conclusion In LOA position the fetal head engages with the sagittal suture in the right oblique diameter, descends, flexes, rotates one-eighth of a circle forwards on the pelvic floor, crowns and is born by extension. It then restitutes and rotates externally as the shoulders rotate, and the shoulders and trunk are born by lateral flexion. These movements are the fetus's adaptation to the shape of the pelvis, and the midwife's skill lies in supporting rather than forcing them.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: (a) Explain the physiology and the signs of the second stage of labour. (4 marks) (b) Describe the management of the second stage of labour, including the conduct of a normal delivery. (8 marks) (c) Explain the immediate care of the mother and the newborn at birth. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Steps in conducting a normal delivery
labels: maintain flexion and support the perineum → slow birth of the head between contractions → feel for cord around the neck → wait for restitution and external rotation → gentle downward traction for the anterior shoulder → upward traction for the posterior shoulder → birth of trunk by lateral flexion → baby dried and placed skin-to-skin on the mother's abdomen

answer_html:
(a) Physiology and signs of the second stage (4 marks)

The second stage begins with full dilatation of the cervix and ends with the birth of the baby.

Physiology

  • Contractions become stronger, longer (60–90 seconds) and more frequent (every 2–3 minutes).
  • Two phases
    • Propulsive (passive) phase – from full dilatation until the head reaches the pelvic floor; the woman may not yet feel an urge to push.
    • Expulsive (active) phase – when the head presses on the pelvic floor, stretch receptors trigger the Ferguson reflex, releasing more oxytocin and producing an involuntary urge to bear down.
  • Secondary powers – the woman takes a breath, closes the glottis and contracts the diaphragm and abdominal muscles, adding to the force of the uterus.
  • Changes in the soft tissues – the vagina becomes a wide tube continuous with the uterus; the levator ani is pushed down and sideways; the perineum is stretched and thinned; the anus dilates and pouts; the vulva gapes.
  • Membranes rupture if they have not already done so.
  • Fetal changes – the head completes internal rotation, moulds, may develop caput, and is born by extension.

Signs of the second stage

  1. Urge to bear down with each contraction – often the first sign.
  2. Stronger, expulsive contractions, sometimes with grunting.
  3. Increased show and often rupture of the membranes with a gush of fluid.
  4. Bulging and thinning of the perineum, gaping of the anus and sometimes passage of a little stool.
  5. Gaping of the vulva and appearance of the presenting part at the introitus.
  6. Vomiting, restlessness or a change in behaviour.
  7. Confirmation – vaginal examination shows no cervix palpable (full dilatation).

Duration – usually up to 3 hours in a first labour and 2 hours in later labours (WHO 2018); it may be longer with epidural analgesia. Progress is judged by descent of the head, not by the clock alone.

(b) Management of the second stage and conduct of normal delivery (8 marks)

1. Preparation

  • Delivery area – clean, private and warm (25–28°C); the newborn corner ready with a radiant warmer switched on, pre-warmed towels, a cap, self-inflating bag and masks (sizes 0 and 1), a suction device, cord clamps and a sterile blade.
  • Sterile delivery tray – gloves, gown, two artery forceps, cord-cutting scissors, cord clamp, gauze, kidney tray, perineal pads, and episiotomy and suturing materials kept ready.
  • Oxytocin 10 IU drawn up in a syringe for the third stage.
  • Hand hygiene and personal protective equipment (apron, gloves, eye protection).
  • Use the "just before pushing" pause point of the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist.
  • Keep the birth companion with her and an assistant available.

2. Care during the second stage

  • Position of her choice – semi-sitting, side-lying, squatting, kneeling or on all fours; avoid lying flat on the back.
  • Pushing – encourage her to push when she feels the urge, in her own way; avoid prolonged, forced breath-holding (directed Valsalva) pushing. With an epidural, pushing can be delayed for 1–2 hours if mother and baby are well.
  • Fetal heart checked every 5 minutes (after each contraction); maternal pulse and BP regularly; contractions and descent observed.
  • Encouragement and comfort – praise, wipe her face, give sips of water, keep the bladder empty.
  • Perineal protection – warm compresses and perineal massage in the late second stage, and a "hands-on" technique to support the perineum and control the head.
  • Episiotomy only when indicated (not routine), and no fundal pressure to push the baby out.

3. Conduct of normal delivery (vertex)

  1. When the head distends the perineum, clean the vulva and perineum from front to back and place a sterile pad under the buttocks.
  2. Delivery of the head
    • Place the fingers of one hand gently on the vertex to maintain flexion and prevent sudden extension, and support the perineum with the other hand over a pad.
    • As the head crowns, ask the woman to stop pushing and to pant or breathe quickly, so that the head is born slowly between contractions, the occiput first, then the face and chin.
    • Routine suction of the mouth and nose is not needed for a baby who is breathing well with clear liquor.
  3. Check for the cord around the neck – if loose, slip it over the head; if tight, clamp it in two places and cut between the clamps.
  4. Wait for restitution and external rotation with the next contraction.
  5. Delivery of the shoulders – with both hands on the sides of the head, apply gentle downward traction to deliver the anterior shoulder under the symphysis, then gentle upward traction to deliver the posterior shoulder over the perineum.
  6. Delivery of the trunk – the body follows by lateral flexion towards the mother's abdomen; support the baby firmly (it is slippery).
  7. Note the time of birth and sex, and place the baby on the mother's abdomen, skin-to-skin.
  8. Palpate the abdomen to exclude another baby and give oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly within one minute (active management of the third stage).
  9. Clamp and cut the cord after 1–3 minutes (delayed cord clamping), unless the baby needs resuscitation – then cut it at once and resuscitate.
  10. Inspect the perineum and vagina for tears after delivery of the placenta.

4. Records – time of full dilatation, birth, sex, birth weight (after the first feed), condition at birth, drugs given and any complications, entered in the delivery register, LCG and MCP card.

(c) Immediate care of the mother and newborn (3 marks)

Newborn – essential newborn care

  1. Dry the baby thoroughly immediately (head, body, limbs) and remove the wet towel; this also stimulates breathing.
  2. Assess breathing – a baby who is crying or breathing well stays with the mother; a baby who is not breathing is moved to the warmer, the airway cleared and bag-and-mask ventilation started within the "golden minute".
  3. Keep warm – skin-to-skin contact, cap and covering with a dry cloth; delay bathing.
  4. Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour.
  5. Cord care – clamp, cut with a sterile instrument and keep the cord clean and dry.
  6. Identification band, APGAR score at 1 and 5 minutes, vitamin K injection, weight after the first feed, a quick check for malformations and birth injuries, and birth-dose vaccines before discharge.

Mother

  1. Complete the third stage with AMTSL and check the placenta for completeness.
  2. Examine and repair any tears, estimate blood loss, check the uterus is firm.
  3. Check pulse, BP and bladder; clean her, give a fresh pad, dry clothing, a warm drink and rest.
  4. Keep mother and baby together and observe both closely in the fourth stage.

Evidence-based measures to prevent perineal trauma

  • Warm compresses on the perineum and perineal massage with a lubricant during the late second stage.
  • Controlled, slow delivery of the head between contractions, with the mother panting rather than pushing at crowning.
  • Hands-on support of the perineum and flexion of the head.
  • Positions that reduce tears, such as side-lying; avoiding the lithotomy position where possible.
  • Restrictive episiotomy – only for clear indications.
  • Delivering the shoulders one at a time, without hurrying.

When to call for help in the second stage

  • No descent after an hour of good pushing, or the second stage exceeding the expected limits.
  • Fetal heart rate below 110 or above 160, or late decelerations.
  • Thick meconium or fresh bleeding.
  • The head delivers but retracts against the perineum ("turtle sign") – suspect shoulder dystocia; call for help and begin the emergency manoeuvres.
  • Maternal exhaustion, rising pulse or BP, or convulsions.

Early recognition and help – for instrumental delivery, caesarean section or newborn resuscitation – prevent birth injury and asphyxia.

Nursing importance The second stage is the shortest but most demanding stage – for the mother, the baby and the midwife. Supportive coaching, a position of the woman's choice, gentle control of the head and perineum and readiness for newborn resuscitation prevent perineal injury, fetal hypoxia and birth asphyxia, and make the moment of birth safe and joyful.

Conclusion The second stage begins with full dilatation and ends with birth; the urge to push, bulging perineum and appearance of the head are its signs. Good management combines preparation, an upright or lateral position, spontaneous pushing, fetal heart monitoring, perineal protection and a controlled delivery of the head, shoulders and trunk, followed immediately by drying, skin-to-skin contact, delayed cord clamping, oxytocin for the mother and early breastfeeding.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: (a) Explain the physiology of the third stage of labour – placental separation, descent, expulsion and control of bleeding. (6 marks) (b) Explain the signs of placental separation and the management of the third stage of labour, with emphasis on active management (AMTSL). (9 marks)
tags: oxytocin 10 IU IM within one minute

diagram.caption: Placental separation and controlled cord traction
labels: (1) Schultze (central) separation – retroplacental clot at the centre
placenta descending fetal surface first with membranes inverted; (2) Matthews Duncan (marginal) separation – separation from the edge with external bleeding
maternal surface sliding down; (3) controlled cord traction – one hand holding the clamped cord with steady downward traction
the other hand above the symphysis pushing the uterus upwards (counter-traction)

answer_html:
Introduction The third stage begins with the birth of the baby and ends with the expulsion of the placenta and membranes. It is the most dangerous stage for the mother – postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), the leading direct cause of maternal death in India, starts here. Correct management of this stage is therefore one of the most important skills of a midwife.

(a) Physiology of the third stage (6 marks)

1. Separation of the placenta

  • After the baby is born, the uterus contracts and retracts strongly; its cavity becomes small and the area of the placental site is reduced to about half.
  • The placenta cannot contract, so it buckles and shears off from the uterine wall through the spongy layer of the decidua basalis.
  • Bleeding from the torn maternal sinuses behind the placenta forms a retroplacental clot, which helps to complete separation.
  • Separation usually occurs with the first one or two contractions after birth, within a few minutes.

Methods of separation

Feature Central (Schultze) method Marginal (Matthews Duncan) method
Separation begins At the centre At the margin (edge)
Retroplacental clot Forms behind the placenta Little clot; blood escapes
Placenta appears at the vulva Fetal surface first – shiny, with membranes inverted like an umbrella and the clot inside Maternal surface first – rough, sliding down sideways
Visible bleeding before expulsion Little More
Frequency Commoner Less common; more risk of retained membranes and bleeding

2. Separation of the membranes – the membranes are peeled off the uterine wall by the contractions and by the weight of the descending placenta.

3. Descent – the separated placenta is pushed by contractions into the lower uterine segment and upper vagina; the fundus rises and the cord lengthens outside the vulva.

4. Expulsion – the placenta is expelled by the mother's bearing-down efforts, by gravity in upright positions, or by controlled cord traction in active management.

5. Control of bleeding (haemostasis) – blood flow to the placental site at term is about 500–750 ml per minute, so bleeding must be stopped quickly:

  1. "Living ligatures" – the interlacing oblique (middle-layer) muscle fibres contract and retract around the blood vessels, kinking and compressing them. This is the most important mechanism, which is why a well-contracted uterus is essential.
  2. Apposition of the uterine walls once the uterus is empty.
  3. Coagulation – the increased clotting factors of pregnancy promote rapid thrombosis of the open sinuses at the placental site.

Normal blood loss – up to about 250–300 ml; a loss of 500 ml or more after vaginal birth is PPH.

(b) Signs of placental separation and management of the third stage (9 marks)

Signs of placental separation

  1. The uterus becomes firm, globular and smaller, and rises in the abdomen, often deviating to the right; it becomes mobile.
  2. Permanent lengthening of the cord outside the vulva – when the uterus is pushed gently upwards from above the symphysis, the cord does not recede if the placenta has separated.
  3. A sudden gush of blood from the vagina (especially with marginal separation).
  4. A suprapubic bulge caused by the placenta in the lower segment.

Methods of management

1. Expectant (physiological) management

  • The midwife waits for the signs of separation and for the placenta to be expelled by the mother's efforts or gravity, without a prophylactic uterotonic or cord traction.
  • It is associated with more blood loss and PPH, and is used only for low-risk women who choose it after counselling, with a uterotonic ready.

2. Active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) – recommended for every woman

Component 1 – Uterotonic drug within one minute of birth

  • After excluding another baby, give oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly (into the thigh) within one minute of the birth of the baby.
  • Oxytocin is the drug of choice; keep it in the cold chain (2–8°C).
  • Alternatives – heat-stable carbetocin where available; misoprostol 600 micrograms orally when oxytocin is not available (for example, in home births); ergometrine only if there is no hypertension or heart disease.

Component 2 – Delayed cord clamping and controlled cord traction (CCT)

  • Clamp and cut the cord 1–3 minutes after birth, unless resuscitation is needed.
  • Controlled cord traction (by a skilled attendant):
    1. Hold the clamped cord close to the perineum with one hand.
    2. Place the other hand just above the symphysis pubis and push the uterus gently upwards (counter-traction) – this prevents inversion of the uterus (the Brandt–Andrews method).
    3. During a contraction, apply steady, gentle downward traction on the cord, following the curve of the birth canal.
    4. If the placenta does not descend within 30–40 seconds, stop, wait for the next contraction and repeat.
    5. As the placenta reaches the vulva, hold it with both hands and turn it gently so that the membranes twist into a rope and come out intact; artery forceps may be used to ease out trailing membranes.
  • Never pull the cord without counter-traction or when the uterus is relaxed.

Component 3 – Uterine massage and monitoring of uterine tone

  • Immediately after delivery of the placenta, massage the uterus through the abdomen until it is firm.
  • Palpate the uterus every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours to make sure it remains contracted, and teach the mother to feel and rub it.

3. Examination of the placenta and membranes – check that the placenta and membranes are complete (no missing cotyledon or vessels running to a torn edge), count the cord vessels and note abnormalities. Incompleteness means retained tissue and a risk of PPH and infection.

4. Examination of the birth canal – inspect the perineum, vagina and, if bleeding continues, the cervix; repair tears and episiotomy.

5. Estimation and recording of blood loss – using a calibrated under-buttock drape or by weighing pads, rather than guessing; record the time of placental delivery, blood loss, drugs and findings.

6. Retained placenta – if the placenta is not delivered within 30 minutes of birth with active management: empty the bladder, repeat CCT; if still retained, start an IV line, call for help and arrange manual removal under anaesthesia (referral if necessary).

7. Precautions

  • Do not massage the uterus or pull the cord before a uterotonic has been given and the uterus has contracted.
  • No fundal pressure or squeezing of the uterus to expel the placenta.
  • Watch continuously for bleeding, pallor, rising pulse or falling BP.

8. Care after the third stage – clean the perineum, apply a sterile pad, make the mother comfortable and warm, keep the baby skin-to-skin and breastfeeding, and begin fourth-stage observation of pulse, BP, uterine tone, bleeding and bladder.

Complications of the third stage – PPH (atonic or traumatic), retained placenta or membranes, acute inversion of the uterus, shock and, rarely, amniotic fluid embolism.

Common errors in the third stage and their consequences

  • Delay in giving oxytocin or giving it before excluding a second twin – loss of the main protective effect, or trapping of the second baby.
  • Pulling the cord without counter-traction or before the uterus contracts – snapping of the cord, retained placenta or acute inversion of the uterus.
  • Kneading or squeezing the fundus before separation – partial separation and heavy bleeding.
  • Not examining the placenta – a retained cotyledon or succenturiate lobe is missed.
  • Guessing blood loss – PPH is recognised late.
  • Leaving the mother unobserved after the placenta is delivered.

Third stage in special situations

  • Home or sub-centre births where oxytocin cannot be kept cold – the ANM or ASHA gives misoprostol 600 micrograms orally immediately after the baby is born, as per government policy.
  • Rh-negative mother – collect cord blood for the baby's blood group and Coombs test before discarding the placenta.
  • Anaemic or high-risk women (previous PPH, twins, prolonged labour) – keep an IV line running, blood grouped and cross-matched, and oxytocin infusion ready.
  • HIV-positive mother – follow universal precautions and ensure the baby receives prophylaxis.

Nursing importance AMTSL is one of the most effective, low-cost interventions known to prevent PPH. The midwife who gives oxytocin within one minute, performs controlled cord traction correctly, keeps the uterus contracted, checks the placenta and measures blood loss accurately can prevent most third-stage deaths.

Conclusion In the third stage, retraction reduces the placental site, the placenta separates through the spongy decidua by the Schultze or Duncan method, and bleeding is controlled by the living ligatures, apposition of the uterine walls and clotting. Signs of separation include a rising, globular uterus, lengthening cord, a gush of blood and a suprapubic bulge. Active management – oxytocin within one minute, delayed cord clamping, controlled cord traction with counter-traction and uterine massage with regular checks of tone – is the standard of care for every woman.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: Explain the theories of the onset of labour and the signs of approaching labour.
answer_html:
Introduction The exact cause of the onset of labour in humans is not fully known. Labour probably begins when several hormonal, mechanical and fetal signals together change the uterus from a quiet, relaxed organ into an active, co-ordinated one, and the cervix from firm to soft (ripening).

Theories of onset of labour

  1. Uterine distension theory – increasing stretch of the uterine muscle near term increases its excitability, gap junctions and oxytocin receptors. This explains early labour in twins and polyhydramnios.
  2. Progesterone withdrawal – progesterone keeps the uterus quiet during pregnancy. Near term, its effect is reduced (a "functional" withdrawal, as blood levels do not fall sharply in humans), removing the block on contractions.
  3. Oestrogen theory – rising oestrogen and a higher oestrogen : progesterone ratio increase oxytocin receptors, gap junctions and prostaglandin production, and soften the cervix.
  4. Fetal role (fetal HPA axis) – the maturing fetal hypothalamus–pituitary–adrenal axis increases fetal cortisol and adrenal androgens; these increase placental oestrogen production, so the fetus helps to "decide" when it is ready to be born.
  5. Placental CRH ("placental clock") – corticotrophin-releasing hormone produced by the placenta rises steeply in the last weeks and stimulates prostaglandins and cortisol.
  6. Oxytocin theory – oxytocin levels change little, but oxytocin receptors in the myometrium increase greatly near term, making the uterus highly sensitive.
  7. Prostaglandin theory – prostaglandins E2 and F2α from the decidua and membranes ripen the cervix and stimulate contractions; this is why prostaglandins can induce labour.
  8. Mechanical (Ferguson) reflex – pressure of the presenting part on the cervix releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, reinforcing contractions.
  9. Inflammatory and immune factors – cytokines and white cells in the cervix and membranes contribute to ripening and the start of contractions.

Signs of approaching labour (pre-labour)

  • Lightening – the head sinks into the pelvis in primigravidae 2–3 weeks before labour; breathing becomes easier.
  • Increased frequency of micturition and pelvic pressure.
  • False labour pains – irregular Braxton Hicks contractions that become more noticeable.
  • Cervical ripening – the cervix becomes soft, shorter and begins to open.
  • Increased vaginal discharge; a show may appear.
  • Backache, slight loss of weight, and a sudden burst of energy ("nesting instinct").

Signs of the onset of true labour

  1. Regular, painful contractions that become stronger, longer and more frequent.
  2. Show – blood-stained mucus.
  3. Effacement and progressive dilatation of the cervix.
  4. Formation of the bag of forewaters; sometimes rupture of the membranes.

Nursing importance – the midwife teaches women the signs of labour and when to come to the facility, and distinguishes pre-labour from true labour to avoid unnecessary early admission and interventions.

Conclusion Labour begins through the combined effect of uterine stretch, changes in the oestrogen–progesterone balance, fetal signals, placental CRH, increased oxytocin sensitivity and prostaglandins. Lightening, false pains and cervical ripening announce its approach, while regular painful contractions with cervical change mark its true onset.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the organisation of a labour room.

diagram.caption: Layout of a standard labour room
labels: entrance → triage and examination area → labour-delivery-recovery (LDR) beds with curtains
each with a newborn care corner (radiant warmer
resuscitation kit) → central nursing station with view of all beds → post-delivery recovery area; side rooms for eclampsia
changing room and birth companion area

answer_html:
Introduction The labour room is where the lives of two people are at risk at the same time. A well-organised labour room ensures that every woman receives safe, respectful and evidence-based care, and that every emergency can be managed without delay. The Government of India's Labour Room Standardization Guidelines and the LaQshya programme give standards for its organisation.

1. Location

  • On the ground floor or easily accessible, with a ramp and clear signage.
  • Close to the operation theatre, blood storage unit and newborn care unit (SNCU/NBSU).
  • 24-hour water, electricity with back-up, and communication.

2. Layout (functional areas)

  • Triage area at the entrance – for rapid assessment and to sort women as normal or emergency.
  • Labour–delivery–recovery (LDR) beds – the woman labours, gives birth and recovers in the same bed, with curtains or partitions for privacy.
  • A newborn care corner beside each delivery bed – radiant warmer, bag and masks, suction, clock with second hand.
  • Nursing station placed to see all beds.
  • Post-delivery (recovery) area for fourth-stage observation.
  • Eclampsia room – quiet and dimly lit; septic room for women with infection.
  • Clean utility (sterile supplies), dirty utility and sluice, attached toilets, store, duty and changing rooms, and a waiting area for birth companions.
  • Room temperature 25–28°C; good lighting with a spotlight; handwashing stations with elbow-operated taps.

3. Equipment and supplies

  • Labour beds, delivery kits, Doppler and Pinard stethoscopes, CTG, BP apparatus, thermometers, radiant warmers, baby weighing scale, oxygen, suction machines, autoclave.
  • Standardised trays – delivery, episiotomy, baby, emergency drugs, PPH and eclampsia trays, checked every shift.
  • Essential drugs – oxytocin (kept at 2–8°C), misoprostol, magnesium sulphate, calcium gluconate, antihypertensives, antibiotics, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, vitamin K and lignocaine.
  • Colour-coded biomedical waste bins, sharps containers and spill kits.

4. Staffing

  • Adequate skilled birth attendants (staff nurses/NPMs) on every shift according to caseload, trained in SBA, Dakshata and newborn resuscitation; doctors and obstetrician on call; housekeeping and security staff.

5. Processes of care

  • Protocols displayed – AMTSL, management of PPH and eclampsia, neonatal resuscitation, referral.
  • WHO Labour Care Guide and Safe Childbirth Checklist for every woman.
  • Respectful maternity care – birth companion, privacy, choice of position, no unnecessary interventions.
  • Strict infection prevention – hand hygiene, sterilisation, cleaning schedules, safe waste disposal.
  • Records – admission, labour room and referral registers, delivery notes, MCP cards, maternal and neonatal death notification forms.

6. Quality assurance

  • A quality circle, regular audits, maternal and perinatal death reviews, emergency drills (for example "PPH drill"), feedback from women.
  • Assessment against the National Quality Assurance Standards for LaQshya certification.

Conclusion A labour room should be accessible, private, warm, clean and well equipped, with skilled staff, standard trays and drugs, clear protocols and respectful care. Such an organisation turns guidelines into safe births every day.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the comfort measures and non-drug methods that help a woman cope with pain during labour.
answer_html:
Introduction Labour pain is real and often severe, but it can be reduced without drugs. Non-pharmacological methods work by reducing fear and tension, closing the "pain gate" in the spinal cord (gate control theory) and releasing the body's own endorphins. WHO (2018) recommends relaxation and manual techniques for healthy women who ask for pain relief; these can be combined with drugs when needed.

Methods

  1. Continuous support and a birth companion – the presence of a trusted person reduces anxiety and the need for analgesia.
  2. Information and reassurance – explaining what is happening breaks the fear–tension–pain cycle.
  3. Breathing techniques
    • Slow, deep breathing during early contractions – in through the nose, out through the mouth.
    • Lighter, faster breathing at the peak of strong contractions.
    • Panting at crowning, to avoid pushing.
  4. Relaxation – progressive muscle relaxation, relaxing the jaw, shoulders and hands between contractions; rest and conserve energy.
  5. Massage and touch – back massage, firm counter-pressure over the sacrum (very helpful in backache labour), gentle stroking of the abdomen.
  6. Warm compresses on the lower back or abdomen; cold packs on the back for some women.
  7. Hydrotherapy – a warm shower or bath in early labour.
  8. Mobility and position changes – walking, rocking, sitting on a birth ball, leaning forward, kneeling or all fours; upright positions shorten labour and reduce pain.
  9. TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) – electrodes on the back stimulate nerves and block pain signals.
  10. Acupressure points, aromatherapy, music, visualisation and attention-focusing, hypnobirthing.
  11. Comfort measures – a calm, dim, private environment, sips of water and light food, emptying the bladder, cool cloth on the face, mouth care.

Advantages

  • Safe for mother and baby, with no drug side effects.
  • Woman remains alert and in control; mobility is maintained; low cost.
  • Increase satisfaction and the sense of a positive birth.

Role of the midwife

  • Teach these methods in antenatal classes and in early labour.
  • Assess pain and respect the woman's choices.
  • Coach breathing and relaxation, involve the companion in massage, and offer pharmacological methods when needed or requested.

Conclusion Support, information, breathing, relaxation, massage, warmth, water and freedom of movement can greatly reduce labour pain. They are simple, safe and inexpensive and should be offered to every woman in labour.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the alternative birthing positions and the role of the midwife.
answer_html:
Introduction For many years women in hospitals were made to give birth lying flat on their backs (lithotomy position) for the convenience of the attendant. Evidence now shows that women should be encouraged to move and to give birth in the position of their choice. WHO (2018) recommends mobility and an upright position in the first stage and a position of choice, including upright positions, in the second stage.

Types of birthing positions

  1. Upright positions
    • Squatting – widens the pelvic outlet and uses gravity; may be supported by the companion or a bar.
    • Kneeling – upright kneeling or leaning forward on a bed or ball.
    • All fours (hands and knees) – helpful in backache and occipitoposterior positions and for shoulder dystocia manoeuvres.
    • Standing or leaning on the companion.
    • Sitting on a birthing stool or chair.
  2. Semi-recumbent (semi-sitting) – back supported at 45° or more; convenient and commonly used.
  3. Lateral (side-lying, left lateral or Sims) – restful, prevents aortocaval compression and reduces perineal tears; useful with fast labour or epidural.
