  4. Supine or lithotomy – needed for instrumental delivery or repair; otherwise discouraged.

Advantages of upright and lateral positions

  • Gravity helps descent; contractions are more efficient.
  • Pelvic outlet diameters increase (especially in squatting) and the sacrum and coccyx can move back.
  • No compression of the aorta and vena cava, so better placental blood flow and fewer abnormal fetal heart patterns.
  • Shorter second stage, fewer instrumental births and episiotomies, less severe pain.
  • The woman feels more in control and is more satisfied.

Possible disadvantages

  • Some upright positions may be associated with slightly more blood loss and second-degree tears.
  • Less convenient for the attendant to see the perineum; the midwife must adapt her technique.
  • Not suitable when there is fetal distress, need for continuous monitoring or instrumental delivery.

Role of the midwife

  1. Discuss birthing positions during antenatal classes so the woman knows her options.
  2. Encourage movement in labour and let the woman choose; help her change positions every so often.
  3. Provide equipment – birth ball, birthing stool, floor mats, pillows, a squatting bar.
  4. Adapt her own technique – deliver kneeling or sitting beside the woman, use a mirror or torch to see the perineum, support the perineum and baby appropriately.
  5. Involve the companion in supporting the woman.
  6. Keep safety in view – clear the area, keep the newborn corner ready, watch the fetal heart, and move to another position if a complication arises.
  7. Document the position used.

Conclusion Upright and lateral birthing positions use gravity, enlarge the pelvic outlet and protect placental blood flow, shortening labour and reducing interventions. The midwife's task is to offer choice, support the woman in her chosen position and adapt her skills to keep the birth safe.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the role of the birth companion, doula and ASHA in supporting a woman in labour.
answer_html:
Introduction Continuous support during labour is one of the most effective and simple ways to improve outcomes. It may be given by a birth companion (a person of the woman's choice), a doula (a trained, non-medical labour supporter) or an ASHA, in addition to the midwife. WHO (2018) recommends a companion of choice for all women, and the Government of India allows a birth companion in public labour rooms; LaQshya sets targets for births with companions.

1. Birth companion

  • Usually a female relative or friend chosen by the woman; some facilities also allow the husband.
  • Roles
    • Emotional support – presence, encouragement, praise, reassurance.
    • Physical comfort – massage, holding her hand, helping her walk and change position, giving sips of water, wiping her face.
    • Communication – telling the staff about her needs and pain; helping her understand instructions.
    • Support with skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding after birth.
  • Orientation – the midwife explains the companion's role, hand hygiene, the use of a gown, and that she should not interfere with clinical care or disturb other women.

2. Doula

  • A trained, experienced woman (not a health professional) who provides continuous physical, emotional and informational support before, during and after birth.
  • She uses comfort measures, positions and breathing, and helps the woman and family make informed decisions; she does not perform clinical tasks.

3. ASHA

  • Identifies pregnant women, helps with the birth plan, arranges transport and accompanies (escorts) the woman to the facility, often staying as a companion.
  • Helps with early breastfeeding and later makes home visits (HBNC).
  • Receives an incentive under JSY for facilitating institutional delivery.

Benefits of continuous support (research evidence)

  • More spontaneous vaginal births and fewer caesarean and instrumental births.
  • Shorter labour and less need for pain-relief drugs.
  • Fewer babies with low five-minute APGAR scores.
  • Less fear and a more positive birth experience; better breastfeeding.
  • Reduced chance of disrespect and abuse, as there is a witness and advocate.

Role of the midwife

  • Welcome and orient the companion; provide a chair, gown and privacy screens.
  • Involve the companion in comfort measures and explain progress to both.
  • Never leave the woman alone even when a companion is present; the midwife remains responsible for clinical care.
  • Respect the woman's choice of companion and her confidentiality.

Conclusion A birth companion, doula or ASHA provides continuous emotional and physical support that makes labour shorter, safer and more satisfying. Welcoming and guiding them is an essential part of respectful maternity care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Define episiotomy. Explain its indications, types, procedure, repair and post-repair care.

diagram.caption: Types of episiotomy
labels: perineum with incisions shown – median (midline towards the anus)
mediolateral (from the fourchette at 45–60° away from the anus

answer_html:
Definition Episiotomy is a surgical incision of the perineum made during the second stage of labour to enlarge the vaginal outlet. Routine or liberal episiotomy is not recommended (WHO, 2018); it should be done only when there is a clear indication (restrictive use).

Indications

  • Rigid or inelastic perineum delaying birth.
  • Imminent severe perineal tear (for example, thinning with "button-holing").
  • Instrumental delivery (forceps; sometimes vacuum).
  • Fetal distress, when the birth must be hastened.
  • Assisted breech delivery, shoulder dystocia manoeuvres, large baby, occipitoposterior delivery (face to pubis) as needed.
  • Previous perineal repair or scarring that may tear.

Types

  1. Mediolateral – from the midpoint of the fourchette, directed 45–60° away from the midline (usually to the right); most commonly used because extension into the anal sphincter is less likely.
  2. Median (midline) – towards the anus; easy to repair and heals well, but may extend to a third- or fourth-degree tear.
  3. Lateral – not recommended (bleeding, injury to the Bartholin's duct).
  4. J-shaped – starts in the midline and curves away from the anus; rarely used.

Procedure

  1. Explain and obtain consent; maintain asepsis.
  2. Timing – when the perineum is thinned and the head is distending it (about 3–4 cm of head visible during a contraction); too early causes bleeding, too late is useless.
  3. Local anaesthesia – infiltrate 1% lignocaine (about 10 ml) along the line of incision, after aspirating to avoid a vessel.
  4. With two fingers inside to protect the head, cut with straight, blunt-ended scissors in a single cut of about 3–4 cm during a contraction.
  5. Control the head to prevent extension of the cut; note the time.

Repair (after delivery of the placenta)

  • Good light, lithotomy position, aseptic technique, adequate anaesthesia; check for extension.
  • Layers
    1. Vaginal mucosa – a continuous suture starting about 1 cm above the apex, up to the hymenal ring.
    2. Perineal muscles – continuous or interrupted sutures, closing the dead space.
    3. Skin – subcuticular continuous or interrupted sutures.
  • Suture material – rapidly absorbable synthetic (polyglactin 910, 2-0 or 3-0).
  • After repair – rectal examination to make sure no suture has passed through the rectum, count swabs and needles, clean the area and apply a sterile pad.

Post-repair care

  • Perineal hygiene – wash after each voiding and bowel movement (front to back), change pads frequently, keep the area dry.
  • Ice pack in the first 24 hours to reduce swelling; warm sitz baths afterwards.
  • Analgesics (paracetamol) as prescribed.
  • Prevent constipation – fluids and fibre; mild laxatives if needed.
  • Inspect daily using REEDA (redness, oedema, ecchymosis, discharge, approximation).
  • Pelvic floor exercises once comfortable; resume intercourse when healed and comfortable.

Complications – bleeding, haematoma, infection, wound breakdown, extension to the anal sphincter, pain and dyspareunia, rarely fistula.

Conclusion Episiotomy is an incision to enlarge the vaginal outlet, used only when indicated. A correctly timed mediolateral incision, careful layered repair and good perineal care allow quick healing with few complications.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the examination of the placenta, membranes and umbilical cord after delivery.
answer_html:
Introduction Every placenta must be examined immediately after delivery. The most important purpose is to make sure that the placenta and membranes are complete, because retained pieces cause postpartum haemorrhage and infection. The examination also gives clues about the baby's condition.

Preparation – wear gloves; rinse off blood clots gently; place the placenta on a flat tray in good light.

1. Membranes

  • Hold the placenta by the cord so that the membranes hang down; identify the hole through which the baby passed.
  • Spread the membranes to see whether they are complete; separate the amnion (smooth, shiny, can be peeled off up to the cord) from the chorion (rough, opaque, continuous with the placental edge).
  • Ragged or missing membranes suggest retained pieces.

2. Fetal surface

  • Covered by amnion; shiny and bluish-grey.
  • Note the insertion of the cord – central or eccentric (normal), marginal (battledore) or velamentous (vessels run through the membranes and can tear).
  • Follow the vessels – vessels running to the edge and ending in a torn membrane suggest a missing succenturiate lobe (an accessory lobe) left in the uterus.

3. Maternal surface

  • Dark red and lobulated, with 15–20 cotyledons covered by a thin layer of decidua.
  • Fit the cotyledons together to check for completeness; a rough, missing area means a retained cotyledon.
  • Note infarcts (white, firm areas), calcification (gritty), and retroplacental clots or depressions (suggest abruption).

4. Umbilical cord

  • Length – normally about 50 cm; very short or long cords cause problems.
  • Vessels – cut surface shows two arteries and one vein; a single umbilical artery is associated with fetal anomalies (especially renal), so inform the paediatrician.
  • Knots – true knots (may obstruct blood flow) or false knots (harmless loops of vessels or jelly); Wharton's jelly; cysts, haematoma.

5. Size and weight – the placenta is about 15–20 cm across and weighs about 500 g (one-sixth of the baby's weight); a very large placenta may be seen in Rh disease, diabetes or syphilis; a small one in growth restriction.

6. Abnormal shapes – bipartite (two lobes), succenturiate lobe, circumvallate (a raised white ring on the fetal surface), membranous placenta.

7. Recording and action

  • Record complete or incomplete, weight, abnormalities, cord vessels and blood loss.
  • If incomplete, inform the doctor at once and watch closely for bleeding; exploration of the uterus may be needed.
  • Send for histopathology when indicated (stillbirth, growth restriction, suspected infection).

8. Disposal – as anatomical (yellow-category) biomedical waste, or handed over to the family according to hospital policy and cultural wishes, with proper documentation.

Conclusion Systematic examination of the membranes, both surfaces of the placenta and the cord confirms completeness and detects abnormalities. A midwife who never skips this step prevents many cases of PPH and infection.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain post-partum intrauterine contraceptive device (PPIUCD) insertion.

diagram.caption: Post-placental IUCD insertion with Kelly's forceps
labels: anterior lip of cervix held with ring forceps; Cu-T held at the edge of the horizontal arm by long Kelly's placental forceps; forceps passed through the cervix into the lower segment
then moved upwards towards the umbilicus while the abdominal hand stabilises the fundus; Cu-T released at the fundus

answer_html:
Introduction Many women do not return for family planning after childbirth, and short birth intervals are dangerous for mother and baby. PPIUCD – insertion of a copper intrauterine device soon after delivery – gives a safe, highly effective, long-acting, non-hormonal method before the woman leaves the facility.

Timing

  • Post-placental – within 10 minutes of delivery of the placenta (lowest expulsion rate among postpartum insertions).
  • Intra-caesarean – after removal of the placenta, before closing the uterus.
  • Immediate postpartum – within 48 hours of delivery.
  • If not inserted within 48 hours, wait until 6 weeks (interval insertion).

Devices – Cu-T 380A (effective for 10 years) and Cu-T 375 (5 years).

Counselling and consent

  • Counsel during antenatal visits and early labour (not in active labour or just after delivery when she is in pain), with her husband if she wishes; explain benefits, side effects and follow-up.
  • Obtain and record informed consent; reconfirm her choice after delivery.

Eligibility – do not insert if

  • Chorioamnionitis, fever in labour, or rupture of membranes for more than 18 hours.
  • Puerperal sepsis, unresolved postpartum haemorrhage.
  • Extensive genital trauma that would be disturbed by insertion.
  • Known uterine anomaly or other WHO MEC category 4 conditions.

Procedure (post-placental, with forceps)

  1. Complete AMTSL; confirm the uterus is contracted and the placenta complete.
  2. Explain to the woman; use sterile instruments – Sims speculum, ring (sponge-holding) forceps and long Kelly's placental forceps.
  3. Visualise the cervix and hold the anterior lip with ring forceps.
  4. Hold the Cu-T with Kelly's forceps at the edge of the horizontal arm, with the vertical stem in line with the forceps.
  5. Pass it through the cervix into the lower segment; then place the other hand on the abdomen to stabilise the fundus and move the forceps upwards towards the umbilicus until the fundus is felt.
  6. Release the device at the fundus, sweep the forceps sideways and withdraw them carefully without pulling the strings.
  7. Check that the device is not visible at the cervix; record the procedure and give the woman an IUCD card.

Advantages – about 99% effective, immediate, convenient (no separate visit), does not affect breastfeeding, long-acting and reversible.

Side effects and problems – expulsion (more than with interval insertion; she should check for it), heavier periods and cramps, strings not visible (they descend later), rarely infection or perforation.

Follow-up and advice

  • Review at 6 weeks (with the postnatal visit) – check the strings and trim them if long.
  • Report fever, foul-smelling discharge, severe lower abdominal pain, heavy bleeding or expulsion.

Conclusion PPIUCD, inserted within 10 minutes of placental delivery or within 48 hours, offers new mothers a safe, effective and long-acting method of spacing births. Good antenatal counselling, correct technique and follow-up make it acceptable and successful.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the management of the fourth stage of labour.
tags: first hour after delivery of placenta
answer_html:
Introduction The fourth stage is the first hour (and up to two hours) after delivery of the placenta. It is a time of great risk – most cases of PPH and many cases of maternal collapse occur now – and also a time of bonding and the first breastfeed. Mother and baby must be observed together, closely.

1. Observation of the mother Every 15 minutes for the first hour, then every 30 minutes for the second hour:

  • Pulse and blood pressure – a rising pulse or falling BP is an early sign of bleeding or shock.
  • Uterus – fundus at or below the umbilicus, firm and central; if soft, massage it and inform the doctor. A uterus displaced upwards and to the right suggests a full bladder.
  • Vaginal bleeding – check pads; more than one soaked pad in a short time or a steady trickle is abnormal.
  • Perineum – bleeding from the repair, increasing pain or swelling (haematoma).
  • Bladder – encourage voiding; a full bladder prevents uterine contraction.
  • Temperature at the end of the first hour; general condition, colour, consciousness.
  • In high-risk women (pre-eclampsia, PPH, prolonged labour) – BP, urine output and reflexes more often.

2. Care of the newborn (with the mother)

  • Skin-to-skin contact continues; check breathing, colour, warmth and cord bleeding every 15 minutes.
  • Initiate breastfeeding within the first hour – help with position and attachment.
  • Give vitamin K, weigh after the first feed, and keep the baby warm; delay bathing.

3. Comfort and care

  • Clean the perineum, change pads and soiled linen, provide dry clothes and a blanket (shivering is common).
  • Give warm fluids and light food.
  • Allow rest; keep the companion with her.
  • Explain her condition and congratulate the family.

4. Health education before transfer

  • How to feel and rub the uterus and recognise heavy bleeding.
  • Danger signs for mother and baby; hygiene; breastfeeding.

5. Documentation and transfer

  • Record observations, blood loss, drugs, condition of the baby and time of the first breastfeed.
  • Use the "soon after birth" pause point of the Safe Childbirth Checklist.
  • Transfer to the postnatal ward only when stable; advise a stay of at least 48 hours after normal delivery.

Conclusion The fourth stage is the "golden hour" of observation and bonding. Close monitoring of pulse, BP, uterine tone, bleeding and bladder, together with skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding, prevents and detects PPH early and gives mother and baby a safe start.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Explain the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist.
tags: just before pushing or caesarean section

diagram.caption: WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist – four pause points
labels: 1 on admission (referral needed? labour monitoring started? antibiotics? magnesium sulphate and antihypertensives? HIV medicines? supplies ready
companion encouraged) → 2 just before pushing or caesarean (antibiotics? MgSO4? oxytocin and newborn supplies ready
within 1 hour (abnormal bleeding? antibiotics? MgSO4? newborn referral
antibiotics or special care? skin-to-skin and breastfeeding started) → 4 before discharge (bleeding controlled? baby feeding well? family planning discussed? follow-up and danger signs explained)

answer_html:
Introduction Most maternal and newborn deaths around the time of birth are caused by a few problems – haemorrhage, infection, obstructed labour, hypertensive disorders and birth asphyxia – for which simple, effective practices exist. These practices are often missed in a busy labour room. The WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist (2015) is a reminder tool, modelled on the Surgical Safety Checklist, that helps birth attendants carry out essential, evidence-based practices for every birth. It was field-tested in Karnataka, India, where adherence to essential practices improved markedly.

Structure – 29 items grouped into four "pause points" in the normal flow of work.

Pause point 1 – On admission

  • Does the mother need referral (by the facility's criteria)?
  • Has labour monitoring (partograph/LCG) been started?
  • Does she need antibiotics (fever, foul-smelling discharge, prolonged rupture of membranes)?
  • Does she need magnesium sulphate and antihypertensive treatment (severe hypertension with proteinuria)?
  • Does she need antiretroviral drugs (HIV-positive)?
  • Are supplies available and is hand hygiene possible?
  • Has she been encouraged to have a birth companion, and has she been told to call for help if she has bleeding, severe pain, headache, visual disturbance or an urge to push?

Pause point 2 – Just before pushing (or before caesarean section)

  • Re-check the need for antibiotics and magnesium sulphate.
  • Are essential supplies at the bedside – for the mother (gloves, hand rub, oxytocin 10 units in a syringe) and for the baby (clean towels, sterile blade, suction, bag and mask)?
  • Is the team prepared to give oxytocin within one minute, deliver the placenta and check the uterus, and to dry, warm and resuscitate the baby if needed?
  • Is an assistant identified and ready?

Pause point 3 – Soon after birth (within 1 hour)

  • Is the mother bleeding abnormally – if so, massage the uterus, give more uterotonic, start IV fluids and call for help.
  • Does the mother need antibiotics or magnesium sulphate?
  • Does the baby need referral, antibiotics or special care (preterm, low birth weight, required resuscitation, breathing problems, poor feeding)?
  • Have skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding been started?
  • Has HIV prophylaxis been given to the baby if required?

Pause point 4 – Before discharge

  • Is the mother's bleeding controlled and BP normal? Does she need antibiotics?
  • Is the baby feeding well and free of danger signs?
  • Have family planning options been discussed and offered?
  • Have follow-up and the danger signs for mother and baby been explained, and does the family know where to seek help?

Benefits – fewer missed essential practices, better teamwork and communication, early recognition of complications, improved preparedness and quality of care; it fits with LaQshya and Labour Care Guide use.

Role of the midwife – use the checklist for every woman, not as a form-filling exercise but as a pause to think, act and communicate; ensure supplies are ready; record and act on the answers.

Conclusion The Safe Childbirth Checklist turns essential birth practices into a simple routine at four critical moments – admission, just before pushing, soon after birth and before discharge. Used consistently, it helps every woman and newborn receive the care that prevents the major causes of death.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Differentiate between true labour and false labour.
answer_html:
Feature True labour False labour
Contractions Regular, with increasing frequency, duration and intensity Irregular, no progressive increase
Pain Starts in the back and radiates to the front; hardening of the uterus Mainly in the lower abdomen and groin; uterus may not harden much
Effect of rest, walking or sedation Not relieved Relieved or disappears
Cervix Progressive effacement and dilatation No change
Show Usually present Absent
Bag of membranes Forms and bulges Not formed
  • If in doubt, the woman is observed for 1–2 hours and re-examined: cervical change confirms true labour; a woman in false labour is reassured and told when to return.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: What is the Bishop score?
answer_html:
• The Bishop score is a scoring system that assesses the readiness (ripeness) of the cervix before induction of labour.
  • Five features are scored by vaginal examination: dilatation (0–3), effacement (0–3), station of the head (0–3), consistency – firm, medium, soft (0–2), and position – posterior, mid, anterior (0–2); maximum 13.
  • A score of 8 or more means a favourable cervix, with a good chance of successful induction; 6 or less is unfavourable, and cervical ripening (for example with prostaglandins or a balloon catheter) is needed first.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: Classify perineal tears.
answer_html:
• First degree – injury to the perineal skin and/or vaginal mucosa only.
  • Second degree – involves the perineal muscles but not the anal sphincter.
  • Third degree – involves the anal sphincter complex:
    • 3a – less than 50% of the external anal sphincter thickness torn;
    • 3b – more than 50% of the external sphincter torn;
    • 3c – both external and internal sphincters torn.
  • Fourth degree – the anal sphincter complex and the anorectal mucosa are torn.
  • First- and second-degree tears are repaired by the midwife or doctor; third- and fourth-degree tears need repair by an experienced obstetrician in the operation theatre.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: What is the modified Ritgen manoeuvre?
tags: pressure on fetal chin through perineum
answer_html:
• The modified Ritgen manoeuvre is a method of controlling the delivery of the fetal head at crowning.
  • With the woman's perineum distended, the midwife places a towel-covered hand on the perineum just in front of the coccyx and applies gentle forward and upward pressure on the fetal chin, while the other hand applies gentle pressure on the occiput to keep the head flexed and control its speed.
  • This allows the head to be born slowly, by controlled extension, between contractions, helping to reduce perineal tears; it is combined with asking the mother to pant rather than push.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: What is a partograph? Name its components.
answer_html:
• A partograph is a graphical record of the progress of labour and the condition of mother and fetus plotted against time; in the modified WHO partograph it starts in the active phase at 4 cm.
  • Components
    • Fetal condition – fetal heart rate, liquor (colour) and moulding.
    • Progress of labour – cervical dilatation (X), descent of the head in fifths (O) and contractions per 10 minutes.
    • Maternal condition – pulse, BP, temperature, urine (volume, protein, acetone), drugs, IV fluids and oxytocin.
  • The alert line rises at 1 cm per hour from 4 cm and the action line lies 4 hours to its right. WHO has now replaced it with the Labour Care Guide.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during Labour
question: What is the Ferguson reflex?
answer_html:
• The Ferguson reflex is a neuroendocrine positive-feedback reflex in labour.
  • Stretching of the cervix, upper vagina and pelvic floor by the presenting part sends impulses to the hypothalamus, causing the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin; oxytocin produces stronger contractions, which push the fetus down further and increase the stretch.
  • It produces the involuntary urge to bear down in the second stage, which is why women are encouraged to push spontaneously when they feel the urge. Epidural analgesia can blunt it.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: (a) Define puerperium and state its phases. (2 marks) (b) Explain the physiological changes during the puerperium – involution of the uterus, lochia, changes in the other reproductive organs, breasts and other body systems – with their nursing implications. (13 marks)

diagram.caption: Involution of the uterus after delivery
labels: abdominal outline showing fundal height just below the umbilicus (about 13.5 cm above the symphysis) after delivery
at about the midpoint by day 6–7 and not palpable abdominally by about day 12–14; side panel showing uterine weight about 1
300 g at two weeks and about 60 g at six weeks; strip of lochia colours – rubra (days 1–4)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and phases (2 marks)

Puerperium is the period following childbirth during which the body tissues, especially the pelvic organs, return approximately to their pre-pregnant state, both anatomically and physiologically. It begins after delivery of the placenta and lasts about 6 weeks (42 days).

Phases

  • Immediate puerperium – the first 24 hours after delivery (the time of greatest risk of PPH and collapse).
  • Early puerperium – up to the end of the first week.
  • Remote (late) puerperium – up to 6 weeks.

(b) Physiological changes in the puerperium (13 marks)

1. Involution of the uterus Involution is the process by which the uterus returns to its non-pregnant size, position and condition.

Changes in size and weight

  • Immediately after delivery the uterus weighs about 1,000 g; it is firm, globular and the fundus is just below the umbilicus, about 13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis.
  • The fundus stays at this level for about a day and then descends about 1.25 cm (one finger-breadth) every 24 hours.
  • It is at about the midpoint between the umbilicus and symphysis by the end of the first week and cannot be felt abdominally by about the 12th–14th day, when it has become a pelvic organ.
  • Weight falls to about 500 g at one week, 300 g at two weeks and about 60 g at six weeks.

Mechanism of involution

  • Autolysis – proteolytic enzymes break down the excess muscle protein; the products are absorbed and excreted in the urine. The number of muscle cells changes little; each cell becomes smaller.
  • Ischaemia – strong contraction and retraction reduce blood supply, so the muscle shrinks; the living ligatures also control bleeding.
  • Phagocytosis – removes elastic and fibrous tissue.

Changes in the endometrium

  • The superficial layer of the decidua becomes necrotic and is shed as lochia.
  • The basal layer regenerates the endometrium in about 2–3 weeks, except at the placental site, which heals more slowly (about 6 weeks) without leaving a scar.

Afterpains – painful contractions of the uterus in the first 2–3 days, more common in multiparae and during breastfeeding (oxytocin release).

2. Lochia

  • Lochia is the vaginal discharge in the puerperium, coming from the uterus, cervix and vagina.
  • Lochia rubra (days 1–4) – red; blood, shreds of decidua, vernix, lanugo and meconium.
  • Lochia serosa (days 5–9) – yellowish or pink; less blood, more serum, white cells, mucus and organisms.
  • Lochia alba (days 10–15, may continue up to 3–6 weeks) – pale white; white cells, decidual and epithelial cells, mucus.
  • It has a mild, stale (not foul) smell; the total amount is about 250 ml; it is more in multiparae and less after caesarean section.
  • Abnormal lochia – foul smell (infection), persistent or returning red lochia (retained products, subinvolution, secondary PPH), very heavy flow or large clots.

3. Cervix

  • Soft, oedematous and lacerated immediately after delivery; it gradually firms and closes.
  • By the end of the first week the external os admits only a finger tip; by about two weeks the internal os is closed.
  • The external os becomes a transverse slit (the parous cervix), instead of the round os of a nulliparous woman.

4. Vagina, vulva and perineum

  • The vagina is smooth and capacious at first; rugae reappear by about three weeks, but it never returns completely to the nulliparous state.
  • The hymen is reduced to small tags (carunculae myrtiformes).
  • The perineum is oedematous; small tears and an episiotomy heal within 1–2 weeks. The pelvic floor regains tone gradually, helped by exercises.
  • Vaginal epithelium is thin in breastfeeding women because of low oestrogen, causing dryness.

5. Ovaries and fallopian tubes – return to the non-pregnant state; ovarian function resumes as described below.

6. Abdominal wall and skin

  • The abdominal wall remains lax and soft; muscle tone returns gradually over 6–8 weeks.
  • Striae fade to silvery white lines; linea nigra and chloasma fade; hair fall may increase a few months after delivery.

7. Breasts (lactation)

  • The fall in oestrogen and progesterone after delivery of the placenta allows prolactin to act; suckling maintains prolactin secretion and releases oxytocin for the let-down reflex.
  • Colostrum in the first 2–4 days → transitional milk → mature milk by about two weeks.
  • Primary engorgement (fullness, warmth, tenderness) commonly occurs on the third or fourth day as milk "comes in".

8. Cardiovascular system

  • Immediately after delivery, blood from the contracting uterus returns to the circulation (autotransfusion) and cardiac output rises – a dangerous time for women with heart disease.
  • Pulse often slows (50–70 per minute) in the first days (puerperal bradycardia); a rising pulse suggests bleeding or infection.
  • Blood volume and cardiac output return towards normal over the next few weeks, helped by diuresis.
  • Varicose veins and oedema of the legs regress.

9. Blood

  • Leucocytosis – the white cell count may be 20,000/mm³ or more in the first days.
  • Haemoglobin may fall slightly at first and then rise as plasma volume falls.
  • Clotting factors and fibrinogen remain high for several weeks – the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism is highest in the puerperium.

10. Urinary system

  • Diuresis on days 2–5, as the extra water of pregnancy is excreted (up to 3 litres of urine a day).
  • The bladder may be oedematous and less sensitive after labour, especially after prolonged labour, instrumental delivery or epidural – causing retention of urine and overflow; a full bladder pushes the uterus up and causes PPH.
  • Dilated ureters and renal pelves return to normal in about 6–8 weeks; urinary infection is common.

11. Gastrointestinal system

  • The woman is hungry and thirsty after delivery.
  • Constipation is common – sluggish bowel, loss of abdominal tone, reduced food in labour, perineal pain and fear of opening the bowels; haemorrhoids may worsen.

12. Endocrine changes

  • Placental hormones fall rapidly – hPL disappears within a day, oestrogen and progesterone fall to low levels within a week, hCG becomes undetectable within a few weeks.
  • Prolactin remains high in breastfeeding women.
  • Insulin resistance disappears quickly; most women with gestational diabetes return to normal sugar levels, and insulin needs of diabetic women fall sharply after delivery.

13. Return of menstruation and ovulation

  • Non-breastfeeding women – ovulation may return as early as 4–6 weeks; menstruation usually by 6–8 weeks.
  • Breastfeeding women – ovulation and menstruation are delayed (lactational amenorrhoea), sometimes for many months, but ovulation may occur before the first period, so pregnancy can occur without a period.

14. Weight, temperature and general changes

  • About 5–6 kg is lost at delivery (baby, placenta, liquor, blood) and a further 2–4 kg over the following weeks, mainly by diuresis.
  • A slight rise of temperature (not above 38°C) may occur in the first 24 hours (reactionary) or with engorgement; a temperature of 38°C or more on two occasions after the first 24 hours suggests puerperal pyrexia and must be investigated.
  • Shivering soon after delivery is common.

15. Musculoskeletal and psychological changes

  • Ligaments and joints regain stability over months; backache and pelvic girdle pain may persist; the rectus muscles may remain separated (diastasis recti).
  • Emotional changes – elation, fatigue, tearfulness; postpartum blues are common and transient, but depression and psychosis need recognition.

Nursing implications

  • Measure fundal height daily at the same time, after the bladder is emptied, and record involution; a uterus that is large, soft or tender suggests subinvolution, retained products or infection.
  • Observe lochia for amount, colour and smell; teach the mother to report heavy bleeding or foul smell.
  • Check the bladder – ensure she passes urine within about 6 hours of delivery; catheterise if the bladder is distended.
  • Prevent thrombosis – early ambulation, leg exercises, hydration.
  • Monitor pulse, temperature and BP; report tachycardia and fever.
  • Support breastfeeding and manage engorgement.
  • Prevent constipation and care for the perineum.
  • Advise contraception before the return of fertility.
  • Give emotional support and watch for depression.

Nursing importance Knowledge of normal puerperal changes allows the midwife to tell the normal from the abnormal – for example, normal bradycardia from the tachycardia of haemorrhage, normal lochia from infected lochia, normal afterpains from the pain of infection. Most postnatal complications – PPH, sepsis, thromboembolism, urinary retention and breast problems – can be prevented or detected early by observing these changes.

Conclusion The puerperium is the six-week period after delivery during which the body returns to its pre-pregnant state. The uterus involutes by autolysis, ischaemia and phagocytosis, falling about 1.25 cm a day and becoming a pelvic organ in two weeks; lochia changes from rubra to serosa to alba; the cervix, vagina and perineum heal; the breasts establish lactation; and the circulatory, urinary, digestive and endocrine systems readjust. Careful observation of these changes is the basis of good postnatal care.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: (a) Explain the postnatal assessment of the mother. (5 marks) (b) Describe the postnatal care of the mother in the facility and at home as per Government of India guidelines, including the schedule of postnatal visits and counselling. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Postnatal care schedule
labels: timeline after delivery – fourth stage observation (first hour
every 15 minutes) → stay in facility at least 48 hours (day 1 check) → day 3 visit → day 7 visit → day 42 (six-week) visit; ASHA HBNC home visits on days 3
28 and 42 marked below; each visit labelled with key checks for mother (BP

answer_html:
Introduction More than half of maternal deaths and most newborn deaths occur in the first days and weeks after birth, yet this period has traditionally received the least attention. Good postnatal care (PNC) detects complications early, supports breastfeeding and recovery, and links the mother to family planning and child health services.

(a) Postnatal assessment of the mother (5 marks)

1. History – how she feels, pain, bleeding, passing urine and stools, sleep, feeding, mood, any complaints; review of delivery notes (type of delivery, blood loss, tears, complications).

2. Vital signs

  • Temperature – 38°C or more after the first 24 hours suggests infection.
  • Pulse – tachycardia suggests haemorrhage, infection, anaemia or thromboembolism.
  • Blood pressure – hypertension may first appear after delivery (postpartum pre-eclampsia).
  • Respiration, pallor, oedema.

3. Systematic examination – "BUBBLE-HE"

  • B – Breasts – soft, filling or engorged; nipples (sore, cracked, flat); redness or lumps; attachment during feeding.
  • U – Uterus – fundal height (in finger-breadths or cm below the umbilicus), firm or boggy, central or displaced, tenderness.
  • B – Bladder – time of first voiding, amount, pain, distension, incontinence.
  • B – Bowel – flatus, bowel movement (usually by day 2–3), haemorrhoids.
  • L – Lochia – colour, amount (scanty, light, moderate, heavy by pad count), clots, smell.
  • E – Episiotomy/perineum – using REEDA (redness, oedema, ecchymosis, discharge, approximation of wound edges); haematoma; caesarean wound if applicable.
  • H – Homan's sign and legs – calf tenderness, swelling, warmth (signs of deep vein thrombosis); varicose veins.
  • E – Emotional status – mood, bonding with the baby, anxiety, tearfulness, sleep; signs of depression.

4. Additional checks – haemoglobin when indicated, urine protein in hypertensive women, blood sugar in women who had GDM, wound and drain care after caesarean section.

(b) Postnatal care in the facility and at home (10 marks)

1. Schedule of postnatal care

  • Stay in the facility for at least 48 hours after a normal delivery (longer after caesarean section or complications).
  • Government of India schedule – postnatal check-ups on day 1 (in the facility, within 24 hours), day 3, day 7 and at 6 weeks (day 42).
  • WHO (2022) recommends at least four postnatal contacts – within 24 hours, on day 2–3, between days 7 and 14, and at 6 weeks.
  • ASHA home visits under HBNC on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 (with an extra visit on day 1 after a home delivery) for both mother and baby.

2. Care in the facility

  • Monitoring – after the fourth stage, check pulse, BP, uterine tone and lochia regularly (about every 4 hours on the first day, then twice daily) and temperature daily; teach her to feel and rub the uterus.
  • Rest and sleep – a quiet environment; rest when the baby sleeps.
  • Early ambulation – encourage her to sit up and walk within a few hours of a normal delivery; this prevents thrombosis, improves bladder and bowel function and lifts mood.
  • Bladder care – encourage voiding within about 6 hours and then regularly; privacy, running tap water, warm water over the perineum; catheterise if retention.
  • Bowel care – fluids, fibre, early ambulation; mild laxative if needed.
  • Diet – a normal, nutritious diet with an extra meal and plenty of fluids; no food restrictions (counter taboos).
  • Perineal care – wash with clean water after each voiding and bowel movement, front to back; change pads every 4–6 hours; ice pack in the first 24 hours, sitz baths later; analgesics.
  • Breast care and breastfeeding – exclusive breastfeeding on demand; help with positioning and attachment; manage engorgement and sore nipples.
  • Hygiene – daily bath, clean clothes and bedding, hand washing before handling the baby.
  • Supplements and prophylaxis – IFA and calcium for 180 days after delivery; anti-D for Rh-negative mothers of Rh-positive babies; Td if not completed.
  • Baby – kept with the mother (rooming-in), skin-to-skin, warmth, cord care, birth-dose vaccines.
  • Before discharge – check the mother and baby, discuss family planning, explain danger signs, give the date for follow-up, complete the MCP card and discharge summary, and help with birth registration and JSY/PMMVY paperwork.

3. Care at home

  • The ANM and ASHA check the mother's general condition, temperature, pulse, BP, breasts, uterus, lochia, perineum, bladder and mood at each visit.
  • They support breastfeeding, check the newborn (weight, warmth, feeding, cord, jaundice, danger signs) and refer when needed.
  • They reinforce nutrition, IFA, hygiene, rest and family planning, and involve the family in supporting the mother.

4. Counselling during the postnatal period

  1. Nutrition – an extra meal, green vegetables, pulses, milk, fruits and fluids; continue IFA and calcium.
  2. Breastfeeding – exclusively for six months; no prelacteal feeds, water or bottles.
  3. Personal hygiene and perineal care.
  4. Rest and gradual return to activity; avoid heavy lifting for some weeks; postnatal exercises.
  5. Danger signs for the mother – heavy bleeding, foul-smelling discharge, fever, severe abdominal pain, severe headache or blurred vision, fits, breathlessness or chest pain, painful swollen calf, painful red breast, burning or difficulty in passing urine, and feelings of deep sadness or thoughts of harming herself or the baby.
  6. Danger signs for the baby – poor feeding, fast breathing, fever or cold body, convulsions, yellow palms and soles, lethargy, umbilical redness or pus.
  7. Family planning – fertility may return before the first period; choose a method (LAM, PPIUCD, injectable, pills, condoms, sterilisation).
  8. Sexual life – resume when the perineum has healed and she feels comfortable, using contraception.
  9. Emotional health – baby blues are common; seek help if low mood lasts more than two weeks.
  10. Immunisation of the baby, growth monitoring and the six-week visit.

5. The six-week (day 42) postnatal check

  • General condition, weight, BP, haemoglobin; breasts and feeding.
  • Abdomen (involution, caesarean scar), perineum, lochia; pelvic examination if indicated; cervical screening if due.
  • Urinary or faecal incontinence; return of menstruation.
  • Adoption of a family planning method.
  • Mental health screening.
  • Follow-up of medical conditions – a blood sugar test for women who had gestational diabetes; BP for hypertensive women.
  • Baby's growth and six-week vaccines.

6. Additional care after caesarean section

  • Monitor pulse, BP, respiration, wound, drain and urine output closely on the first day; give adequate analgesia so that she can move, cough and breastfeed.
  • Start oral fluids early and a normal diet as tolerated; remove the urinary catheter as per protocol and check voiding.
  • Early ambulation (within about 12–24 hours), leg exercises and good hydration to prevent thrombosis; thromboprophylaxis in high-risk women as prescribed.
  • Help her breastfeed in the side-lying or football position, with pillows to protect the wound.
  • Keep the wound clean and dry; watch for redness, discharge or gaping; remove sutures or staples as advised.
  • Advise her to avoid heavy lifting for about six weeks and to keep a gap of at least 18–24 months before the next pregnancy.

7. Postnatal care of high-risk mothers

  • Anaemia – check haemoglobin; continue IFA, give intravenous iron or blood as prescribed; teach an iron-rich diet.
  • Hypertension or pre-eclampsia – measure BP frequently for at least the first few days (eclampsia can occur after delivery), continue antihypertensives and teach warning signs such as headache and blurred vision.
  • Gestational diabetes – stop treatment after delivery as advised, encourage breastfeeding, and arrange a blood sugar test at about 6–12 weeks and yearly thereafter, because the risk of type 2 diabetes is high.
  • Heart disease – watch for breathlessness and tachycardia in the first days; avoid fluid overload.
  • HIV-positive mother – continue ART, ensure infant prophylaxis and follow-up testing, and support her chosen feeding method as per national guidelines.
  • Rh-negative mother – give anti-D within 72 hours if the baby is Rh-positive.
  • Adolescent mothers and women without family support – extra counselling on breastfeeding, nutrition and contraception, and more frequent home visits.

Nursing importance The postnatal period is when women are most often discharged early, left at home and overlooked. A midwife who assesses systematically (BUBBLE-HE), follows the visit schedule and counsels well can prevent deaths from PPH, sepsis, pre-eclampsia and thromboembolism, establish breastfeeding, prevent rapid repeat pregnancy and support the mother's emotional well-being.

Conclusion Postnatal care begins with careful assessment of vital signs and the BUBBLE-HE parameters. The mother should stay at least 48 hours in the facility and receive check-ups on day 1, day 3, day 7 and at six weeks, with ASHA home visits in between. Care covers rest, ambulation, diet, hygiene, perineal and breast care, supplements, family planning, danger signs and emotional support, ending with a complete six-week check.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain the minor disorders of the puerperium and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction After delivery many women have discomforts caused by the normal changes of the puerperium. They are not serious, but they make the mother miserable and may interfere with breastfeeding and bonding. The midwife relieves them and differentiates them from serious complications.

Disorder Cause Management
Afterpains Contractions of the involuting uterus, more in multiparae and during breastfeeding (oxytocin) Reassure; empty the bladder before feeding; warm compress; lie prone with a pillow under the abdomen; paracetamol before feeds if needed; refer if pain is continuous or with fever (infection)
Perineal pain and swelling Bruising, tears, episiotomy Ice pack in the first 24 hours; warm sitz baths later; perineal hygiene; sit on a soft cushion; analgesics; check for haematoma or infection (REEDA)
Breast engorgement (day 3–5) Increased blood flow and milk with poor emptying Frequent, effective feeding; express a little milk to soften the areola; warm compress before and cold compress after feeds; supportive bra; analgesics
Sore or cracked nipples Poor attachment Correct positioning and attachment; start on the less sore side; apply a little hindmilk and air-dry; avoid soap; continue feeding
Retention of urine Bladder oedema and reduced sensation, perineal pain, epidural Privacy, running tap water, warm water over the vulva, upright position, early ambulation, analgesia; catheterise if the bladder is distended or no urine in 6 hours
Constipation Sluggish bowel, lax abdominal muscles, fear of pain, iron tablets Fluids, fibre, fruits, early ambulation; reassure that stitches will not break; mild laxative if needed
Haemorrhoids Pushing in labour, constipation Prevent constipation; sitz baths; cold compress; local soothing applications as prescribed
Excessive sweating (night sweats) Loss of extra body water Reassure; cotton clothing; fluids; frequent change of clothes
Shivering soon after delivery Common physiological reaction Warm blankets and warm drinks; check temperature to exclude fever
Backache and pelvic pain Lax ligaments, posture during feeding Good posture with pillows while feeding, back-care exercises, firm mattress, correct lifting
Fatigue and sleep disturbance Labour, night feeds, anaemia Rest when the baby sleeps, family help, iron-rich diet and IFA
Postpartum blues (days 3–10) Hormonal and emotional changes Reassurance, rest, family support; refer if low mood lasts beyond two weeks or is severe

Health education

  • Explain that these discomforts are normal and temporary.
  • Teach simple self-care measures and when to seek help.

Warning features that need referral – fever, foul-smelling lochia, heavy bleeding, severe or increasing pain, a painful swollen calf, a red, hot, painful area of the breast with fever, or persistent sadness.

Conclusion Minor disorders of the puerperium – afterpains, perineal pain, engorgement, sore nipples, urinary retention, constipation, sweating, backache and blues – are common and usually respond to simple measures. Prompt relief and reassurance help the mother rest, breastfeed and recover.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain the common breastfeeding problems in the early postnatal period and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction Almost every new mother meets some difficulty in breastfeeding, especially in the first week. Most problems arise from poor positioning and attachment and infrequent feeding, and most can be prevented or solved by skilled support without stopping breastfeeding.

Basic skills taught to every mother

  • Positions – cradle, cross-cradle (good for newborns), football (clutch) hold (after caesarean section or for twins), side-lying (rest at night, after caesarean) and laid-back positions.
  • Good positioning – the baby's head and body in line, close to the mother, facing the breast with the nose opposite the nipple, whole body supported.
  • Good attachment – mouth wide open, more areola visible above than below, lower lip turned out, chin touching the breast; slow, deep sucks with audible swallowing.
  • Feed on demand, 8–12 times in 24 hours, letting the baby finish one breast before offering the other.

1. "Not enough milk" (perceived or real low supply)

  • Causes – infrequent or short feeds, poor attachment, prelacteal or formula feeds, anxiety.
  • Management – frequent feeding day and night, skin-to-skin contact, rooming-in, correct attachment, avoid bottles and formula; reassure using signs of adequate intake – at least 6 wet nappies a day after the first few days, regular stools, regaining birth weight by about two weeks and a contented baby.

2. Flat or inverted nipples

  • Check the nipples in pregnancy, but do not "treat" them before birth.
  • After birth – help the baby take a large mouthful of breast, not just nipple; shape the breast; draw the nipple out before feeds with a modified 10 ml syringe (barrel cut and plunger reversed); express milk and give it by cup until the baby attaches well.

3. Sore and cracked nipples

  • Cause – usually poor attachment; sometimes thrush.
  • Management – correct the attachment; begin with the less painful breast; break suction with a finger before removing the baby; apply a few drops of hindmilk and air-dry; avoid soap and creams; if very painful, express and cup-feed for a day or two; treat thrush if present.

4. Breast engorgement

  • Swollen, hard, painful, shiny breasts on day 3–5; the nipple may flatten, so the baby cannot attach.
  • Management – frequent, effective feeding; soften the areola first by expressing a little milk or by gentle "reverse pressure"; warm compress before and cold compress after feeds; gentle massage; supportive bra; analgesics.

5. Blocked duct

  • A tender lump in one part of the breast, without fever.
  • Management – feed frequently from the affected side first, massage towards the nipple during feeding, change positions (baby's chin towards the lump), warmth; avoid tight clothing.

6. Mastitis and breast abscess

  • Mastitis – a red, hot, painful area with fever and flu-like illness.
  • Management – continue breastfeeding or expressing (the milk is safe for the baby), rest, fluids, analgesics, and antibiotics as prescribed; refer early.
  • A breast abscess (fluctuant, very painful swelling) needs drainage; feeding continues from the other breast.

7. Problems related to mother or baby

  • After caesarean section – side-lying or football hold, pillows, early skin-to-skin.
  • Sleepy or preterm baby – wake for feeds, skin-to-skin (KMC), expressed milk by cup or paladai.
  • Twins – football hold for both together.
  • HIV-positive mother on treatment – exclusive breastfeeding as per national guidelines.

Role of the nurse

  • Observe a full feed before discharge and correct problems early.
  • Teach hand expression, encourage rooming-in and exclusive breastfeeding, involve the family, and refer complicated cases.

Conclusion Most early breastfeeding problems – low supply, nipple difficulties, engorgement, blocked ducts and mastitis – result from poor attachment or infrequent feeding. Correct technique, frequent feeding and continued breastfeeding, with patient support from the nurse, solve nearly all of them.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain postpartum family planning (PPFP).
tags: healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy
combined pills after six months if breastfeeding
answer_html:
Introduction Postpartum family planning (PPFP) is the prevention of unintended and closely spaced pregnancies during the first 12 months after childbirth. Many women wish to delay or stop childbearing after delivery, but few use a method, and fertility may return before menstruation. A birth-to-pregnancy interval of at least 24 months (healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy) reduces maternal anaemia and death, preterm birth, low birth weight and infant death.

When to counsel

  • During antenatal visits, in early labour (not in active labour), after delivery, before discharge, at postnatal and immunisation visits.
  • Involve the husband if the woman wishes; use the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria.

Methods and timing

  1. Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) – about 98% effective when all three conditions are met: the baby is under 6 months, the mother is exclusively breastfeeding (day and night), and her periods have not returned. When any condition changes, another method must start.
  2. Postpartum IUCD (Cu-T 380A or 375) – post-placental (within 10 minutes), intra-caesarean or within 48 hours; otherwise wait until 6 weeks. Safe in breastfeeding.
  3. Progestin-only methods
    • Progestin-only pills – suitable for breastfeeding women (from about 6 weeks as per national guidelines; immediately for non-breastfeeding women).
    • Injectable MPA (Antara) every three months – from 6 weeks in breastfeeding women.
  4. Centchroman (Chhaya) – a non-hormonal weekly pill (twice a week for the first three months); can be used by breastfeeding women.
  5. Combined oral contraceptive pills – they can reduce milk, so in breastfeeding women they are usually started after 6 months; non-breastfeeding women can start them from about 3 weeks if there is no risk of thrombosis.
  6. Condoms – can be used at any time; protect against STIs.
  7. Female sterilisation – postpartum (within 7 days of delivery, by minilaparotomy), during caesarean section, or as an interval procedure after 6 weeks.
  8. Male sterilisation (no-scalpel vasectomy) – at any time; the couple uses another method for three months until semen is free of sperm.
  9. Emergency contraception for unprotected intercourse once fertility may have returned.

Programme support – PPIUCD and postpartum sterilisation are available free in public facilities, with compensation to clients under the national family planning programme; ASHAs counsel and follow up.

Role of the nurse

  • Counsel every pregnant and postnatal woman with correct, unbiased information.
  • Provide or refer for the chosen method before discharge; follow up at six weeks.
  • Record the method in the MCP card and register.

Conclusion PPFP uses the time when a woman is already in contact with health services to help her space or limit births. LAM, PPIUCD, progestin-only methods, centchroman, condoms and sterilisation, chosen with good counselling, protect the health of the mother and the next child.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain the transition to parenthood and the role of the nurse in promoting maternal–infant bonding.
answer_html:
Introduction The birth of a baby changes the lives of the mother, father and the whole family. Transition to parenthood is the process by which parents take on their new roles, responsibilities and identity. Healthy bonding between parents and baby lays the foundation for the child's emotional development.

1. Maternal adaptation – Rubin's phases

  • Taking-in phase (first 1–2 days) – the mother is dependent and passive, focused on her own needs for rest, food and comfort; she talks repeatedly about her labour experience. Nurse – meet her physical needs, listen, allow rest.
  • Taking-hold phase (about day 2 to 10) – she becomes independent and eager to learn baby care, but may be anxious about her ability. Nurse – this is the best time for teaching (feeding, bathing, cord care); praise her efforts.
  • Letting-go phase (from about two weeks onwards) – she accepts her new role, adjusts relationships and gives up old roles; the family settles into a new routine.

2. Maternal role attainment (Mercer) – a mother passes through anticipatory, formal, informal and personal stages until she feels confident and comfortable as a mother; support and experience speed this.

3. Paternal adaptation – fathers show engrossment (absorption and interest in the baby); they may feel left out or anxious about responsibilities. Involving them in care strengthens the family.

4. Bonding and attachment

  • Bonding – the strong emotional tie that develops between parents and baby, especially in the first hours after birth.
  • Attachment behaviours – eye-to-eye contact in the en face position, touching (from fingertips to the whole hand), talking in a high-pitched voice, smiling, holding close, naming the baby, responding to cries.
  • Factors that help – skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding, rooming-in, a healthy baby, a supportive partner and family.
  • Factors that hinder – separation (sick or preterm baby), a traumatic birth, maternal illness or depression, an unwanted pregnancy, disappointment about the baby's sex, poverty and lack of support.

5. Family adjustment – changes in the couple relationship and sexual life, fatigue, financial stress, sibling rivalry in older children, and the roles of grandparents.

Role of the nurse

  1. Promote skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding within the first hour, and rooming-in.
  2. Encourage parents to see, touch, hold and talk to the baby; explain the baby's behaviour and cues.
  3. Respect the phases – give rest and care first, then teach.
  4. Involve the father in holding, changing and comforting the baby.
  5. Prepare older siblings (include them, give them small roles and attention).
  6. Allow parents of sick or preterm babies to visit, touch and practise kangaroo mother care.
  7. Observe for poor bonding or depression – lack of interest in the baby, persistent sadness, anxiety – and refer.
  8. Link the family with ASHAs, anganwadi services and community support.

Conclusion Transition to parenthood involves physical recovery, emotional adjustment and the learning of new roles. By understanding Rubin's phases, promoting early contact and involving fathers and families, the nurse helps parents form strong, loving bonds with their baby.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain the cultural practices and taboos related to the postnatal period and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction In India the postnatal period is surrounded by traditional customs, passed on by mothers-in-law, elders and dais. Some protect the mother and baby, some are harmless and some are dangerous. The nurse needs cultural competence – understanding and respecting beliefs while protecting health.

1. Beneficial practices (to be encouraged)

  • Rest and confinement for about 40 days ("sava mahina"), freeing the mother from heavy work.
  • Special nourishing foods – ghee, milk, dry fruits, edible gum (dinka) laddoos, garden cress (aliv) preparations, methi and other energy-rich foods.
  • Oil massage of mother and baby with clean oil, and warm baths.
  • Family support – the mother is cared for at her parents' home; elders help with the baby.
  • Abstinence from intercourse during the puerperium.

2. Harmless practices (to be respected)

  • Prayers and religious rituals, wearing threads or amulets, the naming ceremony (for example on the twelfth day), special songs and celebrations.

3. Harmful practices (to be discouraged)

  • Restricting water and fluids, or giving only dry food – causes dehydration, constipation and poor milk supply.
  • Avoiding "cold" foods such as fruits, vegetables, pulses or curd – reduces vitamins, protein and iron.
  • Discarding colostrum and giving prelacteal feeds (honey, sugar water, ghutti, animal milk) – deprives the baby of protection and causes infection.
  • Applying cow dung, ash or oil to the umbilical cord – risk of neonatal tetanus and sepsis.
  • Putting oil in the baby's ears or nose, applying kajal – infection and aspiration.
  • Keeping the mother and baby in a closed, smoky room or making the mother sit near a fire (shekoti) for long – carbon monoxide poisoning, burns, overheating.
  • Tight abdominal binding soon after delivery; very hot baths for the baby; isolation of the mother as "impure".
  • Delaying medical care for fever or bleeding because the mother "should not go out".

4. Approach of the nurse (Leininger's culture care)

  • Culture care preservation – support beneficial practices (rest, nourishing foods, massage, family care).
  • Culture care accommodation – adapt practices to make them safe (for example, special foods plus plenty of water and vegetables; clean oil for massage but nothing on the cord; ventilation in the room).
  • Culture care repatterning – respectfully change harmful practices (discarding colostrum, prelacteal feeds, applying substances to the cord, fluid restriction) by explaining reasons.

Role of the nurse

  • Begin with a cultural assessment – ask the mother and elders what they plan to do and why.
  • Listen without ridicule; use the local language and examples.
  • Involve mothers-in-law and grandmothers, who make many decisions (for example, through Saas–Bahu meetings), and ASHAs and anganwadi workers as cultural bridges.
  • Use health education, demonstrations and stories of local mothers who followed safe practices.
  • Follow up at home visits to see that advice is followed.

Conclusion Postnatal customs reflect a family's love and concern for the mother and baby. By preserving the beneficial, accommodating the harmless and gently changing the harmful – especially fluid restriction, discarding colostrum, prelacteal feeds and unsafe cord care – the nurse makes tradition work for health.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: Explain postnatal exercises and their importance.
answer_html:
Introduction Pregnancy and childbirth stretch the abdominal and pelvic floor muscles and slow the circulation in the legs. Postnatal exercises are graded exercises begun soon after delivery to restore muscle tone, prevent complications and help the mother regain fitness and confidence.

Benefits

  • Improve circulation and prevent deep vein thrombosis.
  • Restore the pelvic floor, preventing urinary incontinence and genital prolapse.
  • Strengthen the abdominal muscles and help close a diastasis recti.
  • Reduce backache and improve posture.
  • Help weight loss and return of figure; improve mood and reduce the risk of depression; aid bowel function.

Programme of exercises

From the first day (even in bed)

  1. Deep breathing – slow, deep abdominal breathing, 5–10 times, several times a day.
  2. Foot and ankle exercises – bend and stretch the feet and circle the ankles 10–20 times every hour while awake.
  3. Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises – tighten the muscles around the vagina, urethra and anus as if stopping urine flow, hold for 5–10 seconds, relax; repeat 10 times, 3–4 times a day. Continue for life.
  4. Abdominal tightening – while breathing out, pull the navel towards the spine, hold for a few seconds, relax.

From the second or third day

  1. Pelvic tilting – lying on the back with knees bent, flatten the lower back against the bed by tightening the abdomen and buttocks; hold, then relax.
  2. Knee rolling – with knees bent and together, roll them gently from side to side.
  3. Head lift – lying with knees bent, lift the head while pulling in the abdomen; progress to lifting the shoulders.
  4. Bridging – raise the buttocks off the bed and hold, to strengthen the back and buttocks.

After the first week (if no diastasis or once it is closing)

  1. Curl-ups (partial sit-ups) and oblique curl-ups, gradually increased.

After six weeks

  1. Brisk walking, yoga and other activities, gradually returning to normal exercise.

Posture and back care – sit upright with pillows while feeding, bend the knees (not the back) when lifting the baby, change nappies at waist height.

Precautions

  • Start gently and progress slowly; exercises should not cause pain.
  • After caesarean section – breathing, leg, pelvic floor and gentle abdominal tightening from the first day; avoid strenuous abdominal exercises until the wound has healed (about six weeks).
  • Check for diastasis recti before starting curl-ups.
  • Stop and seek advice if there is pain, heavy bleeding, dizziness or breathlessness.

Role of the nurse – demonstrate the exercises before discharge, check that the mother can perform pelvic floor contractions correctly, give a written or pictorial chart, and review at postnatal visits.

Conclusion Simple, graded postnatal exercises – breathing, leg, pelvic floor and abdominal exercises – started early and continued regularly, help prevent thrombosis, incontinence and backache and restore the mother's strength and confidence.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: What is lochia? Name its types.
answer_html:
• Lochia is the vaginal discharge during the puerperium, consisting of blood, decidual tissue and secretions from the healing placental site, cervix and vagina.
  • Types
    • Lochia rubra (days 1–4) – red; blood, decidua, vernix, lanugo.
    • Lochia serosa (days 5–9) – yellowish or pink; serum, white cells, mucus.
    • Lochia alba (days 10–15, may persist up to 3–6 weeks) – pale white; white cells, epithelial cells, mucus.
  • Normal lochia has a stale, not foul, smell. Foul-smelling lochia suggests infection; persistent or returning red lochia suggests retained products or subinvolution.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Physiology, Management and Care during the Puerperium (Postnatal Care)
question: What is diastasis recti abdominis? How is it checked in a postnatal mother?
answer_html:
• Diastasis recti abdominis is the separation of the two rectus abdominis muscles along the linea alba, caused by stretching of the abdominal wall in pregnancy; it is common after delivery, especially in multiparae and after twins.
  • Checking – the mother lies on her back with knees bent and lifts her head and shoulders slightly; the nurse places her fingertips across the midline above and below the umbilicus and counts the finger-widths of the gap. A gap of more than two finger-widths is significant.
  • Management – abdominal tightening and pelvic tilt exercises, good posture, avoid sit-ups and heavy lifting until the gap closes; refer for physiotherapy if it persists beyond 6–8 weeks.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: (a) Explain the physiological adaptation of the newborn to extra-uterine life – respiratory, cardiovascular, haematological, thermoregulatory, hepatic, gastrointestinal, renal, immune and neurological. (12 marks) (b) Explain the nursing care that supports a smooth transition after birth. (3 marks)

diagram.caption: Main adaptations of the newborn at birth
labels: central baby figure with linked boxes – lungs (first breath
surfactant keeps alveoli open); heart (pulmonary resistance falls
foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus close); temperature (brown fat
low vitamin K factors); gut (meconium within 24 hours
small stomach); kidneys (first urine within 24 hours

answer_html:
Introduction At birth the baby must, within minutes, change from a life dependent on the placenta – which breathes, feeds, excretes and keeps it warm – to independent life. The baby must breathe, change its circulation, control its temperature, maintain its blood sugar, feed and excrete, and resist infection. Most babies make this transition smoothly, but the first hours and days are the period of greatest risk of death in life. The midwife's knowledge of these changes is the basis of newborn care.

(a) Physiological adaptation (12 marks)

1. Respiratory adaptation – the first breath

  • In the uterus the lungs are filled with fluid, and the placenta carries out gas exchange.
  • Stimuli that start breathing
    • Chemical – mild hypoxia, rising carbon dioxide and acidosis after labour and cord clamping stimulate the chemoreceptors.
    • Thermal – the sudden fall in temperature (from about 37°C to room temperature) stimulates the skin receptors.
    • Mechanical – compression of the chest in the birth canal ("thoracic squeeze") pushes out part of the lung fluid; the chest then recoils and draws in air.
    • Sensory – touch, light, sound, drying and handling.
  • The first breath needs a high negative pressure to overcome the surface tension of the fluid-filled alveoli; once the alveoli open, surfactant keeps them from collapsing and establishes the functional residual capacity.
  • Lung fluid clearance – by the thoracic squeeze and, mainly, by absorption into the lymphatics and blood vessels, helped by labour hormones. Babies born by caesarean section without labour clear fluid more slowly (transient tachypnoea).
  • Normal breathing – 30–60 breaths per minute, irregular, mainly diaphragmatic (abdominal); newborns are mostly nose breathers. Short pauses (periodic breathing) are normal; pauses of more than 20 seconds (apnoea) are not.
  • Preterm babies with too little surfactant develop respiratory distress syndrome.

2. Cardiovascular adaptation

  • With the first breaths, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and blood flows freely to the lungs; clamping of the cord removes the low-resistance placenta and systemic resistance rises.
  • The pressure in the left atrium becomes higher than in the right, so the flap of the foramen ovale closes (functionally at once; anatomically over months).
  • Rising oxygen and falling prostaglandins constrict the ductus arteriosus – functionally within about the first day, anatomically within a few weeks (it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum).
  • The ductus venosus and umbilical vessels close and become ligaments.
  • Heart rate is about 120–160 per minute; peripheral circulation is sluggish, so blue hands and feet (acrocyanosis) are normal in the first day, while the lips and tongue are pink.
  • Delayed cord clamping gives the baby an extra placental transfusion of blood and better iron stores.

3. Haematological changes

  • High haemoglobin at birth (about 15–20 g/dl), mostly fetal haemoglobin (HbF), which holds oxygen more tightly.
  • Red cells have a shorter life; their breakdown produces bilirubin.
  • White cell count is high in the first days.
  • Vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) are low, because the gut has no bacteria to make vitamin K and breast milk contains little – hence the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding and the need for vitamin K at birth.

4. Thermoregulation

  • The newborn loses heat easily – large surface area relative to weight, thin skin, little subcutaneous fat and a wet body at birth.
  • Heat is lost by evaporation (wet skin), conduction (cold surfaces), convection (draughts) and radiation (to cold walls and windows).
  • Heat is produced mainly by non-shivering thermogenesis – metabolism of brown fat (around the neck, between the scapulae, around the kidneys), which uses oxygen and glucose. Cold stress therefore leads to hypoxia, hypoglycaemia and acidosis.
  • Normal axillary temperature – 36.5–37.5°C.

5. Hepatic adaptation and metabolism

  • Glucose – the fetus received glucose continuously from the mother; after birth, glycogen stores in the liver (laid down in late pregnancy) are used and blood glucose falls, reaching its lowest point at about 1–2 hours, then stabilises with early feeding and gluconeogenesis. Preterm, small and cold babies and infants of diabetic mothers are at risk of hypoglycaemia.
  • Bilirubin – the liver's conjugating enzyme (glucuronyl transferase) is immature, while bilirubin production is high, so many babies develop physiological jaundice after 24 hours (peak on day 3–5 in term babies, fading by about two weeks). Early, frequent feeding helps excretion.
  • Iron stores in a term baby last for about 4–6 months.

6. Gastrointestinal adaptation

  • Sucking, swallowing and breathing are co-ordinated from about 34 weeks; the rooting and sucking reflexes are strong in a term baby.
  • Stomach capacity is very small – about 5–7 ml on day 1, increasing to about 22–27 ml by day 3 and 45–60 ml by the end of the first week – which explains frequent feeds and why colostrum in small amounts is enough.
  • The gut is colonised with bacteria after birth – mainly healthy bifidobacteria and lactobacilli in vaginally born, breastfed babies.
  • Meconium (dark green-black, sticky) is passed within 24 hours in most babies, followed by transitional stools (greenish-yellow) and then yellow, soft "milk stools" of breastfed babies.
  • The cardiac sphincter is lax, so small regurgitations are common; enzymes for fat and starch are limited, but breast milk contains its own lipase.

7. Renal adaptation

  • The kidneys work from birth but are immature – low glomerular filtration rate and limited ability to concentrate urine or handle excess salt and acid.
  • First urine within 24 hours in most babies (always by 48 hours); urine is dilute; pink "brick-dust" staining from urates may be seen in the first days.
  • Physiological weight loss of up to about 7–10% of birth weight occurs in the first week, mainly loss of fluid, and birth weight is regained by about 10–14 days.

8. Immune adaptation

  • Passive immunity – maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects against diseases such as measles, tetanus and diphtheria for some months.
  • Colostrum and breast milk provide secretory IgA, lactoferrin, lysozyme and white cells that protect the gut.
  • The baby's own immunity is immature – IgM is not transferred, neutrophil function is weak and the skin is thin – so newborns are highly susceptible to infection.

9. Neurological and behavioural adaptation

  • Primitive reflexes (rooting, sucking, swallowing, Moro, grasp, stepping) are present and show neurological integrity.
  • Sleep–wake states – deep sleep, light sleep, drowsy, quiet alert, active alert and crying; the quiet alert state is ideal for feeding and bonding.
  • Periods of reactivity – an alert first hour, then sleep, then a second period of activity.
  • Senses – the baby sees best at 20–25 cm (the distance to the mother's face), recognises the mother's voice and smell, and responds strongly to touch – all of which support bonding.

10. Skin and other changes

  • The skin is thin, covered with protective vernix caseosa in folds, with fine lanugo in some babies.
  • Withdrawal of maternal hormones may cause breast swelling and, in girls, a little vaginal bleeding – both normal.

(b) Nursing care that supports transition (3 marks)

  1. Dry the baby immediately and keep it warm – skin-to-skin contact, cap, covering, warm room; delay the first bath.
  2. Ensure breathing – observe colour, breathing and heart rate; resuscitate promptly if needed.
  3. Delayed cord clamping (1–3 minutes) when the baby is breathing well.
  4. Early and frequent breastfeeding, starting within the first hour – supplies glucose, colostrum and immunity, and helps clear meconium and bilirubin.
  5. Vitamin K 1 mg intramuscularly (0.5 mg for babies under 1,000 g).
  6. Monitor temperature, breathing, heart rate, colour, feeding, first urine and meconium, and jaundice.
