  7. Watch for failed transition – grunting, chest indrawing, breathing rate above 60, central cyanosis, temperature instability, jitteriness or lethargy (hypoglycaemia), jaundice within 24 hours, no urine or meconium.
  8. Prevent infection – hand hygiene, clean cord care, rooming-in, immunisation.
  9. Keep mother and baby together and teach the mother the baby's normal behaviour.

Nursing importance Nearly half of newborn deaths occur in the first day of life, mainly from failed transition – asphyxia, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, infection and complications of prematurity. A midwife who understands normal adaptation can support it with simple measures – warmth, breathing support, early breastfeeding, vitamin K and infection prevention – and can recognise at once a baby who is not coping.

Conclusion At birth the newborn begins breathing as lung fluid is cleared and surfactant opens the alveoli; the circulation changes as the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus close; brown fat provides heat; liver glycogen maintains glucose; the gut, kidneys and immune system begin independent work; and the brain shows reflexes, states and periods of reactivity. Warmth, early breastfeeding, vitamin K, close observation and infection prevention help every baby complete this transition safely.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: Explain the birth injuries of the newborn's head – caput succedaneum, cephalhaematoma and subgaleal haemorrhage.

diagram.caption: Layers of the scalp and sites of swellings
labels: sutures); caput succedaneum shown as oedema in the subcutaneous tissue crossing the suture; cephalhaematoma as blood under the periosteum limited by the sutures; subgaleal haemorrhage as blood spreading in the subgaleal space across sutures

answer_html:
Introduction During labour the fetal head is pressed against the cervix and pelvis, and instruments may be used to deliver it. This can cause swellings of the scalp. The midwife must recognise them, explain them to parents and identify the dangerous ones.

1. Caput succedaneum

  • Definition – a diffuse, oedematous swelling of the soft tissues of the scalp over the presenting part.
  • Cause – after rupture of the membranes, the scalp encircled by the dilating cervix (girdle of contact) is not pressed, so venous and lymphatic return from it is obstructed; seen after prolonged labour. A similar swelling after vacuum delivery is called a chignon.
  • Features – present at birth; soft, pitting, poorly defined; crosses suture lines; may have bruising.
  • Course – largest at birth and disappears within 24–48 hours without treatment.

2. Cephalhaematoma

  • Definition – a collection of blood under the periosteum of a skull bone, usually a parietal bone.
  • Cause – rupture of small vessels by friction or pressure during difficult labour, vacuum or forceps delivery; occasionally after normal birth.
  • Features – not obvious at birth; appears after some hours and may enlarge over a day or two; firm, later fluctuant, well defined; does not cross suture lines because the periosteum is attached at the sutures; may be on both sides, separated by a groove.
  • Course – resolves slowly over 2–6 weeks; may calcify, leaving a hard lump for some time.
  • Complications – jaundice (breakdown of the collected blood), anaemia, rarely infection or an underlying linear skull fracture.

3. Subgaleal haemorrhage

  • Definition – bleeding into the space between the galea aponeurotica and the periosteum.
  • Cause – mainly vacuum extraction, sometimes forceps or coagulation disorders.
  • Features – a boggy, fluctuant swelling that crosses sutures and may extend from the forehead to the neck; ears may be pushed forward.
  • Danger – the space is large and can hold a large part of the baby's blood volume, leading to hypovolaemic shock and death within hours. It is an emergency.

Differences between caput and cephalhaematoma

Feature Caput succedaneum Cephalhaematoma
Nature Oedema of scalp tissue Blood under the periosteum
Time of appearance Present at birth Appears after a few hours
Suture lines Crosses them Limited by them
Consistency Soft, pits on pressure Firm, later fluctuant, does not pit
Disappears Within 1–2 days Within weeks
Complications None Jaundice, anaemia, rarely infection

Nursing care

  • Examine the scalp after every birth, especially after prolonged or instrumental delivery; record the size and site of any swelling.
  • Explain to parents that caput and cephalhaematoma are usually harmless and will disappear; ask them not to massage or press the swelling.
  • Never aspirate a cephalhaematoma (risk of infection).
  • Give vitamin K; monitor for jaundice and anaemia; arrange phototherapy if needed.
  • In suspected subgaleal haemorrhage – measure head circumference regularly, monitor heart rate, colour, capillary refill, BP and haemoglobin, inform the doctor at once and prepare for fluid resuscitation and blood transfusion.
  • Handle the head gently and position the baby on the unaffected side if comfortable.

Conclusion Caput succedaneum is a harmless oedema present at birth that crosses sutures and disappears in a day or two; cephalhaematoma is a subperiosteal blood collection that appears later, stays within the sutures and takes weeks to resolve. Subgaleal haemorrhage, usually after vacuum delivery, can be life-threatening and demands close monitoring and urgent treatment.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: Explain Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC).
tags: extra visits for low birth weight
answer_html:
Introduction Most newborn deaths occur at home in the first week after birth, often because danger signs are not recognised. Home-Based Newborn Care (HBNC), started under the National Health Mission in 2011 (guidelines revised in 2014), takes essential newborn and postnatal care to every home through the ASHA.

Objectives

  • To ensure essential newborn care for every baby – warmth, exclusive breastfeeding, hygiene and cord care.
  • To detect danger signs and illness early and refer.
  • To give extra care to preterm and low birth weight babies.
  • To check the mother for postnatal complications and support family planning.

Schedule of home visits

  • Institutional delivery – six visits on days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42.
  • Home delivery – seven visits, with an additional visit on day 1 (within 24 hours).
  • Extra visits for low birth weight and preterm babies and those discharged from SNCUs.

HBNC kit of the ASHA – a weighing scale, digital thermometer, watch or timer to count breathing, baby blanket and the HBNC visit format.

Activities during each visit

For the baby

  • Check temperature, count breathing for one full minute, observe colour, activity, sucking and attachment at the breast.
  • Look at the cord (bleeding, redness, pus), eyes, skin (pustules, jaundice).
  • Weigh the baby (as per schedule) and identify LBW babies.
  • Look for danger signs – poor feeding, fast breathing (60 or more per minute), chest indrawing, fever or cold body, lethargy, convulsions, yellow palms and soles, pus or redness around the cord.

For the mother

  • Ask about bleeding, fever, foul discharge, breast problems, pain and mood; check IFA intake and diet.

Counselling

  • Exclusive breastfeeding, keeping the baby warm (skin-to-skin, KMC for LBW babies), hand washing, dry cord care, no applications on the cord, delaying the bath, immunisation, birth registration and family planning.

Referral and follow-up – a sick baby or mother is referred with a referral slip to the PHC, CHC or SNCU; the ASHA accompanies or arranges transport and follows up after return.

Recording and incentive – visits are recorded in the HBNC format and MCP card; the ASHA receives a performance-based incentive (₹250) for completing the scheduled visits with proper records.

Continuation – Home-Based Care for Young Child (HBYC) continues home visits at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 months.

Role of the nurse / ANM

  • Train and supervise ASHAs, verify visits and check the quality of records.
  • Examine babies referred by ASHAs and ensure treatment.
  • Ensure supply and maintenance of HBNC kits.
  • Track LBW and SNCU-discharged babies on the due list.

Conclusion HBNC extends newborn care beyond the hospital, with an ASHA visiting every mother and baby six or seven times in the first six weeks. Through simple checks, counselling and timely referral, it helps reduce neonatal deaths in the community.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: Explain the prevention of infection in the newborn at birth and in the postnatal ward.
tags: chlorhexidine for cord in home births
answer_html:
Introduction Infection (sepsis, pneumonia, cord infection, tetanus) is a major cause of newborn death in India. Newborns are highly susceptible – their immune system is immature, the skin is thin and the cord stump is an open wound. Most newborn infections are preventable by simple, consistent practices.

1. At birth – clean birth practices ("cleans")

  1. Clean hands of the birth attendant – hand washing with soap and water or alcohol rub, and sterile gloves.
  2. Clean perineum of the mother.
  3. Clean delivery surface.
  4. Clean (sterile) blade or scissors to cut the cord.
  5. Clean cord tie or clamp.
  6. Clean towels and cloth to dry and wrap the baby. - In facilities, use sterile delivery kits, standard trays and personal protective equipment, and follow strict asepsis for any procedure.

2. Care of the cord

  • Dry cord care – keep the cord clean, dry and exposed (nappy folded below it); clean with clean water if soiled and dry it.
  • Never apply oil, ash, cow dung, turmeric or other substances.
  • Where births take place at home in high-mortality settings, WHO recommends chlorhexidine (7.1%) application to the cord.

3. Feeding and contact

  • Skin-to-skin contact at birth colonises the baby with the mother's friendly bacteria.
  • Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour and exclusive breastfeeding – colostrum supplies antibodies and protective factors; avoid prelacteal feeds, water and bottles.
  • Rooming-in – keeping the baby with the mother reduces cross-infection from nursery care.

4. Skin and eye care

  • Delay the first bath for at least 24 hours (keep vernix, which is protective); wipe off blood and meconium gently.
  • Clean the eyes with sterile water from the inner to the outer canthus; give eye prophylaxis where the protocol recommends it.

5. Immunisation – BCG, OPV-0 and hepatitis B birth dose (within 24 hours) before discharge; prophylaxis for HIV-exposed babies as per guidelines.

6. Measures in the postnatal ward and nursery

  • Hand hygiene by everyone – staff (WHO "five moments"), mothers and visitors – before and after touching the baby.
  • Individual equipment (thermometers, clothes, linen) for each baby; clean and disinfect shared equipment.
  • Cleaning of the environment by schedule; adequate space between beds; good ventilation.
  • Limit visitors; keep away people with colds, diarrhoea or skin infections, including staff.
  • Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures (injections, suction, catheters).
  • Safe disposal of biomedical waste and sharps.

7. Educating the mother and family

  • Hand washing, cord care, clean clothes, exclusive breastfeeding, keeping the baby warm.
  • Avoid harmful practices such as kajal, oil in the ears, applications on the cord and prelacteal feeds.
  • Warning signs to report – fever or cold body, poor feeding, lethargy, fast breathing, pus or redness around the cord, skin pustules, eye discharge, jaundice.

Conclusion Clean birth practices, dry cord care, early and exclusive breastfeeding, rooming-in, delayed bathing, immunisation, hand hygiene and an educated family form a strong barrier against newborn infection. These simple measures save more newborn lives than any expensive treatment.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: Explain family-centred maternity and newborn care, including family participation in newborn units.
answer_html:
Introduction Childbirth is a family event, not only a medical one. Family-centred care is an approach in which the mother, newborn and family are treated as one unit of care, and the family is respected and involved as a partner in planning and giving care, from pregnancy to the postnatal period and in newborn units.

Principles

  1. Dignity and respect – care respects the family's values, beliefs, culture and choices.
  2. Information sharing – complete, honest and timely information in a way the family understands.
  3. Participation – the family is encouraged to take part in care and decisions at the level they choose.
  4. Collaboration – families and professionals work together in planning care, and in improving services.

Components in maternity and newborn care

  • Antenatal – classes for couples and families; involvement of the husband and mother-in-law in birth planning.
  • Labour and birth – a birth companion of the woman's choice, choice of position, privacy, involvement of the father where possible.
  • After birth – skin-to-skin contact, early breastfeeding, rooming-in, keeping mother and baby together (the mother–baby dyad), flexible visiting for the father and siblings.
  • Sick and small newborns – unrestricted access for parents in SNCUs, kangaroo mother care, and Family Participatory Care, in which mothers and family members are trained to provide basic care (feeding, KMC, hygiene, observation) under nurses' supervision.
  • Discharge and home care – teaching the family to care for the baby, recognise danger signs and use follow-up services; linking them with ASHAs and HBNC.
  • Culturally sensitive care – respecting harmless customs and negotiating changes in harmful ones.

Benefits

  • Better bonding and higher rates of exclusive breastfeeding.
  • Greater confidence and competence of parents; less anxiety.
  • Fewer infections and shorter hospital stay for newborns; better weight gain in LBW babies.
  • Higher satisfaction with care; better follow-up and continuation of care at home.
  • Stronger family relationships, including the father's role.

Role of the nurse

  • See the family as partners, not visitors; welcome and orient them.
  • Teach skills (breastfeeding, KMC, bathing, cord care) by demonstration and return demonstration.
  • Share information regularly and involve parents in decisions.
  • Adapt rules to support family presence while maintaining infection control and privacy.
  • Provide emotional support, especially to parents of sick babies.

Conclusion Family-centred care recognises the family as the constant presence in the baby's life. By respecting, informing and involving families from pregnancy to discharge – and especially in newborn units – nurses improve the health of mothers and babies and prepare families to care confidently at home.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: What are the periods of reactivity in a newborn?
answer_html:
• Periods of reactivity describe the predictable pattern of behaviour of a healthy newborn in the first hours after birth.
  • First period of reactivity (birth to about 30–60 minutes) – the baby is alert, active, cries, roots and sucks; heart rate and breathing are rapid; mucus may be present. Ideal time for skin-to-skin contact and the first breastfeed.
  • Period of decreased responsiveness (about 1–2 hours) – the baby sleeps deeply; heart and breathing rates slow.
  • Second period of reactivity (about 2–8 hours after birth) – the baby wakes and becomes alert again; may gag, pass meconium and show feeding cues; observe for apnoea or colour changes.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Assessment and Care of the Normal Neonate
question: What is rooming-in? State its advantages.
answer_html:
• Rooming-in is the practice of keeping the mother and her newborn together in the same room (or bed) 24 hours a day from birth, unless there is a medical reason for separation. It is one of the steps of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative.
  • Advantages
    • Breastfeeding on demand and better milk supply.
    • Bonding and early recognition of the baby's cues.
    • The mother learns baby care under supervision and gains confidence.
    • Less infection than in crowded nurseries; less crying; better sleep for both.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: (a) Classify the methods of contraception. (3 marks) (b) Explain intrauterine contraceptive devices – types, mechanism of action, timing of insertion, advantages, side effects and complications. (8 marks) (c) Describe the procedure of interval IUCD insertion, with the instructions and follow-up. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Cu-T 380A and its insertion
labels: (1) Cu-T 380A with copper sleeves on the arms and copper wire on the stem

threads below; (2) loading in the sterile package with the arms folded into the inserter tube and the depth gauge set to the uterine depth; (3) withdrawal technique – white rod held still while the inserter tube is pulled back to release the arms at the fundus; (4) device in the uterine cavity with threads cut 3–4 cm from the external os

answer_html:
(a) Classification of contraceptive methods (3 marks)

A. Temporary (spacing) methods

  1. Barrier methods
    • Physical – male condom (Nirodh), female condom, diaphragm, cervical cap.
    • Chemical – spermicides (foam tablets, jelly, cream, film).
  2. Intrauterine devices – copper-bearing (Cu-T 380A, Cu-T 375) and hormone-releasing (levonorgestrel intrauterine system).
  3. Hormonal methods
    • Oral pills – combined oral contraceptives (Mala-N) and progestin-only pills.
    • Injectables – DMPA (Antara, intramuscular and subcutaneous).
    • Implants – single-rod subdermal implant.
    • Others – vaginal ring, patch; emergency contraceptive pills.
  4. Non-hormonal pill – centchroman (Chhaya), weekly.
  5. Natural and behavioural methods – fertility awareness methods (calendar, Standard Days, basal body temperature, cervical mucus, symptothermal), withdrawal (coitus interruptus), lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM), abstinence.

B. Permanent (terminal or limiting) methods

  • Female sterilisation (tubectomy – minilaparotomy, laparoscopic).
  • Male sterilisation (vasectomy – conventional or no-scalpel).

(b) Intrauterine contraceptive devices (8 marks)

Definition – an IUCD is a small, flexible device inserted into the uterine cavity to prevent pregnancy. It is one of the most effective, long-acting and reversible methods, and is offered free in the national family planning programme.

Types (generations)

  1. First generation – inert devices (for example, Lippes loop); no longer used.
  2. Second generation – copper-bearing devices
    • Cu-T 380A – T-shaped polyethylene frame with copper on the stem and arms (380 mm² of copper); effective for 10 years.
    • Cu-T 375 (Multiload 375) – effective for 5 years.
    • These two are supplied in the government programme.
  3. Third generation – hormone-releasing devices
    • Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) – releases a small daily dose of levonorgestrel; effective for several years; reduces menstrual bleeding.

Mechanism of action

  • Copper ions are toxic to sperm and ova – they reduce sperm motility and viability and so prevent fertilisation.
  • A sterile inflammatory (foreign body) reaction in the endometrium makes the uterus hostile to sperm and to implantation.
  • LNG-IUS thickens the cervical mucus, thins the endometrium and may suppress ovulation in some women.
  • IUCDs work mainly by preventing fertilisation, not by causing abortion.

Effectiveness – more than 99%; fewer than 1 pregnancy per 100 women in the first year with Cu-T 380A.

Timing of insertion

  • Interval – at any time during the menstrual cycle when the provider is reasonably sure the woman is not pregnant, usually within 12 days of the start of the menstrual period.
  • Postpartum – within 10 minutes of placental delivery, during caesarean section or within 48 hours; otherwise after 6 weeks.
  • Post-abortion – immediately after an uncomplicated first-trimester abortion, or within 12 days.
  • Emergency contraception – within 5 days of unprotected intercourse.

Advantages

  • Highly effective and long-acting (5–10 years) after a single decision.
  • Fertility returns promptly after removal.
  • No daily action needed; does not interfere with intercourse.
  • No systemic hormonal effects (copper IUCD) and safe during breastfeeding.
  • Inexpensive; can be inserted by trained nurses and ANMs.
  • Can be used as emergency contraception.

Side effects

  • Heavier and longer periods, spotting between periods and cramps, especially in the first 3–6 months; usually settle.
  • Increased vaginal discharge.

Complications

  • At insertion – pain, vasovagal reaction (fainting, bradycardia), rarely uterine perforation.
  • Expulsion – most often in the first three months and during menstruation; the woman should check the strings.
  • Pelvic inflammatory disease – risk mainly in the first 20 days, related to existing infection at the time of insertion; screen and use aseptic technique.
  • Pregnancy with IUCD in place – rare; risk of miscarriage and septic abortion; if the strings are visible in early pregnancy, the device is removed. If pregnancy occurs, ectopic pregnancy must be excluded.
  • Missing strings – may mean expulsion, perforation or strings drawn up into the uterus; use a back-up method and refer for ultrasound.

Contraindications (WHO MEC category 4 for starting) – pregnancy, puerperal sepsis, immediately after septic abortion, unexplained vaginal bleeding before evaluation, current pelvic inflammatory disease or purulent cervicitis, cervical or endometrial cancer awaiting treatment, a uterine cavity distorted by fibroids or anomalies, and pelvic tuberculosis.

(c) Procedure of interval IUCD insertion, instructions and follow-up (4 marks)

Preparation

  • Counselling (using the Balanced Counselling Strategy) and informed consent.
  • History – LMP, use the pregnancy checklist to rule out pregnancy, risk of STIs, bleeding pattern.
  • Examination – abdominal palpation; speculum examination (cervix, discharge); bimanual examination for size, position, mobility and tenderness of the uterus.
  • Equipment – sterile IUCD pack, Cusco's or Sims speculum, sponge-holding forceps, vulsellum (tenaculum), uterine sound, scissors, antiseptic solution, gloves, swabs and a good light.

Steps

  1. Ask the woman to empty her bladder; position her in lithotomy; wash hands and wear sterile gloves.
  2. Perform a bimanual examination; insert the speculum and clean the cervix and vagina with antiseptic.
  3. Hold the anterior lip of the cervix gently with a tenaculum and apply light traction to straighten the canal.
  4. Sound the uterus gently to measure its depth and direction (usually 6–9 cm).
  5. Load the Cu-T in its sterile package (no-touch technique) – fold the arms into the inserter tube and set the blue depth gauge at the measured depth.
  6. Insert the loaded tube through the cervix until the gauge touches the cervix (or slight resistance at the fundus).
  7. Withdrawal technique – hold the white rod still and pull the inserter tube back to release the arms; then push the tube gently up again to place the device high at the fundus.
  8. Remove the rod and the tube; cut the strings 3–4 cm from the external os; remove the tenaculum and check for bleeding; remove the speculum.
  9. Let the woman rest for 15–30 minutes and observe for pain or fainting; dispose of waste safely; record the details and give her an IUCD card with the type, date of insertion and date of removal.

Instructions to the client

  • Cramps and spotting for a few days are normal; mild analgesics may be taken.
  • Check the strings after each period, especially in the first few months; do not pull them.
  • Report at once if any warning sign ("PAINS") appears – Period late or abnormal bleeding; Abdominal pain or pain during intercourse; Infection exposure or abnormal discharge; Not feeling well, fever or chills; Strings missing, shorter or longer.
  • The device can be removed at any time she wishes; return for removal when it is due.

Follow-up – after the first period (3–6 weeks), then at three months and yearly, or at any time she has a problem.

Management of common problems with IUCDs

Problem Management by the nurse / provider
Heavy or prolonged bleeding Reassure that it usually improves in 3–6 months; give an NSAID such as ibuprofen for a few days during bleeding and iron tablets; check haemoglobin; look for other causes (pregnancy, infection); remove the device if bleeding is severe or causes anaemia, and help her choose another method
Cramps and pain NSAIDs; exclude partial expulsion, perforation, infection or ectopic pregnancy if pain is severe or persistent
Missing strings Exclude pregnancy; give a back-up method (condoms); refer for ultrasound to locate the device (in the uterus, expelled or outside the uterus)
Partial expulsion (device felt in the cervix) Remove it and, if she wishes, insert a new one after excluding pregnancy and infection
Pelvic inflammatory disease Start antibiotics promptly as per protocol; the IUCD need not be removed if she wishes to continue and improves within 48–72 hours; remove if she does not improve
Pregnancy with IUCD Exclude ectopic pregnancy; in an intrauterine pregnancy in the first trimester with visible strings, remove the device gently after explaining the risks; refer
Partner feels the strings Explain; trim the strings slightly if needed

Removal of an IUCD

  • It can be removed at any time the woman wishes – to plan a pregnancy, because of side effects or at the end of its effective life.
  • Removal is easier during menstruation. After a speculum examination, the strings are grasped with forceps and the device is removed with gentle, steady traction; if the strings are not visible, refer.
  • If she wants to continue, a new IUCD can be inserted immediately; otherwise counsel her about another method so that she is not left unprotected. Fertility returns promptly after removal.

Nursing importance The IUCD is one of the most effective and cost-effective spacing methods, and trained nurses and ANMs are its main providers. Good counselling, careful screening, aseptic insertion and proper follow-up increase continuation, reduce complications and help women space their children safely.

Conclusion Contraceptive methods are temporary (barrier, intrauterine, hormonal, non-hormonal and natural) or permanent (male and female sterilisation). Copper IUCDs such as Cu-T 380A act mainly by preventing fertilisation, are over 99% effective for up to 10 years and are safe in breastfeeding, though they may cause heavier periods and rarely expulsion, infection or perforation. Correct interval insertion using the no-touch withdrawal technique, clear instructions and follow-up ensure safe and successful use.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: (a) Explain the methods of female sterilisation. (5 marks) (b) Explain the eligibility criteria, timing and pre-operative preparation of a client for tubectomy. (5 marks) (c) Explain the post-operative care, discharge instructions and complications of tubectomy. (5 marks)
tags: Standards for Female and Male Sterilization Services 2014

diagram.caption: Methods of tubal occlusion
labels: (1) modified Pomeroy – a loop of the isthmic part of the tube lifted

tied at its base with absorbable suture and the knuckle excised; (2) Falope ring – a loop of tube drawn into the applicator and a silastic band placed around its base through the laparoscope; positions of minilap incisions – suprapubic (interval) and subumbilical (postpartum)

answer_html:
Introduction Female sterilisation (tubectomy) is a permanent method of contraception in which the fallopian tubes are blocked or cut so that sperm and ovum cannot meet. It is the most widely used method in India. Because it is permanent, it must be chosen voluntarily, with full information, and done to high standards, as laid down in the Government of India's Standards for Female and Male Sterilization Services.

(a) Methods of female sterilisation (5 marks)

1. Minilaparotomy (minilap)

  • A small abdominal incision (2–3 cm) through which the tubes are brought out and occluded.
  • Interval minilap – a suprapubic transverse incision; a uterine elevator inserted through the cervix raises the uterus to bring the tubes near the incision.
  • Postpartum minilap – within 7 days of delivery, through a small subumbilical incision, because the uterus is still high.
  • Usually done under local anaesthesia with light sedation; requires simple equipment; suitable at CHCs and district hospitals.
  • Modified Pomeroy technique (most common) – a loop of the isthmic portion of the tube is lifted, tied at its base with absorbable suture and the top of the loop (knuckle) is excised; the cut ends separate as the suture dissolves.

2. Laparoscopic sterilisation

  • Done as an interval procedure (at least 6 weeks after delivery) or along with a first-trimester abortion.
  • Under local anaesthesia and sedation, the abdomen is distended with gas (pneumoperitoneum) and a laparoscope is inserted through a small incision below the umbilicus.
  • A loop of each tube is drawn into the applicator and a Falope ring (silastic band) is placed around it, causing necrosis and blockage of the loop (clips or electrocoagulation are other options).
  • Quick, small scar and early discharge; needs a trained, certified surgeon, equipment and careful asepsis.

3. Sterilisation at caesarean section – the tubes are ligated (Pomeroy) or removed during the operation; salpingectomy (removal of the tubes) is increasingly preferred because it may also reduce the risk of ovarian cancer.

4. Other methods – vaginal approach (rarely used); hysteroscopic methods have been withdrawn.

Effectiveness – about 99.5%; effective immediately. Failure may occur years later and carries a higher chance of ectopic pregnancy.

(b) Eligibility, timing and pre-operative preparation (5 marks)

Eligibility criteria (GoI standards)

  1. The client should be ever-married.
  2. The woman should be 22–49 years of age.
  3. The couple should have at least one child more than one year old, unless sterilisation is medically indicated.
  4. Neither partner should have been sterilised before (except after failure of a previous sterilisation).
  5. The client must be of sound mind and understand the permanent nature of the procedure; a mentally ill client needs certification by a psychiatrist and consent of the legal guardian.
  6. The decision must be voluntary, with written informed consent on the prescribed form.

Timing

  • Interval – preferably within 7 days of the start of a menstrual period, or any time if pregnancy can be excluded.
  • Postpartum – within 7 days of delivery (preferably within 48 hours), by minilap.
  • Post-abortion – immediately after an uncomplicated first-trimester abortion (minilap or laparoscopy).
  • With caesarean section.
  • Delay the procedure in the presence of infection, severe anaemia, fever, uncontrolled medical conditions or a recent complicated delivery.

Pre-operative preparation

  1. Counselling – permanence, the option of other effective methods (including vasectomy for the husband), small risk of failure, no protection against STIs, the procedure and recovery; ensure there is no coercion.
  2. Informed consent – signed by the client on the standard consent form, after she has understood the information.
  3. History – medical, surgical, obstetric, LMP, allergies; examination – general condition, pulse, BP, weight, heart and lungs, abdominal and pelvic examination.
  4. Investigations – haemoglobin, urine for albumin and sugar, pregnancy test if pregnancy is suspected, others as indicated.
  5. Nil by mouth for about 4–6 hours; bath; remove jewellery; clip hair only if necessary.
  6. Empty the bladder just before the procedure.
  7. Check vital signs, give pre-medication as ordered, ensure the OT, emergency drugs and resuscitation equipment are ready.

(c) Post-operative care, discharge instructions and complications (5 marks)

Immediate post-operative care

  • Observe pulse, BP, respiration and level of consciousness frequently (every 15 minutes at first) until stable; watch the wound for bleeding.
  • Keep her in a comfortable position; give analgesics as prescribed.
  • Give oral fluids when fully awake and not nauseated, then a light diet.
  • Early ambulation and voiding before discharge.
  • Discharge after interval procedures when she is fully conscious, walking, has passed urine, vital signs are stable and there is no bleeding – usually at least 4 hours after the procedure; postpartum women stay as for postnatal care.

Discharge instructions

  • Rest for a day or two; resume light work after about 48 hours and normal work after a week; avoid heavy lifting for a week.
  • Keep the wound clean and dry; return for stitch removal or wound check on about the 7th day.
  • Take analgesics as advised; resume intercourse after about a week when comfortable; no other contraception is needed.
  • Return immediately if there is fever, dizziness or fainting, severe or increasing abdominal pain, bleeding or pus from the wound, or a missed period (possible pregnancy or ectopic pregnancy).
  • Follow-up at one week and after the first menstrual period, when the sterilisation certificate is issued.
  • Information about compensation for wage loss and the Family Planning Indemnity Scheme.

Complications

  • Anaesthetic complications – reactions to local anaesthetic or sedation.
  • During surgery – bleeding from the mesosalpinx; injury to the bladder or bowel; in laparoscopy, injury from the trocar, vessel injury or gas embolism.
  • After surgery – wound infection, haematoma, pain, fever, urinary infection.
  • Late – failure and pregnancy (with a higher proportion of ectopic pregnancies), regret (more common in young women and those sterilised hurriedly after delivery), menstrual complaints.
  • Death – rare, usually from anaesthesia, haemorrhage or sepsis.
  • Reversal (recanalisation) is possible only by microsurgery, with uncertain success, so the procedure should be treated as permanent.

Role of the nurse in the operation theatre

  • Check that the consent form, eligibility checklist and investigations are complete and that the client has emptied her bladder.
  • Ensure sterile instruments – minilap set or laparoscope, Falope ring applicator and rings, sutures – and working emergency drugs, oxygen, suction and resuscitation equipment.
  • Position the client correctly (supine for minilap; a slight head-down tilt for laparoscopy) and maintain asepsis.
  • Because the client is awake under local anaesthesia, talk to her and reassure her throughout ("verbal anaesthesia").
  • Monitor pulse, BP, respiration and oxygen saturation during sedation; watch for reactions to the local anaesthetic.
  • Count swabs and instruments, label any specimen, and record the procedure in the sterilisation register.

Female sterilisation compared with vasectomy

Feature Tubectomy Vasectomy (no-scalpel)
Procedure Abdominal operation, needs an OT Minor procedure under local anaesthesia through a tiny puncture in the scrotum
Time and recovery Longer; rest for a few days About 10–15 minutes; back to light work the next day
Risk of serious complications Higher Much lower
Effective from Immediately Only after about 3 months, when semen is free of sperm (another method used till then)
Cost Higher Lower

Because vasectomy is simpler, safer and cheaper, the nurse should present it as an equal option when a couple chooses a permanent method, and encourage male participation in family planning.

Nursing importance The nurse is the counsellor, the person who checks eligibility and prepares the client, the OT assistant and the one who gives post-operative care and follow-up. Her vigilance ensures voluntary, informed choice, safe surgery under the national standards and early detection of complications, protecting women's health and rights.

Conclusion Female sterilisation, by minilaparotomy (interval or postpartum) or laparoscopy, is a safe and highly effective permanent method. Clients must meet the eligibility criteria and give voluntary written consent after counselling. Careful pre-operative preparation, post-operative monitoring, clear instructions and follow-up minimise complications, while the indemnity scheme protects both clients and providers.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the barrier methods of contraception.
answer_html:
Introduction Barrier methods prevent pregnancy by stopping sperm from reaching the ovum, either by a physical barrier, by a chemical that kills sperm, or both. Condoms are the only methods that also protect against STIs and HIV (dual protection).

1. Male condom

  • A thin latex (or polyurethane) sheath worn on the erect penis; supplied free as Nirodh and through social marketing.
  • Correct use – check the expiry date and the packet; use a new condom for every act; put it on the erect penis before any genital contact; pinch the tip to leave space for semen and unroll to the base; after ejaculation, withdraw while the penis is still erect, holding the rim; tie and dispose of it safely.
  • Use only water-based lubricants with latex condoms; oil-based ones (oil, petroleum jelly) damage latex.
  • Effectiveness – about 98% with perfect use, but lower (about 87%) with typical use.
  • Advantages – easily available, cheap, no hormones, STI/HIV protection, involves the man, no medical supervision needed.
  • Disadvantages – must be used every time, may reduce sensation, may slip or break, rare latex allergy.

2. Female condom

  • A soft, loose polyurethane or nitrile pouch with an inner and an outer ring, inserted into the vagina before intercourse (up to several hours earlier).
  • Woman-controlled; protects against STIs; can be used with oil-based lubricants.
  • Less effective with typical use than the male condom, costlier and less familiar.

3. Diaphragm and cervical cap

  • A dome-shaped rubber or silicone cup that covers the cervix; it must be fitted for size by a trained provider and used with a spermicide.
  • Inserted before intercourse and left in place for at least 6 hours afterwards (not more than 24 hours).
  • May cause urinary infections; less used in India.

4. Spermicides

  • Chemicals (usually nonoxynol-9) in the form of foam tablets, jelly, cream or film, placed deep in the vagina shortly before intercourse.
  • Less effective when used alone; better combined with a barrier.
  • Frequent use can irritate the vaginal lining and may increase the risk of HIV, so they are not recommended for women at high risk of HIV.

General advantages and limitations

  • No systemic side effects; can be used by breastfeeding women and those who cannot use hormones.
  • Used only at the time of intercourse.
  • Effectiveness depends heavily on correct and consistent use; emergency contraception should be taken if a condom breaks or slips.

Role of the nurse

  • Demonstrate correct use on a model; encourage open discussion with couples; ensure supply (including condom boxes at facilities).
  • Promote dual protection – condoms with another method for couples at risk of STIs.
  • Inform about emergency contraception.

Conclusion Condoms, the female condom, the diaphragm and spermicides are simple, user-controlled methods without hormonal effects. Condoms, used correctly every time, give the unique benefit of protection against both pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the fertility awareness-based (natural) methods of family planning.
answer_html:
Introduction Fertility awareness-based methods help a couple identify the fertile days of the menstrual cycle and avoid unprotected intercourse (or use a barrier) on those days. They rely on the facts that ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next period, the ovum survives about 24 hours and sperm survive up to about 5 days in the female tract.

1. Calendar (rhythm) method (Ogino–Knaus)

  • The woman records the length of her cycles for 6–12 months.
  • First fertile day = shortest cycle − 18; last fertile day = longest cycle − 11.
  • Example – cycles of 26–30 days → fertile from day 8 to day 19.
  • Not suitable for irregular cycles.

2. Standard Days Method (SDM)

  • For women whose cycles are usually 26–32 days long.
  • Days 8 to 19 of every cycle are considered fertile.
  • CycleBeads – a colour-coded string of beads (a red bead for day 1 of the period, white beads for fertile days and brown beads for non-fertile days) helps her keep track; she moves a ring one bead each day.

3. Basal body temperature (BBT) method

  • The woman takes her temperature every morning before getting out of bed and plots it.
  • After ovulation, progesterone raises the temperature by about 0.2–0.5°C.
  • The infertile phase begins after three consecutive days of raised temperature and lasts until the next period; it does not identify the start of the fertile phase.

4. Cervical mucus (Billings ovulation) method

  • The woman observes her vaginal secretions daily.
  • Fertile mucus is clear, slippery and stretchy, like raw egg white (spinnbarkeit), appearing before ovulation; the last day of such mucus is the "peak day".
  • She avoids unprotected intercourse from the first day of wet mucus until the fourth day after the peak day.
  • The simpler TwoDay Method – if she notices secretions today or yesterday, she considers herself fertile.

5. Symptothermal method – combines temperature, mucus and other signs (cervical changes, mid-cycle pain) for greater accuracy.

6. Withdrawal (coitus interruptus) – the man withdraws before ejaculation; widely practised but less reliable because of pre-ejaculatory fluid and poor control.

7. Lactational amenorrhoea method (LAM) – a natural method for the first six months after birth (discussed under postpartum family planning).

Effectiveness – good with correct and consistent use (SDM about 95% with correct use), but lower with typical use because they need motivation and partner co-operation.

Advantages

  • No cost, no side effects, no drugs or devices.
  • Acceptable to couples with religious or cultural objections to other methods.
  • Increase the woman's knowledge of her body; involve the male partner; can also help couples who want to conceive.

Disadvantages

  • Need daily observation, record keeping and periods of abstinence.
  • Less reliable in irregular cycles, after childbirth, during breastfeeding, near menopause and in illness or stress.
  • No protection against STIs.

Role of the nurse

  • Assess suitability (regular cycles, motivation, partner support).
  • Teach charting and the use of CycleBeads with demonstrations.
  • Review records at follow-up and offer a barrier method or emergency contraception as back-up.

Conclusion Natural methods – calendar, Standard Days, BBT, cervical mucus and symptothermal – identify the fertile window so that couples can avoid pregnancy without drugs or devices. They are safe and inexpensive but require good teaching, regular cycles and a committed couple.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) for contraceptive use.
tags: sterilisation categories accept caution delay special
answer_html:
Introduction Women with medical conditions often wonder – or are wrongly told – that they "cannot use" family planning. The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) give evidence-based guidance on which methods can be used safely by women with particular health conditions or characteristics. First published in 1996, the 6th edition was released in November 2025, together with the 4th edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations, which explain how to use methods safely.

The four MEC categories

Category Meaning With clinical judgement Limited clinical judgement
1 A condition for which there is no restriction for the use of the method Use the method in any circumstances Yes – use
2 Advantages generally outweigh the theoretical or proven risks Generally use the method Yes – use
3 Theoretical or proven risks usually outweigh the advantages Use is not usually recommended unless other methods are not available or acceptable; needs careful follow-up No – do not use
4 An unacceptable health risk Method not to be used No – do not use

Where trained clinicians are not available (for example, at sub-centres), the simplified system groups categories 1 and 2 as "yes" and 3 and 4 as "no".

Examples (from WHO MEC)

  • Combined oral contraceptives – category 4 in breastfeeding women under 6 weeks postpartum, women aged 35 or more who smoke heavily, severe hypertension, current or past deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, migraine with aura, current breast cancer, and complicated valvular heart disease.
  • Copper IUCD – category 4 for current pelvic inflammatory disease, puerperal sepsis, immediately after septic abortion, unexplained vaginal bleeding (before evaluation), pelvic tuberculosis and cervical cancer awaiting treatment.
  • Progestin-only methods are suitable for many women who cannot use oestrogen, such as breastfeeding women, smokers over 35 and those with a history of hypertension; current breast cancer is category 4 for all hormonal methods.
  • Condoms and fertility awareness methods have almost no medical restrictions.

Sterilisation uses a different classification – A (accept), C (caution), D (delay) and S (special arrangements) – for example, delay in acute infection or severe anaemia; special settings for women with certain heart conditions.

Tools for use – the MEC wheel and app, quick-reference charts and checklists help providers apply the criteria quickly during counselling.

Importance

  • Removes unnecessary medical barriers so that more women can use effective contraception.
  • Protects women with genuine risks from harm.
  • Standardises practice across providers and facilities.

Role of the nurse

  • Take a focused history of relevant conditions; use the MEC wheel with the client during counselling; refer category 3 situations for clinical judgement; never refuse a method on the basis of myths.

Conclusion The WHO MEC classify conditions into four categories that tell providers whether a method can be used safely. Applied during counselling, they widen safe contraceptive choice and protect women with genuine health risks.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)

question: Explain the Balanced Counselling Strategy (BCS) for family planning.

diagram.caption: Balanced Counselling Strategy – three phases
labels: lay out method cards and set aside those not suitable) → method choice (discuss remaining methods
check medical eligibility) → post-choice (provide or refer

answer_html:
Introduction Good counselling is the key to informed choice and continued use of family planning. The Balanced Counselling Strategy (BCS), developed by the Population Council, is an interactive, client-centred method of counselling that uses simple job aids to give balanced information about the methods suitable for each client, in a short time. BCS Plus adds screening and counselling for STIs and HIV.

Job aids used

  • A counselling algorithm (step-by-step flow chart).
  • Method cards – one card for each method with a picture on the front and key information (effectiveness, how to use, side effects) on the back.
  • Method brochures to give to the client.
  • A pregnancy checklist to exclude pregnancy.

Phases of BCS

1. Pre-choice phase

  • Greet the client, establish rapport and ensure privacy.
  • Assess her reproductive intentions – does she want more children, and when?
  • Rule out pregnancy using the pregnancy checklist (or a test).
  • Lay out all the method cards and explain that together they will select the best methods for her.
  • Set aside cards that do not fit her needs, by asking simple questions – for example:
    • wants more children → set aside sterilisation;
    • breastfeeding a baby under 6 months → set aside combined pills;
    • partner will not co-operate with condoms → set aside condoms;
    • cannot remember to take a pill daily → set aside daily pills.

2. Method choice phase

  • Discuss the remaining methods in detail – how effective they are, how they are used, common side effects and their management.
  • Let the client choose; respect her decision.
  • Check medical eligibility for the chosen method using the WHO MEC; if she is not eligible, return to the remaining options.

3. Post-choice phase

  • Provide the method (or refer).
  • Explain how to use it, possible side effects, warning signs and what to do.
  • Discuss dual protection with condoms if she is at risk of STIs/HIV.
  • Make sure she has understood (ask her to repeat key points), give the brochure and fix the follow-up date; tell her she can return at any time to change the method.

Advantages

  • Gives balanced, unbiased information without overloading the client.
  • Saves time while improving quality; easy for nurses and ANMs to learn.
  • Encourages active participation and informed choice, leading to higher satisfaction and better continuation of methods.

Related approach – GATHER – Greet, Ask, Tell, Help, Explain, Return; used widely in the Indian programme.

Role of the nurse – keep job aids ready, counsel in privacy with respect, avoid personal bias, include the partner if the client wishes and document the counselling.

Conclusion The Balanced Counselling Strategy leads the client through pre-choice, method choice and post-choice phases using method cards and a simple algorithm. It ensures that each woman receives clear, balanced information and chooses a method that truly suits her needs.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the impact of early and frequent childbearing on the health of the mother and child.
tags: healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy
answer_html:
Introduction When a woman has children and how close together are as important for health as how many she has. Early childbearing (before 18–20 years), frequent childbearing (birth-to-pregnancy interval of less than 24 months) and high parity (four or more births) all increase the risk of death and illness for mother and child. In India, NFHS-6 found that 20.1% of women aged 20–24 had married before 18, and teenage pregnancy remains about 6.7%.

1. Effects of early (adolescent) childbearing On the mother

  • The girl's body, especially the pelvis, is not fully grown – risk of obstructed labour, obstetric fistula and caesarean section.
  • Higher risk of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, anaemia, puerperal infections and unsafe abortion.
  • Interrupted education, early dependence, poor decision-making power, depression and violence.

On the baby

  • Preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth, neonatal death; poorer child care and nutrition by a young mother.

2. Effects of frequent childbearing (short birth intervals) On the mother

  • Maternal depletion syndrome – the body has no time to recover nutritional stores (iron, folate, calcium) between pregnancies → anaemia, weakness, poor lactation.
  • Increased risk of PPH, premature rupture of membranes and, after a previous caesarean, uterine rupture.
  • Continuous burden of pregnancy and child care.

On the child

  • Preterm birth, low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age babies.
  • Higher neonatal, infant and under-five mortality.
  • Early weaning of the older child when the mother becomes pregnant again → malnutrition, infections and developmental delay; competition between children for care.

3. Effects of high parity

  • PPH, malpresentation, uterine rupture, genital prolapse, anaemia and placenta praevia; increased maternal mortality.

4. Effects on family and society – poverty, reduced education of girls, poorer health of the whole family and rapid population growth.

WHO recommendations for healthy timing and spacing of pregnancy (HTSP)

  • Delay the first pregnancy until at least 18 years (ideally 20).
  • After a live birth, wait at least 24 months before trying for the next pregnancy.
  • After a miscarriage or abortion, wait at least 6 months.

Strategies and the role of the nurse

  • Prevent child marriage (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006) and keep girls in school; adolescent health services (RKSK).
  • Counsel newly married couples on delaying the first pregnancy (for example, through the Nayi Pehel kit under Mission Parivar Vikas).
  • Promote postpartum and post-abortion family planning – LAM, PPIUCD, injectables, pills, condoms.
  • Improve nutrition and correct anaemia between pregnancies.
  • Involve husbands and mothers-in-law; address son preference.

Conclusion Early, frequent and many pregnancies drain the mother's health and endanger her children. Spacing births at least two years apart and delaying the first pregnancy until adulthood are among the most effective ways to save mothers' and children's lives.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the legal and human rights aspects of family planning in India.
tags: Standards for Female and Male Sterilization Services
answer_html:
Introduction Family planning is not only a health intervention; it is a human right. The International Conference on Population and Development (ICPD, Cairo, 1994) affirmed the right of all individuals and couples to decide freely and responsibly the number, spacing and timing of their children and to have the information and means to do so. India follows this rights-based approach: it adopted the target-free approach in 1996 and its FP2030 commitments stress voluntary, informed choice.

Rights-based principles

  1. Voluntarism – no coercion, pressure, targets or incentives that override free choice; compensation is only for loss of wages.
  2. Informed choice – full, accurate information about all suitable methods, including effectiveness, side effects and alternatives.
  3. Informed consent – especially written consent for sterilisation; the client may change her mind at any time before the procedure.
  4. Privacy and confidentiality of information and examination.
  5. Quality of care – a choice of methods, competent providers, respectful interaction, follow-up and continuity (Bruce framework).
  6. Equity and non-discrimination – services for poor, rural, unmarried, adolescent and disabled persons, without judgement.
  7. Accountability – grievance redressal and compensation for harm.

Legal framework and court directions

  • Supreme Court – Ramakant Rai v. Union of India (2005) – directed uniform standards for sterilisation, quality assurance and compensation for death, complications and failure. This led to the Family Planning Insurance (now Indemnity) Scheme and Quality Assurance Committees at state and district levels.
  • Supreme Court – Devika Biswas v. Union of India (2016) – after deaths in sterilisation camps, the Court recognised reproductive rights as part of the right to life (Article 21), directed that sterilisation camps be discontinued within three years, and called for quality, consent and adequate compensation.
  • Standards for Female and Male Sterilization Services (GoI, 2014) – eligibility, consent, facility standards, surgeon empanelment, record keeping and audits of deaths and complications.
  • Family Planning Indemnity Scheme – compensation to clients for death, failure and complications following sterilisation, and indemnity cover for providers; the amounts were doubled from January 2017 (for example, ₹4 lakh for death in hospital or within 7 days of discharge).
  • MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021 – failure of a contraceptive method used by any woman or her partner is an accepted ground for termination up to 20 weeks.
  • PCPNDT Act – family planning must never be linked with sex selection.
  • Consent of persons with mental illness – through a legal guardian after psychiatric certification.

Rights of special groups

  • Adolescents and young people – right to information and youth-friendly services; providers must respect confidentiality while following child-protection laws.
  • Unmarried and single women – access to contraception and emergency contraception without moral judgement.
  • Persons with disability – accessible information and services; no forced sterilisation.

Role of the nurse

  • Counsel all clients fully and without bias; never pressurise or set personal targets.
  • Ensure valid consent and correct documentation.
  • Maintain confidentiality and privacy.
  • Inform clients of their entitlements – free services, compensation and the indemnity scheme.
  • Report complications and deaths promptly for audit and claims.
  • Advocate for clients' rights and quality services.

Conclusion Family planning in India is guided by the principles of voluntary, informed choice and quality care, reinforced by Supreme Court judgments, national sterilisation standards and the indemnity scheme. Nurses uphold these rights every time they counsel, obtain consent and provide a method.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: Explain the role of the nurse-midwife in identifying and responding to gender-based violence.
tags: medico-legal care of survivors of sexual violence
answer_html:
Introduction Gender-based violence (GBV) is any act of violence based on gender that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual or psychological harm or suffering to women, including threats, coercion or deprivation of liberty, in public or private life. Violence often begins or worsens during pregnancy and causes miscarriage, antepartum haemorrhage, preterm birth, low birth weight, fetal injury, unsafe abortion, depression and suicide. Because almost every woman meets a nurse-midwife during pregnancy and childbirth, the midwife has a unique chance to identify and help survivors.

1. Providing gender-sensitive health services

  • Privacy for examination and counselling; a female provider when the woman prefers.
  • Respect for the woman's own decisions, including in family planning – no method should be forced by the husband or family.
  • Non-judgemental attitude; confidentiality of records; involving men positively.

2. Identification

  • Routine, private enquiry during antenatal and postnatal care, when the woman is alone and it is safe to ask (for example, "Has anyone at home hurt you or threatened you?").
  • Warning signs – repeated or unexplained injuries, bruises of different ages, injuries to the breasts or abdomen, inconsistent explanations, late or missed antenatal visits, frequent visits with vague complaints, a partner who never leaves her side or answers for her, depression, anxiety, repeated STIs or unwanted pregnancies.

3. First-line support – WHO "LIVES"

  • L – Listen closely, with empathy and without judging.
  • I – Inquire about her needs and concerns – emotional, physical, social and practical.
  • V – Validate – show that you believe and understand her and that she is not to blame.
  • E – Enhance safety – discuss a safety plan (where to go, whom to call, keeping documents and money ready).
  • S – Support – connect her with services and support.

4. Clinical care of survivors of sexual violence (MoHFW Guidelines and Protocols, 2014)

  • Free treatment at any public or private hospital; immediate care of injuries.
  • Informed consent for examination, treatment and evidence collection; she may refuse any part.
  • The "two-finger test" is prohibited; examination must be gentle, private and dignified, with a female attendant.
  • Emergency contraception, prophylaxis for STIs, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (within 72 hours), tetanus and hepatitis B vaccination, and a pregnancy test.
  • Psychological first aid and referral for counselling.
  • Careful documentation in the prescribed medico-legal format and intimation to the police as required by law; for a survivor under 18, mandatory reporting under the POCSO Act.

5. Referral and linkages

  • One Stop Centre (Sakhi) for integrated medical, police, legal and shelter support.
  • Women Helpline 181, emergency number 112, child helpline 1098.
  • Protection Officers under the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005; free legal aid from the District Legal Services Authority; shelter homes and counsellors.

6. Special courts and laws (awareness)

  • Fast Track Special Courts for rape and POCSO cases, POCSO Special Courts and Family Courts speed up justice for abused women and children.
  • Relevant laws include the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (rape, dowry death, cruelty by husband or relatives), the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961, the POCSO Act, 2012, the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 and the PCPNDT Act, 1994.

7. Prevention and advocacy – educate communities on gender equality, engage men and boys, support girls' education, challenge son preference and promote respectful relationships.

Conclusion The nurse-midwife can be the first person a survivor of violence trusts. By offering gender-sensitive services, asking safely, responding with LIVES, providing complete clinical and medico-legal care, maintaining confidentiality and linking the woman with One Stop Centres, legal aid and special courts, she helps protect both the woman and her baby.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: What is the Pearl index?
answer_html:
• The Pearl index measures the failure rate of a contraceptive method, expressed as the number of unintended pregnancies per 100 woman-years (HWY) of exposure.
  • Formula – Failure rate per HWY = (Total accidental pregnancies × 1,200) ÷ Total months of exposure (1,200 = 100 women × 12 months). In the denominator, 10 months are deducted for each full-term pregnancy and 4 months for each abortion.
  • The lower the Pearl index, the more effective the method – for example, it is below 1 for IUCDs and sterilisation, and much higher for withdrawal and spermicides.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: What is unmet need for family planning?
answer_html:
• Unmet need for family planning refers to women (usually currently married, aged 15–49) who are fecund and sexually active and who want to delay the next birth by two years or more (unmet need for spacing) or want no more children (unmet need for limiting), but are not using any method of contraception.
  • According to NFHS-6 (2023–24), unmet need in India has fallen to 8.5%.
  • Common reasons – lack of knowledge, fear of side effects, opposition from husband or family, poor access and religious beliefs. Reducing unmet need is a major goal of the family planning programme.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: What is Mission Parivar Vikas?
answer_html:
• Mission Parivar Vikas was launched by MoHFW in 2016 to substantially increase access to contraceptives and family planning services in 146 high-fertility districts (TFR 3 or more) of seven high-focus states – Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Assam.
  • It has since been expanded to all districts of these states and six north-eastern states.
  • Key activities – Nayi Pehel kits for newly married couples, Saas–Bahu Sammelans, SAARTHI awareness vans, condom boxes at health facilities, and wider availability of injectable contraceptives and other spacing methods.

subject: Midwifery/Obstetrics and Gynaecology (OBG) Nursing I (including SBA module)
unit_title: Family Welfare Services
question: What is the pregnancy checklist used before starting a contraceptive method?
answer_html:
• The pregnancy checklist is a simple set of questions that helps a provider be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant before starting a method, without a pregnancy test.
  • If she has no signs of pregnancy and any one of the following is true, she can be considered not pregnant: she has not had intercourse since her last normal period; she has been using a reliable method correctly; she is within 7 days of the start of her period (12 days for an IUCD); she is within 4 weeks after delivery (not breastfeeding); she is within 7 days of an abortion or miscarriage; or she is fully breastfeeding, has no periods and is less than 6 months after delivery.
  • If none applies, do a pregnancy test or ask her to use condoms until her next period.
